title: 交互式证明 (Interactive Proofs)
text:
The interaction process can be viewed as a dialogue between the Verifier (V) and the Prover (P).

One-round interaction: a_1 = V(x), \quad a_2 = P(x,a_1), \quad \text{Output} = V(x,a_1,a_2)
Two-round interaction: a_1 = V(x), \quad a_2 = P(x,a_1), \quad a_3=V(x,a_1,a_2), \quad \text{Output} = V(x,a_1,a_2,a_3)

More generally, the definition of k-round interaction is as follows:


Even-round interaction (2i rounds): 
\begin{aligned}
&a_1 = V(x), a_2=P(x,a_1);\\
&a_3 = V(x,a_1,a_2),a_4 = P(x,a_1,a_2,a_3);\\
&\cdots\\
&a_{2i+1} =V(x,a_1,\cdots,a_{2i}), \\
&\text{Output}= V(x,a_1,\cdots,a_{2i+1})
\end{aligned}


Odd-round interaction (2i+1 rounds): 
\begin{aligned}
&a_1 = V(x), a_2=P(x,a_1);\\
&a_3 = V(x,a_1,a_2),a_4 = P(x,a_1,a_2,a_3);\\
&\cdots\\
&a_{2i+1} =V(x,a_1,\cdots,a_{2i}), \\
&a_{2i+2} = P(x,a_1,\cdots,a_{2i+2});\\
&\text{Output}= V(x,a_1,\cdots,a_{2i+2})
\end{aligned}

title: 交互式证明 (Interactive Proofs)
text:
2 2. Deterministic Interactive Proof (\mathsf{dIP})






NoteDefinition: \mathsf{dIP}



L \subset \{0,1\}^* belongs to \mathsf{dIP} if and only if there exists a deterministic Turing machine V:\{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}^* such that for input x:

Completeness: If x \in L, then there exists a multi-round proof function P (mapping \{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}^* with no computational restrictions), such that after k \sim \text{poly}(|x|) rounds of interaction the output is 1.
Soundness: If x \notin L, then for any multi-round proof function P, after k \sim \text{poly}(|x|) rounds of interaction, the output is 0.

Note: The running time of each step in the interactive process must be polynomial \text{poly}(|x|).








ImportantTheorem



\mathsf{dIP} = \mathsf{NP}








NoteProof (click to expand)





Idea: \mathsf{dIP} can be designed as an \mathsf{NP} problem.
For inputs in L, consider either a 2i or 2i+1 round interaction. A Turing machine simulating the calls of V for i+2 times and viewing a_1, \dots, a_{2i+1} (or a_{2i+2}) as Certificates can be used.
This polynomial-time Turing machine with proof does the following simulation: V(x), V(x,a_1,a_2), \dots, V(x, a_1, \dots, a_{2i+1}) When it outputs a_1, a_3, \dots and finally \text{Output} = 1, the output is 1. Thus, examples in L must output 1. Additionally, for those that output 1, since no restrictions are placed on Prover’s capabilities (function P), they must be in \mathsf{dIP}.

title: 交互式证明 (Interactive Proofs)
text:
3 3. Probabilistic Interactive Proof (\mathsf{IP})






NoteDefinition: \mathsf{IP}[k]



L \subset \{0,1\}^* belongs to \mathsf{IP}[k] if and only if there exists a probabilistic Turing machine V:\{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}^* such that for input x:

Completeness: If x \in L, then there exists a proof function P such that the probability of outputting 1 after k \sim \text{poly}(|x|) rounds of interaction is greater than 2/3.
Soundness: If x \notin L, then for any proof function P, the probability of outputting 0 after k \sim \text{poly}(|x|) rounds of interaction is greater than 2/3.



[Image of complexity classes diagram showing P, NP, PH, IP, PSPACE]
Intuition and Discussion: \mathsf{IP} likely exceeds \mathsf{NP} (just as we do not know the relationship between \mathsf{BPP} and \mathsf{P}). Intuitively, many problems in \mathsf{coNP} are unknown to be in \mathsf{NP} because the \forall in the definition of \mathsf{coNP} requires traversing an exponential number of Certifications. However, \mathsf{IP} can establish a distribution over these exponentially many Certifications, thereby verifying some problems in \mathsf{coNP}.

3.1 Example: QNR (Quadratic Non-Residue)
This is a problem that is unknown to be in \mathsf{NP} but confirmed to be in \mathsf{IP}.
Problem: Given (a, p) where p is prime. Determine if a is not a quadratic residue modulo p (Quadratic Non-Residue).
Protocol (one-round interaction):

Verifier:

Establishes a probability distribution Q over quadratic residues modulo p: randomly selects r, computes x = r^2 \pmod p.
Randomly offsets this distribution with a: randomly chooses b \in \{0,1\} and calculates r_1 = a^b \cdot x \pmod p.

(Case a) If a is a quadratic residue, then r_1 remains a quadratic residue (since multiplication forms a group), the distribution remains unchanged.
(Case b) If not, the product changes the random distribution of quadratic residues to Q' (r_1 becomes non-quadratic).

Sends r_1 to Prover.

Prover:

Responds with a value that depends on whether a is a QNR or QR.








NoteDefinition: Randomized NP (\mathsf{MA})



L \subset \{0,1\}^* belongs to \mathsf{MA} if and only if there exists a probabilistic Turing machine V such that for input x:

If x \in L, there exists a Certification r (provided by Prover) such that \Pr[V(x,r)=1] > 2/3.
If x \notin L, for any Certification r, \Pr[V(x,r)=0] > 2/3.









ImportantTheorem



\mathsf{AM}[k] = \mathsf{AM}[2] = \mathsf{BP} \cdot \mathsf{NP}




3.2 Graph Isomorphism (GI)
Definition (\mathsf{GI}): Given graphs G_1=(V_1,E_1), G_2=(V_2,E_2), determine if there exists a vertex permutation \pi such that G_1 \cong G_2.

title: Basics of Shadow Tomography
text:
Single-copy shadow tomography restores single copy of \rho, repeats randomized measurements, and try to use these measurement results to estimate MANY properties of \rho, which includes linear property \text{tr}(O_i\rho), non-linear properties \text{tr}(O_i \rho^{t_i}), and even their products \prod_{i}\text{tr}(O_i \rho^{t_i}). The procedure of shadow tomography firstly includes the sampling of classical shadow, as shown in Algorithm [alg:classical_shadow]. Note that in Algorithm [alg:classical_shadow], virtually means restore the classical description of circuit U and length-n bit string \mathbf b. As shown in Lemma [lemma:single_shadow_unbiased], to estimate many properties includes \text{tr}(O \hat \rho^k), ones compute based only those sampled classical shadow.


Sample U \sim \mathcal{U} with certain unitary ensemble \mathcal{U}. Measure the state U\rho U^\dagger on the computational basis with result \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}}. Virtually computes the shadow matrix \hat \rho:= \mathcal{M}^{-1}(U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}} U), where \mathcal{M} is the entanglement-breaking linear map \rho \to \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \mathcal{U}} \sum_{\mathbf b}\bra{\mathbf b}U \rho U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}} \cdot  U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b} U.








ImportantLemma



 The estimator \hat{o}^{(k)} := \text{tr}(O \hat \rho_1\cdots \hat \rho_k) is an unbiased estimator for the expectation \text{tr}(O \rho^k), where \hat{\rho}_i is sampled according to the Algorithm [alg:classical_shadow].








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. \begin{align}
        \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \text{tr}(O \hat \rho_1\cdots \hat \rho_k) &= \mathbb{E}_{U_i \sim \mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}_i \sim U_i \rho U_i^\dagger} \text{tr}\left[O \prod_{i =1}^{k}\mathcal{M}^{-1}(U_i^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}_i}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}_i} U_i)\right]\\
        &=  \text{tr}\left[O \prod_{i =1}^{k}\mathcal{M}^{-1}(\mathbb{E}_{U_i \sim \mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}_i \sim U_i \rho U_i^\dagger}U_i^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}_i}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}_i} U_i)\right]=\text{tr}(O \rho^k).
\end{align} ◻



While we do not care about the computational complexity in the most case, the computation of \text{tr}(O \hat \rho^k) can be reconstructed as \bra{\mathbf b}(U\mathcal{M}^{-1, \dagger}(O)U^\dagger) \ket{\mathbf b}, thus might be processed efficiently if the randomized unitaries U is classical tractable and the target operator O can be decomposed into poly(n) numbers of simple operators.
The sampling complexity of any classical shadows scheme depends on both the choice of unitary distribution \mathcal{U} and the particular set of properties O of interest.


The explicit form of channel \mathcal{M} rely on the choice of unitary ensembles. Results of \mathcal{M} are known for global and on site 2-design unitary ensembles, 2-design unitary ensemble, fermionic Gaussian unitary ensemble, manybody Gaussian unitary ensemble, and locally scrambled unitaries ensemble. In this subsection we summarized these results.






ImportantLemma



 A k-site 2-design unitary ensembles \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)^{\otimes n} separates n\cdot k numbers of qudits in to n parts, and independently implements k-qudit 2-design unitary, as defined in Definition [def:t_design], within each part. In other words, \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)^{\otimes n}:=\{\bigotimes_{i  =1}^n U_i| U_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)\}. This ensemble induces the channel \begin{align}
        \mathcal{M}(\rho) = (\mathcal{D}_{1/(2^k + 1)})^{\otimes n}(\rho), \text{with~} \mathcal{D}_{1/(2^k + 1)}(\cdot) = \frac{1}{2^k +1}(\cdot) + \frac{\text{tr}(\cdot)}{2^k + 1}{\mathbb{I}(d^k)}.
\end{align} Specifically, the global 2-design unitary ensemble takes the case n = 1, U \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k),and the channel \mathcal{M}(\rho) ={(d^k + 1)^{-1}} \rho + {d^k{(d^k + 1)^{-1}}  \text{tr}\rho \cdot }({\mathbb{I}(d^k)}/{d^k}). The local 2-design unitary ensemble takes the case k = 1, U \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d)^{\otimes n},and the channel \mathcal{M}(\rho) = {(d + 1)}^{-1} \rho + {d({d + 1})^{-1} \text{tr}\rho} \cdot ({\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d}).








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. For tensor product inputs \otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i, \rho_i \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}(d^k)), the channel \mathcal{M} in this case became \begin{align}
    \mathcal{M}(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i)
    &=\mathbb{E}_{\substack{U = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n\text{U}_i \\ \text{U}_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)}} \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{kn}} \bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U} (\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i) \text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}} \cdot \text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}}\!\bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U} \notag\\
    &=\mathbb{E}_{\substack{U = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n\text{U}_i \\ \text{U}_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)}} \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{kn}} \text{tr}_{\bar A} \left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)} \otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right)\cdot  (\text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}}\! \bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U})^{(\bar A)} \otimes (\text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}}\!\bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U})^{(A)} \right)\notag\\
    &= \text{tr}_{\bar A}\left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right) \cdot \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \sum_{\mathbf{r}_i \in \mathbb{F}_d^k} \mathbb{E}_{\substack{\text{U}_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)}}  (\text{U}_i^{\dagger} \ket{\mathbf{r}_{i}}\bra{\mathbf{r}_{i}} \text{U}_i)^{(\bar A)} \otimes (\text{U}_i^{\dagger} \ket{\mathbf{r}_{i}}\!\bra{\mathbf{r}_{i}} \text{U}_i)^{(A)} \right)\notag\\
    &=  \text{tr}_{\bar A}\left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right) \cdot \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \sum_{\mathbf{r}_{i}\in \mathbb{F}_d^{k}} \Phi_2(\ket{\mathbf{r}_{i}}\!\bra{\mathbf{r}_{i}}^{\otimes 2})^{(\bar A A)} \right)\notag \\
    &= \text{tr}_{\bar A}\left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right) \cdot \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n d^{k} \frac{\mathbb{I}^{(\bar A)}(d^k)\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^k)+ \mathbb{P}_{(12)}^{d,(\bar A A)}}{(d^k+1) \cdot d^k}\right).\label{eq:k_copy_shadow_channel}
\end{align} Here in the second line, we use the fact that \ket{{r}_x {r}_z} =H_z \text{CNOT}_{zx} \ket{\Phi_{r_xr_z}}, with H_z \text{CNOT}_{zx} \in \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k). If we expand \rho on separable basis \rho = \bigotimes_{i =1}^n \rho_{i}, plug in Eq. [eq:k_copy_shadow_channel], and use the fact that \text{tr}_{\bar A}(\mathbb{P}_{(12)}^{d,(\bar A A)}\cdot \rho^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}) = \rho^{(A)}, we get the channel output \begin{align}
    \mathcal{M}(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i)
    &= \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \text{tr}(\rho_i) \frac{\mathbb{I}(d^k)}{d^k + 1} + \frac{1}{d^k +1}\rho_i = \mathcal{D}^{\otimes n}_{{1}/{(d^k +1)}}(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i).
\end{align} By the linearity of \mathcal{M}, we conclude that its inverse \mathcal{D}_{{1}/{(d^k +1)}}^{-1}(\rho) = (d^k + 1)\rho - \text{tr}\rho \cdot \mathbb{I}(d^k) constitute an unbiased estimator of \rho \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}(d^{nk})) through the transformation \begin{align}
     \hat \rho_{U,\mathbf b} =\mathcal{M}^{-1}(\text{U}^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b} \text{U})=\bigotimes_{i =1}^n\left((d^k +1)\text{U}_i^{\dagger} \ket{\mathbf{b}_i}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}_i} \text{U}_i - \mathbb{I}(d^k)\right).
\end{align} ◻



This 2-design unitary ensemble includes the Clifford randomized measurement and the randomized Pauli basis measurement, as proposed in  [huang2020predicting?]. Consider the unitary ensemble \mathcal{E} that Following the previous research, we review the estimation variance in the case with (i)the Clifford ensemble  [huang2020predicting?,mele2024introduction?], (ii)the local Clifford ensemble  [huang2020predicting?], and (iii). the Matchgate ensemble.




The first case is the Clifford shadow. It turns out that this ensemble is suitable for low-rank operators O whose trace norm \text{tr}(O^2) is small. This condition is satisfied for entangled pure-state projectors but not for Pauli observables.






ImportantLemma



 In the case of {U} \sim \text{Cliff}(2^n) and \hat{o}:= \text{tr}(O\hat \rho), we have: \begin{align}
        \text{Var}(\hat o)= \frac{(2^n +1)}{(2^n+2)}\left[\text{tr}(O_0^2) +2\text{tr}(\rho O_0^2)\right] - \text{tr}^2(O_0\rho) \leq 3\text{tr}(O_0^2)
\end{align}








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. To calculate the variance of this estimator, we note that \text{Var}(\hat o):= \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}_0^2 - [\text{tr}(O_0\rho)]^2, where O_0 is the traceless version of O. Then we give the value of \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}^2 as \begin{align}
        \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}^2 &= \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b} \sim U \rho U^\dagger} \text{tr}^2\left[O\mathcal{M}^{-1}(U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}} U)\right]
        =\mathbb{E}_{U \sim \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b} \sim U \rho U^\dagger} \text{tr}^2\left[\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O)U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}} U\right]
\end{align} This average can also be reduced to the Weingarten calculus through: \begin{align}
        \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}^2 &=  \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cl}(n)}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b} \sim U\sigma U^\dagger}\bra{\mathbf b}U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}^2\\
        &=\mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cliff}_2}\sum_{\mathbf b}\bra{\mathbf b}U \rho U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}} \bra{\mathbf b}U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} \bra{\mathbf b}U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}\\
        &= \text{tr}\left[(\rho \otimes \mathcal{M}^{-1}(O)\otimes \mathcal{M}^{-1}(O))\cdot \sum_{\mathbf b}  \Phi_{3}(\ket{\mathbf{bbb}}\!\bra{\mathbf{bbb}})\right],
\end{align} where the last step use the fact that the Clifford group forms a 3-design. Cite the Lemma [lemma:state_trajectory] again gives \begin{align}
    &\Phi_3(\ket{\mathbf{bbb}}\!\bra{\mathbf{bbb}}) = \frac{\sum_{\pi \in S_3} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n}}{(2^n+2)(2^n+1)},\\
    \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}^2 &=\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\rho) \mathrm{tr}^2(\mathcal{M}^{-1}) + \mathrm{tr}(\rho) \mathrm{tr}((\mathcal{M}^{-1})^2) +2\mathrm{tr}(\rho \mathcal{M}^{-1}) \mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{M}^{-1}) + 2\mathrm{tr}(\rho(\mathcal{M}^{-1})^2)}{(2^n+2)(2^n+1)}.
\end{align} Use the fact that O_0 is traceless, \mathcal{M}^{-1}(O_0)= (2^n +1)O_0, we give the final result \begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \hat{o}^2 &= \frac{(2^n +1)^2\left[\text{tr}(\rho)\text{tr}(O_0^2) +2\text{tr}(\rho O_0^2)\right]}{(2^n+2)(2^n+1)},\\
    \text{Var}(\hat o) &=\frac{(2^n +1)}{(2^n+2)}\left[\text{tr}(\rho)\text{tr}(O_0^2) +2\text{tr}(\rho O_0^2)\right] - \text{tr}^2(O_0\rho).
\end{align} ◻








The second case is the local Clifford shadow, which chooses uniform ensemble on {U} \sim \text{Cliff}_2^{\otimes n}. It turns out that this ensemble is suitable for operators O that only supports on constant sized qubits. This condition, in contrast with the Clifford shadow, is satisfied for Pauli observables but not for entangled pure-state projectors. Given an operator O = \sum_{P} \alpha_{P} P decomposed on the Pauli basis, we have \hat o (\{U,\mathbf{b}\}) =  \mathrm{tr}\left(O\hat{\rho}_{U,\mathbf{b}} \right) = \bra{\mathbf b}U\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}({O}) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} since \mathcal{M}^{-1} = \mathcal{M}^{-1,\dagger}. Use the fact that \tilde {\mathcal{M}}= (\mathcal{D}_{1/3})^{\otimes k} and the identity \mathcal{D}_{1/3}^{-1}(P) = 3P - \text{tr}(P)\mathbb{I} =f(P) P := \begin{cases}3P& \text{if~} P = X,Y,Z \\ \mathbb{I} &\text{if~} P = \mathbb{I}\end{cases}, we extend this definition to n-qubit case through f(P,Q) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(P_i, Q_i), with f(P_i, Q_i) = \begin{cases}3 \delta_{P_i,Q_i}& \text{if~} P_i,Q_i \in \{X,Y,Z\} \\ 1 &\text{if else}\end{cases}. Noted that U\ket{\mathbf{b}} is an eigenvector of Pauli operator P_{U} with eigenvalue s(U,\mathbf{b}). We conclude that \hat o (\{U,\mathbf{b}\})= \sum_{P}\alpha_P f(P,P_{U})s(\mathbf{b}). Then the variance of the estimator \hat{o} can be calculated below.






ImportantLemma



 Given a the k-local operator with Pauli decomposition O =\mathbb{I}_{n-k}\otimes  \sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}(k)} \alpha_{P} P, the unbiased estimator \hat{o} above has variance \begin{align}
        \mathbb{E}_{U,\mathbf{b}}(\hat{o}^2) =\text{tr} \left(\tilde{\rho} \cdot \sum_{P,Q}\alpha_P \alpha_Q f(P,Q)P\cdot Q \right) \leq 4^k\|O\|_{\infty}^2.
\end{align}








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. Similarly, we first noted that given an observable O = \tilde{O} \otimes \mathbb{I}_{n-k} that supports on k-qubits, we have \begin{align}
\label{eq:ave_of_square_LCshadow}
        \langle \hat{o}^2 \rangle_{\rho} =\mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cliff}(2)^{\otimes k}}\sum_{\mathbf b}\bra{\mathbf b}U \tilde{\rho} U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}} \bra{\mathbf b}U\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}(\tilde{O}) U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}^2,
\end{align} where \tilde{\rho} is the reduced state of \rho that supports on k-qubits. After this, we expand the k-qubit non-identity part within \tilde{O} into the linear combination of Pauli operators as \tilde{O} = \sum_{P \in \{\mathbb{I},X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes k}} \alpha_{P} P as well as the reduced state \tilde{\rho} = \sum_{s} \beta_s \bigotimes_{i =1}^n\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i. It is thus sufficient to calculate Eq.[eq:ave_of_square_LCshadow] pointwise as \begin{align}
        \langle \hat{o}^2 \rangle_{\rho} &= \sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\prod_{i = 1}^n \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cliff}(2)} \!\!\!\sum_{b_i \in \{0,1\}}\!\!\! \bra{b_i}U \tilde{\rho}_j^{(s)} U^\dagger \ket{b_i} \bra{b_i}U\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}(P_i) U^\dagger\ket{b_i}\bra{b_i}U\tilde{\mathcal{M}}^{-1}(Q_i) U^\dagger\ket{b_i}\\
        &=\sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\prod_{i = 1}^n f(P_i)f(Q_i)\sum_{b_i \in \{0,1\}} \left[(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i \otimes P_i \otimes Q_i)\cdot \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cliff}(2)} U^{\otimes 3}\ket{b_i}\!\bra{b_i}^{\otimes 3}U^{\otimes 3,\dagger}\right].
\end{align}
Again from Lemma [lemma:state_trajectory], \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \text{Cliff}(2)} U^{\otimes 3}\ket{b_i}\!\bra{b_i}^{\otimes 3}U^{\otimes 3,\dagger} = (4 \times 3 \times 2)^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_3} \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d =2}, which gives \begin{align}
     \langle \hat{o}^2 \rangle_{\rho} = (\frac{1}{12})^n\sum_{P,Q}\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\sum_s \beta_s\prod_{i = 1}^n f(P_i)f(Q_i)&\left[ \text{tr}(P_i)\text{tr}(Q_i)\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i)+\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i P_i)\text{tr}(Q_i) + \text{tr}(P_i)\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i Q_i)\right.\notag\\
    & \left.+\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i)\text{tr}(P_iQ_i) + \text{tr}(P_i \tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i Q_i)+\text{tr}(Q_i \tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i P_i)\right]\label{eq:mid_sqr_ave}.
\end{align} Depending on three cases, we calculate the RHS after the \sum_{s} \beta_{s}\prod_i signal as \begin{align}
    \sum_{s} \beta_{s}\prod_{i = 1}^n[\cdots] =
    \begin{cases}
        \prod_{i = 1}^n1\cdot 1\cdot [4+2+2+2+1+1] &\text{if~} P_i=Q_i = \mathbb I,\\
        \sum_{s} \beta_{s}\prod_{i = 1}^n1 \cdot 3 \cdot[2 + 1 + 1]\cdot \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i Q_i)]&\text{if~} P_i = \mathbb I\neq Q_i,\\
        \sum_{s} \beta_{s}\prod_{i = 1}^n3 \cdot 1 \cdot[2 + 1 + 1]\cdot \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i P_i)]&\text{if~} Q_i = \mathbb I\neq P_i,\\
        \sum_{s} \beta_{s}\prod_{i = 1}^n3 \cdot 3 \cdot[2 +1+1] \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i)\delta_{P_i,Q_i}&\text{if~} Q_i, P_i \neq \mathbb I.
    \end{cases}
\end{align} Here in the last equality, we use the fact that \mathcal{C}(P_i) = \{P_i, \mathbb{I}\} and \begin{align}
    \forall Q_i, P_i \neq \mathbb I, \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i \{Q_i,P_i\}) = \begin{cases}0 &\text{if~} Q_i \notin \mathcal{C}(P_i)\backslash \mathbb{I}\\2\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i Q_iP_i)  &\text{if~} Q_i \in \mathcal{C}(P_i)\backslash \mathbb{I} \end{cases} = 2\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i)\delta_{P_i,Q_i}.
\end{align} Plug this equation into Eq.[eq:mid_sqr_ave] gives us the final results \begin{align}
    \langle \hat{o}^2 \rangle_{\rho} &= \left\{\begin{aligned}
        &\sum_{P,Q}\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q \text{~if~} P_i=Q_i = \mathbb I,\\
        &\sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\prod_i\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i  \mathbb{I} \cdot Q_i)\text{~if~} P_i = \mathbb I\neq Q_i,\\
        &\sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\prod_i\text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i  P_i\cdot \mathbb{I})\text{~if~} Q_i = \mathbb I\neq P_i,\\
        &\sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s\alpha_{P}\alpha_Q\prod_i3\delta_{P_i,Q_i}\text{~if~} Q_i,P_i \neq \mathbb I
    \end{aligned}\right.:= \sum_{P,Q,s}\beta_s \alpha_P \alpha_Q\prod_i f(P_i,Q_i) \text{tr}(\tilde{\rho}^{(s)}_i P_iQ_i)\\
   &=\text{tr} \left(\tilde{\rho} \cdot \sum_{P,Q}\alpha_P \alpha_Q \left(\prod_{i = 1}^n f(P_i,Q_i)\right)P\cdot Q \right):=\text{tr} \left(\tilde{\rho} \cdot \sum_{P,Q}\alpha_P \alpha_Q f(P,Q)P\cdot Q \right) .
\end{align} To show the upper bounds, we noted that (i). If P,Q can both be obtained from replacing certain parts of S \in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k} with idendity \mathbb I, which we denoted as P,Q\subset S, then f(P,Q) \neq 0, and (ii). If f(P,Q) \neq 0, we count the number of position at which P_i = Q_i = \mathbb{I} as {k-|P\cup Q|}. Then this implies there are 3^{k-|P\cup Q|} numbers of S \in \{X,Y,Z\}^k s.t. P,Q\subset S. Such a non-zero value f(P,Q) is decided by the length of the overlap parts between P,Q\subset S, which satisfied f(P,Q) =3^{|P| +|Q| -|P \cup Q|}. This gives \begin{align}
    \sum_{P,Q}\alpha_P \alpha_Q f(P,Q)P\cdot Q &= \sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\sum_{P,Q \subset S} 3^{|P\cup Q| - k}\alpha_P \alpha_Q f(P,Q) P\cdot Q \\
    &=\sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\sum_{P,Q \subset S} 3^{|P|+ |Q| - k} \alpha_P P \cdot \alpha_Q Q  = 3^{-k}\sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\!\!\left(\sum_{P\subset S} 3^{|P|} \alpha_P P \right)^2.
\end{align} Then we can upper bound the variance based on the fact that \sum_{P\subset S} 3^{|P|} = (3+1)^{|S|} = 4^k, \begin{align}
    \langle \hat{o}^2 \rangle_{\rho} &\leq 3^{-k}\left\|\sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\left(\sum_{P\subset S} 3^{|P|}\alpha_P P \right)^2\right\|_{\infty} \leq 3^{-k} \sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\left(\sum_{P\subset S} 3^{|P|}\alpha_P \right)^2\\
    &\leq 3^{-k} \sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}}\left(\sum_{P\subset S} 3^{|P|}\right) \left(\sum_{P\subset S}3^{|P|}\alpha_P^2 \right) = 4^k \sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}} \left(\sum_{P\subset S}3^{|P| - k}\alpha_P^2 \right).
\end{align} Notice that \forall P \in \{I,X,Y,Z\}^{k}, \exists 3^{|P| - k} numbers of S \in \{X,Y,Z\} s.t. P \subset S (S that generated from replacing \mathbb{I} within P by \{I,X,Y\}). This means that \begin{align}
    \sum_{S\in \{X,Y,Z\}^{k}} \left(\sum_{P\subset S}3^{|P| - k}\alpha_P^2 \right) = 4^k\sum_{P \in \{I,X,Y,Z\}^{k}} \alpha_P^2 = 2^k \text{tr}(\tilde{O}^2) \leq 4^k \|\tilde{O}\|_{\infty}.
\end{align} ◻



The Local shadow above can be reframed into biased one and introduce adaptive strategy.






ImportantLemma












Then we discuss the power of classical shadow in estimating exponentially many linear properties \text{tr}(O_i\hat \rho), \forall i \in \{1,\cdots,M\}, as shown in Problem [prob:linear_shadow] and Lemma [lemma:linear_sing_shadow] below.

 Given output state \rho and any collection of operators \mathcal{O}:=\{O_1,\cdots,O_M\} with \|O_i\|_{\infty} \leq 1, to get enough classical descriptions that estimates \text{tr}(O_x \rho), \forall O_x \in \mathcal{O} within \varepsilon additive error and 1 - \delta success probability.







ImportantLemma



 To solve Problem [prob:linear_shadow], We can either (i).measure on the eigenbasis of O_1,\cdots ,O_M separately, each one for \varepsilon^{-2}\ln(M/\delta) times, or (ii).use global Clifford shadow tomography and generate N = 2^{\text{rank}(\mathcal{O})}\varepsilon^{-2}\log(M/\delta) numbers of classical shadows.








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. ◻



Unfortunately, Lemma [lemma:linear_sing_shadow] implies the inefficiency of global Clifford classical shadow in estimating linear properties \mathcal{O}, if \text{tr}(O_i^2) is exponentially large. A practical example involves \mathcal{O}:=\{\mathbb{I},X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n}, which we called the Pauli shadow tomography and requires sampling complexity N \sim 4^n \cdot n for case(i) and N \sim 2^n\cdot n for case(ii). Both of them are exponentially hard. Interestedly, there exists simple local two-copy strategy that solve the Pauli shadow tomography, as described in Algorithm [alg:est_Pauli_const] below. Combining the lower bound proof in section [sec:lb_shadow], this manifests a sharp transition of sampling complexity between the single copy strategy and the two-copy strategy for Pauli shadow tomography.
Consuming only \mathcal{O}(n) numbers of \rho, Algorithm [alg:est_Pauli_const] collects enough classical Bell shadow that are able to estimate |\text{tr}(\rho P)|^2 within constant error for each Pauli operator. The power of Algorithm [alg:est_Pauli_const] derived from the common unbiased estimator for \text{tr}(\rho \otimes \rho \cdot \sigma_{\mathbf r} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf r})


n-qubit density matrix \rho and a set of target Pauli operator \{\sigma_{\mathbf{y}^{(1)}},\cdots,\sigma_{\mathbf{y}^{(M)}}\}. Collect enough classical information such that \forall i, |\text{tr}(\rho \sigma_{\mathbf{y}^{(i)}})|^2 can be estimated within \varepsilon additive error and 1 - \delta success rate. Implements N \sim 4 \ln(2M/\delta)/\varepsilon^2 times Bell measurement and restore the result \mathbf{r}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{r}_N with \mathbf{r}_i \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}. To estimate |\text{tr}(\rho \sigma_{\mathbf{y}})|^2, take the xz decomposition of \mathbf y = (\mathbf{y}_x, \mathbf{y}_z) Calculate the average and return R =({1}/{N})\cdot\sum_{i = 1}^N(-1)^{[\mathbf r_i, \mathbf y]+\mathbf y_{x} \cdot \mathbf y_z}.


After that, we show






NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof of Algorithm [alg:est_Pauli_const]. We first show the unbiasedness. Use the property of Bell sampling in Theorem [theo: Bell_prob], we conclude that for \rho = \sum_{\mathbf{u}}c_{\mathbf{u}} \sigma_{\mathbf{u}}, \begin{align}
        \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{r} \sim P(\mathbf r)}(-1)^{[\mathbf r, \mathbf y]+\mathbf y_{x} \cdot \mathbf y_z} &= \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} \text{tr}(\rho \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \rho^* \sigma_{\mathbf{r}})(-1)^{[\mathbf r, \mathbf y]+\mathbf y_{x} \cdot \mathbf y_z}=\sum_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} c_{\mathbf{u}}c_{\mathbf{v}}^*\text{tr}(\sigma_{\mathbf{u}} \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} (-1)^{\mathbf{v}_x \cdot \mathbf{v}_y}\sigma_{\mathbf{v}} \sigma_{\mathbf{r}})(-1)^{[\mathbf r, \mathbf y]+\mathbf y_{x} \cdot \mathbf y_z} \notag \\
        &=\sum_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} c_{\mathbf{u}}c_{\mathbf{v}}^*2^n\delta_{\mathbf u, \mathbf v}(-1)^{[\mathbf r, \mathbf y + \mathbf v]+\mathbf y_{x} \cdot \mathbf y_z +\mathbf{v}_x \cdot \mathbf{v}_y} = 4^n |c_{\mathbf{y}}|^2= |\text{tr}(\rho \sigma_{\mathbf y})|^2.
\end{align} ◻



Discussion above can be generalized to c-copy strategy for the d = c Weyl-Heisenberg shadow tomography, as defined below

Given a n-qudit state \rho, design a sampling method to estimate the value |\text{tr}(W_{\mathbf{a}}\rho)| with a constant additive error \varepsilon for all n-qudit Weyl-Heisenberg operator \{W_{\mathbf{a}}\}_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{n}}.

Unlike the qubit-Pauli operator, in this case \{W_{\mathbf{a}}^{\otimes d}\} are mutually commutant because W_{\mathbf{a}}^{\otimes d} W_{\mathbf{b}}^{\otimes d} =\omega^{d[\mathbf{b},\mathbf{a}]} (W_{\mathbf{b}}W_{\mathbf{a}})^{\otimes d} according to lemma [lemma:properties_WHop] and \omega^{d} = 1. We thus find the common eigenbasis for operators \{W_{\mathbf{a}}^{\otimes d}\}_{\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{F}_{d}^n}. In the case with n = 1, it turns out that those eigenvectors can be specified by labels I \in \mathbb{F}_{d}^{d - 1} and q \in \mathbb{F}_{d} as \ket{\phi_{I,q}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}} \sum_{k = 0}^{d - 1} \omega^{kq} \ket{(0,I) + k \mathbf{1}}, with X^{\otimes d}\ket{\phi_{I,q}} = \omega^{-q} \ket{\phi_{I,q}} and Z^{\otimes d}\ket{\phi_{I,q}} = \omega^{|I|} \ket{\phi_{I,q}}.






ImportantLemma



Define a coarse-grained projector \Pi_{s_x, s_z} = \sum_{I \in \mathbb{F}_{d}^{d-1}, |I| = s_x} \ket{\phi_{I,s_z}}\!\bra{\phi_{I,s_z}} and its tensor product operator \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} = \Pi_{\mathbf{s}_x, \mathbf{s}_z}:= \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \Pi_{s_{x,i}, s_{z,i}}. Then we have: \begin{align}
        (X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z})^{\otimes d} = \sum_{\mathbf{s}\in \mathbb{F}_d^{2n}} \omega^{[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}}, \quad \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} =d^{-2n} \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{2n}}\omega^{-[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]}(X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z})^{\otimes d}.
\end{align} The average of operator X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z} can be estimated by post-processing the d-copy generalized Bell measurement result \mathbf{s}\sim \text{tr}\left(\Pi_{\mathbf{s}}\rho^{\otimes d}\right) on d-copy state \rho^{\otimes d} as \left|\text{tr}\left(\left(X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z}\right) \rho\right)\right| = \left|\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{s}}~\omega^{[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]}\right|^{1/d}.








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. We note the relation that \begin{align}
        &X^{\otimes d} = \sum_{{s}_x, {s}_z} \omega^{-s_z}\sum_{I \in \mathbb{F}_{d}^{d-1}, |I| = s_x}\ket{\phi_{I,s_z}}\!\bra{\phi_{I,s_z}} = \sum_{{s}_x, {s}_z} \omega^{-s_z} \Pi_{s_x,s_z},\\
        &Z^{\otimes d} = \sum_{{s}_x, {s}_z} \omega^{s_x}\sum_{I \in \mathbb{F}_{d}^{d-1}, |I| = s_x}\ket{\phi_{I,s_z}}\!\bra{\phi_{I,s_z}} = \sum_{{s}_x, {s}_z} \omega^{s_x} \Pi_{s_x,s_z}
\end{align} For a d-copies of n-qudit state \rho^{\otimes d}, we get a generalized relation by defining the tensor product operator \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} = \Pi_{\mathbf{s}_x, \mathbf{s}_z}:= \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \Pi_{s_{x,i}, s_{z,i}} with \mathbf{s}\in \mathbb{F}^{2n}_{d} and symplectic product in finite field \mathbb{F}_d^{2n} as [\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}] = \mathbf{s}_x \cdot \mathbf{r}_z - \mathbf{s}_z \cdot \mathbf{r}_x, which write (X^{\mathbf{r}_x})^{\otimes d} = \sum_{\mathbf{s}} \omega^{-\mathbf{r}_x\cdot \mathbf{s}_z} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} and (Z^{\mathbf{r}_z})^{\otimes d} = \sum_{\mathbf{s}} \omega^{\mathbf{r}_z \cdot \mathbf{s}_x} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}}. Product those two terms and use the fact that \Pi_{\mathbf{s}}\Pi_{\mathbf{s}'} = \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} \delta_{\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}'} gives \begin{align}
        (X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z})^{\otimes d} = \sum_{\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}'} \omega^{-\mathbf{r}_x \cdot \mathbf{s}_z} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} \cdot  \omega^{\mathbf{r}_z \cdot \mathbf{s}_x'} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}'} = \sum_{\mathbf{s}} \omega^{[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]} \Pi_{\mathbf{s}}.
\end{align} Use the identity \sum_{\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{2n}}\omega^{[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}']} = d^{2n} \delta_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}'}, we get the inverse transition \Pi_{\mathbf{s}} =d^{-2n} \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{2n}}\omega^{-[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]}(X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z})^{\otimes d}. This then gives \left[\text{tr}\left(\left(X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z}\right) \rho\right)\right]^{d} = \text{tr}\left(\left(X^{\mathbf{r}_x}Z^{\mathbf{r}_z}\right)^{\otimes d} \rho^{\otimes d}\right) = \sum_{\mathbf{s}\in \mathbb{F}_d^{2n}} \omega^{[\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{r}]}\text{tr}\left(\Pi_{\mathbf{s}}\rho^{\otimes d}\right) and proved the result. ◻






Then we discuss the power of classical shadow in estimating the non-linear property \text{tr}(O\rho^k). Notice that \text{tr}(O\rho^k) = \text{tr}(O' \cdot \text{SWAP}_{k}^{\otimes n}\rho^{\otimes k}) with O' = O\otimes \mathbb{I}_n^{\otimes (k-1)}. To estimate the non-linear property \text{tr}(O\rho^k) for k>1, directly applied the Clifford shadow and the local Clifford shadow to operator O'\text{SWAP}_{k}^{\otimes n} on a k-copies system gives exponentially large sampling complexity. According to the lower bound shown in Lemma [lemma:Clifford_shadow] and Lemma [lemma:LC_shadow]. This is because 
\begin{align}
    &\mathrm{tr}(O' \cdot \text{SWAP}_{k}^{\otimes n}\cdot O' \cdot \text{SWAP}_{k}^{\otimes n}) = 2^{n(k-2)} \text{tr}^2(O) ,\\
    &4^{\text{supp}(O'\cdot \text{SWAP}_{k}^{\otimes n})} = 4^{k\cdot n}
\end{align}
 are both exponentially large in the qubit number n.




In this section, we try to present the exponential sampling complexity upper bound for the single-copy shadow methods in estimating (i). A bunch of high-weight Pauli average O \in \{X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n},\text{tr}(O \rho) and (ii) A bunch of second-order value O \in \mathcal{O}, \text{tr}(O\rho^2).





We first reduced the linear-shadow task in Problem [prob:linear_shadow] into a new version of discrimination problem.






ImportantLemma



 Given a set of operators \{O_x\}_{x = 1}^M such that \text{tr}(O_x) = 0, \text{tr}(O_x^2) = 2^n, if an algorithm \mathcal{A} estimates \text{tr}(O_x \rho), \forall x= 1 ,\cdots,M within additive error \varepsilon and success rate 1 - \delta, then this algorithm can distinguish two cases with success rate 1 - \delta: (i). the maximum mixed state, (ii) one of the states within \{2^{-n}(\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon O_x)\}.








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. In the case (i), we have \text{tr}(O_x \rho) = 0, \forall x because O_x is traceless by definition. This means that M^{-1}\mathrm{tr}(\sum_{x \in M}O_x \rho) = 0. While in the case (ii), we know \exists x \in \{1,\cdots,M\} s.t. \text{tr}(O_x \rho) = 3\varepsilon. Based on these observations, we design the algorithms below: (a). \forall x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}, use algorithm that solves problem [prob:linear_shadow], we get result r_x such that \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) - \varepsilon< r_x < \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) + \varepsilon. (b). If \forall x, r_x <2 \varepsilon, accept case (i), If \exists x, r_x \geq 2 \varepsilon, accept case (ii). Note that \exists x, r_x \geq 2 \varepsilon \Rightarrow \exists x, \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) > \varepsilon, this means case (i) is impossible. Similarly, \forall x, r_x < 2 \varepsilon \Rightarrow \forall x, \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) < 3\varepsilon, which means case (ii) is impossible. Then we prove the correctness of the reduction. ◻



The reduction presented in Lemma [lemma:red_shad2distin] required computing \mathrm{tr}(\rho O_x) for all x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}, which is computationally hard if M \sim \text{exp}(n). To fill this gap, one can reframe the distinguishing problem into an adversarial scenario.

Alice (the adversary) first choose \mathbf{x}_0 \in \{1,\cdots,M\} according to arbitrary distribution \mathcal{D}.
Then Alice chooses to send N-copies of state \rho = \rho_{\mathbf{x}_0}:= 2^{-n}(\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon O_x) or \rho = \mathbb{I}/d to Bob.
Bob repeatedly receives \rho and measures with restricted POVMs.
After measurements ends, Alice tells Bob \mathbf{x}_0 and Bob decides whether Alice choose \rho = \rho_{\mathbf{x}_0} or \rho = \mathbb{I}/d through classical post-processing.

We say Bob wins this game if his decision is coincident to Alice’s choice. If there exists a shadow algorithm \mathcal{A} for \text{tr}(O_x \rho), \forall x= 1 ,\cdots,M within additive error \varepsilon and success rate 1 - \delta using N copies, then no matter how Alice changes the distribution \mathcal{D}, Bob can win the game with probability 1 - \delta by first run the shadow algorithm \mathcal{A} and then check the value of \mathrm{tr}(O_{\mathbf{x}_0} \rho).

title: Basics of Shadow Tomography
text:
Single-copy shadow tomography restores single copy of \rho, repeats randomized measurements, and try to use these measurement results to estimate MANY properties of \rho, which includes linear property \text{tr}(O_i\rho), non-linear properties \text{tr}(O_i \rho^{t_i}), and even their products \prod_{i}\text{tr}(O_i \rho^{t_i}). The procedure of shadow tomography firstly includes the sampling of classical shadow, as shown in Algorithm [alg:classical_shadow]. Note that in Algorithm [alg:classical_shadow], virtually means restore the classical description of circuit U and length-n bit string \mathbf b. As shown in Lemma [lemma:single_shadow_unbiased], to estimate many properties includes \text{tr}(O \hat \rho^k), ones compute based only those sampled classical shadow.


Sample U \sim \mathcal{U} with certain unitary ensemble \mathcal{U}. Measure the state U\rho U^\dagger on the computational basis with result \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}}. Virtually computes the shadow matrix \hat \rho:= \mathcal{M}^{-1}(U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}} U), where \mathcal{M} is the entanglement-breaking linear map \rho \to \mathbb{E}_{U \sim \mathcal{U}} \sum_{\mathbf b}\bra{\mathbf b}U \rho U^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}} \cdot  U^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b} U.








ImportantLemma



 The estimator \hat{o}^{(k)} := \text{tr}(O \hat \rho_1\cdots \hat \rho_k) is an unbiased estimator for the expectation \text{tr}(O \rho^k), where \hat{\rho}_i is sampled according to the Algorithm [alg:classical_shadow].








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. \begin{align}
        \mathbb{E}_{\hat \rho} \text{tr}(O \hat \rho_1\cdots \hat \rho_k) &= \mathbb{E}_{U_i \sim \mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}_i \sim U_i \rho U_i^\dagger} \text{tr}\left[O \prod_{i =1}^{k}\mathcal{M}^{-1}(U_i^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}_i}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}_i} U_i)\right]\\
        &=  \text{tr}\left[O \prod_{i =1}^{k}\mathcal{M}^{-1}(\mathbb{E}_{U_i \sim \mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}_i \sim U_i \rho U_i^\dagger}U_i^\dagger \ket{\mathbf{b}_i}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}_i} U_i)\right]=\text{tr}(O \rho^k).
\end{align} ◻



While we do not care about the computational complexity in the most case, the computation of \text{tr}(O \hat \rho^k) can be reconstructed as \bra{\mathbf b}(U\mathcal{M}^{-1, \dagger}(O)U^\dagger) \ket{\mathbf b}, thus might be processed efficiently if the randomized unitaries U is classical tractable and the target operator O can be decomposed into poly(n) numbers of simple operators.
The sampling complexity of any classical shadows scheme depends on both the choice of unitary distribution \mathcal{U} and the particular set of properties O of interest.


The explicit form of channel \mathcal{M} rely on the choice of unitary ensembles. Results of \mathcal{M} are known for global and on site 2-design unitary ensembles, 2-design unitary ensemble, fermionic Gaussian unitary ensemble, manybody Gaussian unitary ensemble, and locally scrambled unitaries ensemble. In this subsection we summarized these results.






ImportantLemma



 A k-site 2-design unitary ensembles \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)^{\otimes n} separates n\cdot k numbers of qudits in to n parts, and independently implements k-qudit 2-design unitary, as defined in Definition [def:t_design], within each part. In other words, \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)^{\otimes n}:=\{\bigotimes_{i  =1}^n U_i| U_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)\}. This ensemble induces the channel \begin{align}
        \mathcal{M}(\rho) = (\mathcal{D}_{1/(2^k + 1)})^{\otimes n}(\rho), \text{with~} \mathcal{D}_{1/(2^k + 1)}(\cdot) = \frac{1}{2^k +1}(\cdot) + \frac{\text{tr}(\cdot)}{2^k + 1}{\mathbb{I}(d^k)}.
\end{align} Specifically, the global 2-design unitary ensemble takes the case n = 1, U \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k),and the channel \mathcal{M}(\rho) ={(d^k + 1)^{-1}} \rho + {d^k{(d^k + 1)^{-1}}  \text{tr}\rho \cdot }({\mathbb{I}(d^k)}/{d^k}). The local 2-design unitary ensemble takes the case k = 1, U \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d)^{\otimes n},and the channel \mathcal{M}(\rho) = {(d + 1)}^{-1} \rho + {d({d + 1})^{-1} \text{tr}\rho} \cdot ({\mathbb{I}(d)}/{d}).








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. For tensor product inputs \otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i, \rho_i \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}(d^k)), the channel \mathcal{M} in this case became \begin{align}
    \mathcal{M}(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i)
    &=\mathbb{E}_{\substack{U = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n\text{U}_i \\ \text{U}_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)}} \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{kn}} \bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U} (\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i) \text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}} \cdot \text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}}\!\bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U} \notag\\
    &=\mathbb{E}_{\substack{U = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n\text{U}_i \\ \text{U}_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)}} \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_d^{kn}} \text{tr}_{\bar A} \left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)} \otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right)\cdot  (\text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}}\! \bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U})^{(\bar A)} \otimes (\text{U}^{\dagger} \ket{{\mathbf r}}\!\bra{{\mathbf r}} \text{U})^{(A)} \right)\notag\\
    &= \text{tr}_{\bar A}\left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right) \cdot \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \sum_{\mathbf{r}_i \in \mathbb{F}_d^k} \mathbb{E}_{\substack{\text{U}_i \sim \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k)}}  (\text{U}_i^{\dagger} \ket{\mathbf{r}_{i}}\bra{\mathbf{r}_{i}} \text{U}_i)^{(\bar A)} \otimes (\text{U}_i^{\dagger} \ket{\mathbf{r}_{i}}\!\bra{\mathbf{r}_{i}} \text{U}_i)^{(A)} \right)\notag\\
    &=  \text{tr}_{\bar A}\left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right) \cdot \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \sum_{\mathbf{r}_{i}\in \mathbb{F}_d^{k}} \Phi_2(\ket{\mathbf{r}_{i}}\!\bra{\mathbf{r}_{i}}^{\otimes 2})^{(\bar A A)} \right)\notag \\
    &= \text{tr}_{\bar A}\left( \left(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^{kn})\right) \cdot \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n d^{k} \frac{\mathbb{I}^{(\bar A)}(d^k)\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}(d^k)+ \mathbb{P}_{(12)}^{d,(\bar A A)}}{(d^k+1) \cdot d^k}\right).\label{eq:k_copy_shadow_channel}
\end{align} Here in the second line, we use the fact that \ket{{r}_x {r}_z} =H_z \text{CNOT}_{zx} \ket{\Phi_{r_xr_z}}, with H_z \text{CNOT}_{zx} \in \mathbf{D}_{2}(d^k). If we expand \rho on separable basis \rho = \bigotimes_{i =1}^n \rho_{i}, plug in Eq. [eq:k_copy_shadow_channel], and use the fact that \text{tr}_{\bar A}(\mathbb{P}_{(12)}^{d,(\bar A A)}\cdot \rho^{(\bar A)}\otimes \mathbb{I}^{(A)}) = \rho^{(A)}, we get the channel output \begin{align}
    \mathcal{M}(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i)
    &= \bigotimes_{i = 1}^n \text{tr}(\rho_i) \frac{\mathbb{I}(d^k)}{d^k + 1} + \frac{1}{d^k +1}\rho_i = \mathcal{D}^{\otimes n}_{{1}/{(d^k +1)}}(\otimes_{i = 1}^n \rho_i).
\end{align} By the linearity of \mathcal{M}, we conclude that its inverse \mathcal{D}_{{1}/{(d^k +1)}}^{-1}(\rho) = (d^k + 1)\rho - \text{tr}\rho \cdot \mathbb{I}(d^k) constitute an unbiased estimator of \rho \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}(d^{nk})) through the transformation \begin{align}
     \hat \rho_{U,\mathbf b} =\mathcal{M}^{-1}(\text{U}^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b} \text{U})=\bigotimes_{i =1}^n\left((d^k +1)\text{U}_i^{\dagger} \ket{\mathbf{b}_i}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}_i} \text{U}_i - \mathbb{I}(d^k)\right).
\end{align} ◻



This 2-design unitary ensemble includes the Clifford randomized measurement and the randomized Pauli basis measurement, as proposed in  [huang2020predicting?]. Consider the unitary ensemble \mathcal{E} that Following the previous research, we review the estimation variance in the case with (i)the Clifford ensemble  [huang2020predicting?,mele2024introduction?], (ii)the local Clifford ensemble  [huang2020predicting?], and (iii). the Matchgate ensemble.

title: Basics of Shadow Tomography
Basics of Shadow Tomography
Basics of Shadow Tomography
text:
In this section, we try to present the exponential sampling complexity upper bound for the single-copy shadow methods in estimating (i). A bunch of high-weight Pauli average O \in \{X,Y,Z\}^{\otimes n},\text{tr}(O \rho) and (ii) A bunch of second-order value O \in \mathcal{O}, \text{tr}(O\rho^2).





We first reduced the linear-shadow task in Problem [prob:linear_shadow] into a new version of discrimination problem.






ImportantLemma



 Given a set of operators \{O_x\}_{x = 1}^M such that \text{tr}(O_x) = 0, \text{tr}(O_x^2) = 2^n, if an algorithm \mathcal{A} estimates \text{tr}(O_x \rho), \forall x= 1 ,\cdots,M within additive error \varepsilon and success rate 1 - \delta, then this algorithm can distinguish two cases with success rate 1 - \delta: (i). the maximum mixed state, (ii) one of the states within \{2^{-n}(\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon O_x)\}.








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. In the case (i), we have \text{tr}(O_x \rho) = 0, \forall x because O_x is traceless by definition. This means that M^{-1}\mathrm{tr}(\sum_{x \in M}O_x \rho) = 0. While in the case (ii), we know \exists x \in \{1,\cdots,M\} s.t. \text{tr}(O_x \rho) = 3\varepsilon. Based on these observations, we design the algorithms below: (a). \forall x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}, use algorithm that solves problem [prob:linear_shadow], we get result r_x such that \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) - \varepsilon< r_x < \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) + \varepsilon. (b). If \forall x, r_x <2 \varepsilon, accept case (i), If \exists x, r_x \geq 2 \varepsilon, accept case (ii). Note that \exists x, r_x \geq 2 \varepsilon \Rightarrow \exists x, \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) > \varepsilon, this means case (i) is impossible. Similarly, \forall x, r_x < 2 \varepsilon \Rightarrow \forall x, \mathrm{tr}(O_x \rho) < 3\varepsilon, which means case (ii) is impossible. Then we prove the correctness of the reduction. ◻



The reduction presented in Lemma [lemma:red_shad2distin] required computing \mathrm{tr}(\rho O_x) for all x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}, which is computationally hard if M \sim \text{exp}(n). To fill this gap, one can reframe the distinguishing problem into an adversarial scenario.

Alice (the adversary) first choose \mathbf{x}_0 \in \{1,\cdots,M\} according to arbitrary distribution \mathcal{D}.
Then Alice chooses to send N-copies of state \rho = \rho_{\mathbf{x}_0}:= 2^{-n}(\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon O_x) or \rho = \mathbb{I}/d to Bob.
Bob repeatedly receives \rho and measures with restricted POVMs.
After measurements ends, Alice tells Bob \mathbf{x}_0 and Bob decides whether Alice choose \rho = \rho_{\mathbf{x}_0} or \rho = \mathbb{I}/d through classical post-processing.

We say Bob wins this game if his decision is coincident to Alice’s choice. If there exists a shadow algorithm \mathcal{A} for \text{tr}(O_x \rho), \forall x= 1 ,\cdots,M within additive error \varepsilon and success rate 1 - \delta using N copies, then no matter how Alice changes the distribution \mathcal{D}, Bob can win the game with probability 1 - \delta by first run the shadow algorithm \mathcal{A} and then check the value of \mathrm{tr}(O_{\mathbf{x}_0} \rho).

title: Maximal Likelihood Decoding
text:
Maximal Likelihood Decoding (MLD) involves finding the most likely string \mathbf{c} given a syndrome \mathbf{s}. To do this, we need prior knowledge of which errors are more likely to occur, i.e., the error weight distribution p(\mathbf{e}).
The so-called MLD problem is rigorously modeled as: 
\begin{cases}
\min_{c \in \mathbb{F}_2^n} \sum_{i \in [n]} w_i c_i\\
\text{s.t.~} \sum_{i \in [n]}H[j,i] c_i = s_j, \forall j \in [m] \cup\{0\}
\end{cases}\quad \text{(MLD)}
 where w_i = \ln \frac{1 - p[i]}{p[i]}.


If every column of H has at most 2 non-zero elements (each error triggers at most 2 detectors), MLD can be reduced to MWPM with boundaries.
Definition (Detector Graph): G=(E,V), where V = [m] \cup \{0\}. Edges correspond to the columns of H. * If |\mathbf{e}_i|=2 (triggers x_1, x_2): Edge is (x_1, x_2). * If |\mathbf{e}_i|=1 (triggers x): Edge is (x, 0) (connecting to boundary).






ImportantLemma (MLD to MWPM)



The MLD problem on this class of H matrices can be deterministically reduced to MWPM on a Detector Graph in polynomial time.








TipProof (Click to expand)





Add a row such that every column of the matrix \mathbf{H}\in \mathbb{F}_2^{m+1} \times \mathbb{F}_2^n has weight |\mathbf{e}_i| = 2. Correspondingly construct the Detector graph G, edge vector \mathbf c \in \mathbb{F}_2^n, and vertex vector \mathbf s \in \mathbb{F}_2^{m+1}. The \mathbf{H} matrix, reflecting errors to syndromes, becomes the boundary mapping \partial from the edge vector \mathbf c \in \mathbb{F}_2^n to the vertex vector \mathbf s \in \mathbb{F}_2^{m+1} on G. For a given vertex vector \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{m+1}, take the index positions D \subset V of the first m non-zero bits. This corresponds to the boundary of the edges. The constraint is interpreted as: Find a set of edges on the DG that has the boundary D.
Minimization is equivalent to the following two steps: First, exhaust all point pairs (u,v), u\in D,v\in D \cup \{0\}. This requires repeating \frac{|D|(|D| - 1)}{2} + |D| times. Use Dijkstra’s algorithm to calculate the shortest path u \to v, constructing a fully connected weighted graph of |D| vertices and its boundary point \{0\}. Second, solve the \text{MWPM}_b problem on this fully connected weighted graph with boundary point \{0\}.
These two steps are guaranteed to give the solution to \text{MLD}. Therefore, \text{MLD} can be deterministically reduced to \text{MWPM}_b in polynomial time.

title: Maximal Likelihood Decoding
text:
2.1 Definitions and Primal Problem






NoteDefinition 1: Weighted Graph



A weighted graph is defined as G = (V=\{v_i\},E = \{(v_i,v_j), \forall i \neq j\},W= \{w_e \in \mathbb{R}, \forall e \in E\}).

A Matching of G is a subset M of E such that no two edges in M share a vertex.
A Perfect Matching of G further requires that every vertex is included in some edge in M.



For e \in E, M \subset E, define the vector \mathbf{x}_M = (x_e)_{e \in E} such that: 
{x}_e =\chi_M(e) := \begin{cases}x_e = 1& \text{if~} e \in M\\x_e = 0& \text{if~} e \notin M\end{cases}

The minimization task (Integer Weighted Perfect Matching, IWPM) becomes:

\begin{align}
\begin{cases}
&\min_x \sum_{e \in E} w_e x_e \\
&\text{s.t.} \sum_{e \in \delta(\{v_i\})} x_e = 1, \forall v_i \in V  \\
&\quad \quad \quad x_e \in \{0,1\}, \forall e \in E
\end{cases}\quad \text{(IWPM)}
\end{align}

Its feasible region is a finite set of |E|-dimensional vectors with components in \{0,1\}, corresponding to perfect matchings on the graph.
To perform Relaxation, we introduce the following lemma:






NoteTheorem 1: The Matching Polytope



Define the odd set: \mathcal{O}(G) = \{U \mid U \subseteq V, |U| = 3, 5, \dots \text{ is odd and } \geq 3\}

\begin{align}
P_1(G) &:=\text{conv}\{\mathbf{x} \mid \forall e \in E, x_e \in \{0,1\}; \forall v\in V, \sum_{e \in \delta(\{v\})} x_e = 1 \} \\
P_2(G) &:= \text{conv}\{\mathbf{x} \mid \forall e \in E, x_e \geq 0; \forall v \in V, \sum_{e \in \delta(\{v\})} x_e = 1; \forall U \in \mathcal{O}(G), \sum_{e \in \delta(U)} x_e \geq 1\}
\end{align}

If w_e \in \mathbb{Q}, then P_1(G) = P_2(G).








TipProof Idea for Theorem 1





Reference: https://theory.stanford.edu/~jvondrak/CS369P/lec5.pdf

P_1 \subseteq P_2: A set U consisting of an odd number of vertices cannot realize a perfect matching internally, so there must be edges connecting to the outside, i.e., \sum_{e \in \delta(U)} x_e \geq 1 must hold.
P_2 \subseteq P_1: Since P_2 is a convex polytope, we only need to prove that the vertices of P_2 are contained in P_1. Take such a vertex \mathbf{x}=(x_e)_{e \in E} \in P_2.

Without loss of generality, we can require 0 < x_e < 1. If 0 or 1, we can reduce the problem by removing edges or removing edges and vertices to construct a new graph G'.
Examine degrees: If |E| = |V|, corresponding to a cycle, \mathbf{x} = (\alpha, 1 - \alpha, \dots). Being a vertex implies \alpha \in \{0,1\}, which is reducible.
Therefore |E| > |V|. Since \mathbf{x} as an |E|-dimensional vector is a vertex, constraints must be tight (equalities). There exists U \in \mathcal{O}(G) such that \sum_{e \in \delta(U)}x_e = 1.
Examine the contracted graphs G_a=G/U and G_b =G/(V-U) and the vector restrictions \mathbf{x}_a, \mathbf{x}_b on them.
Verify feasibility: The newly added vertices after contraction satisfy degree constraints. Thus \mathbf{x}_a \in P_{2}(G_a), \mathbf{x}_b \in P_{2}(G_b).
Induction: If \mathbf{x}_a \in P_{1}(G_a) and \mathbf{x}_b \in P_{1}(G_b), then \mathbf{x} \in P_{1}(G). Since weights are rational, they can be written as a convex combination of perfect matchings.


Lemma 1: For a linear function f(x) and a constraint set C:=\text{conv}\{x_1,\cdots,x_t\}, the extremum of f can always be attained at the vertices of the constraint.



In summary, by relaxing x_e \in \{0,1\} \to x_e \geq 0 and adding the Blossom Condition (\forall U \subseteq V, |U| = \text{odd}, \sum_{e \in \delta(U)} x_e \geq 1), we form the (MWPM) problem. If the optimal solution to (MWPM) is integer, then it must also be the optimal solution to (IWPM), thus completely transforming the integer programming problem into a linear programming problem.

title: Maximal Likelihood Decoding
Maximal Likelihood Decoding
text:
3.1 Definitions

M-alternating walk: A sequence (v_0,v_1,\cdots,v_t), t\geq 2 such that \forall i = 1,\cdots,t-1, |M\cap \{v_{i-1}v_i, v_i v_{i+1}\}|=1.
M-flower: An M-alternating walk where t is odd, and \exists i < t such that v_t = v_i, and \forall i,j<t~ v_i \neq v_j. The subgraph formed by (v_{i+1},\cdots,v_t) is called its M-blossom.
M-augmenting path: An M-alternating walk satisfying v_0, v_t \notin M, and is a simple path.







NoteLemma 3 (Structure of Alternating Walks)



Let X be the set of unmatched points. Take an undecomposable M-alternating walk (v_0,\cdots,v_t) with v_0, v_t \in X. Then it is either an M-augmenting path, or it contains an M-flower (v_0,\cdots,v_j), where v_j is the index where the repetition first occurs.


Definition 3 (Contraction and Uncontraction): Given a graph G=(E,V) and V_S \subset V: * Contraction: G \to (G/V_S, G_S), where G/V_S replaces V_S with a single point. * Uncontraction: (G', G_S) \to G, the reverse process of contraction.

title: Maximal Likelihood Decoding
text:
3.2 Algorithm 1 (Blossom)
Input: G = (V,E), \{w_{e}\}. Output: MWPM.

Initialization: \Omega = \{\{v\}|v \in V\}, y(\{v\}) = 0, M = \emptyset, G' = (V, \emptyset).
Loop until M is a perfect matching of G':

Find free points X in G', determine if there exists an M-alternating walk starting from X and ending in X.
If it exists, choose the shortest walk P=(V_P, E_P):

Augmenting path: Update M = M \oplus E_P. End this step.
M-flower: By Lemma 3, it must contain an M-Blossom B.

Take its M-Blossom B=(V_B, E_B).
Contract V_B into a single point in V'.
Update M = M - E_B.
Update dual info \Omega = \Omega \cup \{V_B\}, y(V_B) = 0. End this step.


If it does not exist, classify vertices in V' as V' = S \cup T:

v' \in S \Leftrightarrow \exists odd length M-alt walk from X to v'.
v' \in T \Leftrightarrow \exists even length M-alt walk from X to v'.


Dual Update: 
\begin{cases}
y(v') = y(v') + \delta & \text{if~} v' \in T\\
y(v') = y(v') - \delta & \text{if~} v' \in S
\end{cases}
 Choose the largest \delta such that dual feasibility conditions hold:

\lambda_e \geq 0, \forall e \in E.
y_O \geq 0, \forall O \in \Omega.

Check Boundary:

If (1) hits boundary (new edge \lambda_e=0): Add these edges to E'. End this step.
If (2) hits boundary (y_O=0, O \in \Omega \cap \mathcal{O}(G)): Uncontract Blossom (G', O). End this step.










NoteComplexity Theorem



Algorithm 1 halts after at most 2|V|^2 loops. After halting, uncontracting all Blossoms gives an MWPM of G.








TipComplexity Proof Idea






Dual objective function is monotonically non-decreasing.
Primal/dual feasibility and complementary slackness are maintained throughout.
Upper limit on iteration count:

Augment (Case b-i): At most |V|/2 times.
Uncontract (Case c-iv): At most 2|V| times (hierarchical structure).
Contract (Case b-ii): At most 2|V| times.
Add Edge (Case c-iii): At most 3|V|+1 times.
Total iterations \approx 3.5|V|^2.

Single loop time is at most O(|E|).

title: Maximal Likelihood Decoding
text:
3.3 Regarding Graphs with Boundaries
For graphs with a boundary vertex v_0, the perfect matching covers all vertices except v_0. The formula requires slight adjustments (equality constraints become inequalities, or handled via convex hull optimization).

title: Maximal Likelihood Decoding
text:
4.1 Dual Space and Primal Initialization

Dual space initialization y_v = 0.
Primal space initialization: Mark every vertex as +.
Increase y_v by step size \delta_v.

title: Maximal Likelihood Decoding
text:
4.2 Auxiliary Graph
To effectively manage alternating trees, dynamically maintain an Auxiliary Graph (V_{aux}, E_{aux}): * Nodes: Auxiliary graph node T \in V_{aux} corresponds to an alternating tree in the original graph. * Structure: Stored using adjacency lists. * Priority Queue (PQ): * Node-level PQ (Per tree T): * pq^{++}(T): Edges between + nodes inside tree T. * pq^{+\emptyset}(T): Edges from + nodes in tree T to free points (\emptyset). * pq^{-}(T): - nodes inside tree T that are Blossoms. * Edge-level PQ (Per edge (T, T')): * pq^{++}(T, T'): Edge connecting + point in T and + point in T'. * pq^{+-}(T, T'): Edge connecting + in T to - in T'. * pq^{-+}(T, T'): Edge connecting - in T to + in T'.

title: Maximal Likelihood Decoding
text:
4.3 Variable Management

Node Dual Variables: Store base value \bar{y}_v and tree cumulative quantity \Delta_T.

Real value y_v = \bar{y}_v \mp \Delta_T (depends on +/- mark).

Edge Slack: Store base slack \text{slack}(a).

Real slack adjusted based on \Delta_T of the trees the endpoints belong to.

title: Maximal Likelihood Decoding
text:
4.4 Dynamic Maintenance (GROW Operation)
GROW: When a free matching edge (u,v) is added to tree T and u \to -, v \to - are set: 1. If u is a Blossom, add to pq^{-}(T). 2. Update neighbors of u: Remove from pq^{+\emptyset}, move to pq^{-+} or discard. 3. Update neighbors of v: Remove from pq^{+\emptyset}, move to pq^{++} or pq^{+-}. 4. Lazy Update: Use CURRENT_EDGE pointer to avoid O(|V|^2) static memory overhead.

title: BP-OSD Decoding
text:
The MLD algorithm has the following shortcomings:

Knowing the probability of each error occurring a priori, as in MLD, is not a natural assumption.
The occurrence of each error is mutually unrelated. In quantum error correction codes, this means assuming two Pauli errors are independent.
MLD remains NP-hard for arbitrary error correction codes.

The Belief Propagation algorithm is an approximate decoding algorithm that performs approximate decoding by iteratively updating the probabilities of each vertex.

title: BP-OSD Decoding
text:
3.1 The Message Passing Mechanism
Belief Propagation, often called the sum-product algorithm, is an iterative message-passing algorithm on a factor graph.






TipGoal



The objective is to compute the marginal probability for each bit j: P_1(e_j) = P(e_j = 1 | \mathbf{s}) Given that \mathbf{s} = H \cdot \mathbf{e} is the syndrome of the error. This “soft decision” indicates how likely a specific bit is to be flipped.



3.1.1 Log-Likelihood Ratios (LLR)
To ensure numerical stability during computation, BP operates using Log-Likelihood Ratios rather than raw probabilities.
\text{LLR}(e_j) = \log \left( \frac{P(e_j = 0)}{P(e_j = 1)} \right)

LLR > 0: e_j = 0 is more likely (the bit is probably correct).
LLR < 0: e_j = 1 is more likely (the bit is probably flipped).
|LLR|: The magnitude indicates the confidence level of the decision.

For a channel with error probability p, the initial channel LLR is: p_l = \frac{\log(1 - p)}{p}

title: BP-OSD Decoding
text:
3.2 BP Algorithm: Step-by-Step
The algorithm iterates through specific phases to update beliefs.

3.2.1 Step 1: Initialization
Before any message passing occurs, the only information available is the channel prior. We initialize all messages from data nodes (v_j) to parity nodes (u_i) with the channel LLR.
m_{v_j \to u_i} := p_l \quad \text{for all edges } (v_j, u_i)


3.2.2 Step 2: Parity-to-Data Messages
Each parity node u_i sends a message to each connected data node v_j. This step enforces the parity constraints (XOR logic).
m_{u_i \to v_j} = (-1)^{s_i} \cdot \alpha \cdot \prod_{v'_j \in V(u_i) \setminus v_j} \text{sign}(m_{v'_j \to u_i}) \cdot \min_{v'_j \in V(u_i) \setminus v_j} |m_{v'_j \to u_i}|
Where: * s_i is the i-th syndrome bit. * \alpha = 1 - 2^{-t} is a damping factor at iteration t to aid convergence. * The message excludes the target node v_j (extrinsic information).


3.2.3 Step 3: Data-to-Parity Messages
Each data node v_j collects evidence from the channel and its neighboring parity checks to send an update back to the parity nodes.
m_{v_j \to u_i} = p_l + \sum_{u'_i \in U(v_j) \setminus u_i} m_{u'_i \to v_j}
Intuition: Why exclude u_i? This prevents “echo effects.” If v_j simply returned the information u_i just gave it, positive feedback loops would artificially inflate confidence without adding new evidence.


3.2.4 Step 4: Compute Soft Decisions
We calculate the total posterior belief for bit j by summing the channel prior and all incoming messages (no exclusion).
P_1(e_j) = p_l + \sum_{u_i \in U(v_j)} m_{u_i \to v_j}


3.2.5 Step 5: Make Hard Decisions
We convert the soft LLR beliefs into binary estimates.
 e_j^{\text{BP}} = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } P_1(e_j) < 0 \quad (\text{likely flipped}) \\
0 & \text{otherwise} \quad (\text{likely correct})
\end{cases} 


3.2.6 Step 6: Convergence Check
Finally, we verify if the estimated error vector satisfies the syndrome equation.
H \cdot \mathbf{e}^{\text{BP}} = \mathbf{s} \quad ?

If Yes: The algorithm has converged; return \mathbf{e}^{\text{BP}}.
If No: Return to Step 2 and repeat until the maximum iteration count is reached.

title: BP-OSD Decoding
text:
3.3 4. Detailed Code Implementation
Below is the Python implementation of the core logic. The code has been modularized to separately handle model loading, BP inference, and OSD post-processing.

3.3.1 4.1 Environment Preparation and Data Loading
First, we need to load the error physical model (DEM) and the test data.
import numpy as np
from bpdecoderplus.pytorch_bp import (
    read_model_file, BeliefPropagation,
    belief_propagate, compute_marginals, apply_evidence
)
from bpdecoderplus.dem import load_dem, build_parity_check_matrix
from bpdecoderplus.syndrome import load_syndrome_database
from bpdecoderplus.osd import OSDDecoder

# 1. Load factor graph model (.uai) and error model (.dem)
model = read_model_file('datasets/sc_d3_r3_p0010_z.uai')
dem = load_dem('datasets/sc_d3_r3_p0010_z.dem')

# 2. Load pre-generated Syndrome dataset
syndromes, observables, _ = load_syndrome_database('datasets/sc_d3_r3_p0010_z.npz')

print(f"Test set size: {len(syndromes)}")


3.3.2 4.2 Initialize Decoder
Here, we construct the parity check matrix and initialize the BP and OSD decoder instances.
# Initialize BP decoder
bp = BeliefPropagation(model)

# Construct parity check matrix H, which is the basis for OSD equation solving
H, priors, obs_flip = build_parity_check_matrix(dem)

# Initialize OSD decoder
# Note: This is the Robust OSD module we rewrote specifically to solve the "rank deficiency" problem
osd = OSDDecoder(H)

print(f"Parity check matrix shape: {H.shape}")


3.3.3 4.3 Decoding Loop (The Loop)
This is the core of the entire program. For each test sample, we sequentially execute BP and OSD.
predictions = []
# Iterate through the first 1000 samples
for idx, syndrome in enumerate(syndromes[:1000]):
    
    # --- Step 1: Run BP (Detective Phase) ---
    # Inject Syndrome into the factor graph
    evidence = {i+1: int(syndrome[i]) for i in range(len(syndrome))}
    bp_ev = apply_evidence(bp, evidence)
    
    # Iteratively calculate marginal probabilities (Marginals)
    state, _ = belief_propagate(bp_ev, max_iter=20, tol=1e-6, damping=0.2)
    marginals = compute_marginals(state, bp_ev)
    
    # --- Step 2: Run OSD (Judge Phase) ---
    # Determine the index range of error variables
    num_detectors = len(syndromes[0])
    error_var_start = num_detectors + 1

    # Call OSD solver
    # osd.solve will sort columns based on marginals and solve the linear equation system
    # osd_order=0 indicates the basic OSD-0 algorithm
    estimated_errors = osd.solve(syndrome, marginals, error_var_start, osd_order=0)
    
    # --- Step 3: Verification ---
    # Check if a logical error occurred
    predictions.append(np.dot(estimated_errors, obs_flip) % 2)

# Calculate accuracy
logical_error_rate = np.mean(np.array(predictions) != observables[:1000])
print(f"Logical error rate: {logical_error_rate:.4f}")
print(f"Decoder accuracy: {(1 - logical_error_rate):.4f}")

title: Virtual Distillation for Quantum Error Mitigation
text:
Abstract
The manuscript addresses the fundamental limit of estimating the expectation value \text{Tr}(\rho H) of an observable H using a quantum state \rho, specifically when restricted to shallow parameterized quantum circuits (PQC). - Proposes practical algorithms (Greedy Projection and Tensor Network decomposition), - The derivation of a sample complexity lower bound that depends on the circuit’s depth and structure.






NoteDefinition: The Circuit Capability Parameter \delta(H_0)



Let U_L(\theta) be an L-depth parameterized quantum circuit acting on n qubits. Let \mathcal{S} be the set of all states reachable by applying the adjoint circuit to computational basis states: \mathcal{S} := \{ U_L(\theta)^\dagger \ket{b} \mid \forall \theta, b \in \{0,1\}^n \} Let H_0 = H - \frac{\text{Tr}(H)}{2^n}\mathbb{I} be the traceless part of the target observable. The parameter \delta(H_0) is defined as the square of the maximum expectation value achievable within the set \mathcal{S}: \delta(H_0) := \sup_{\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal{S}} \bra{\psi}H_0\ket{\psi}^2








ImportantTheorem (Sample Complexity Lower Bound for Shallow Circuits)



For any single-copy adaptive strategy relying solely on the parameterized circuit U_L(\theta) and computational basis measurements, the number of samples T required to estimate \text{Tr}(\rho H) to additive error \epsilon with success probability \geq 2/3 is lower bounded by: T = \Omega\left(\frac{\text{Tr}(H_0^2)^2}{\epsilon^2 \delta(H_0) 4^n}\right)


Toy Example: Consider a single qubit (n=1) and a target observable H = Z (Pauli-Z). H_0 = Z.

Good Circuit : \mathcal{S} includes \ket{0} and \ket{1}, \bra{0}Z\ket{0} = 1, \delta(H_0) = 1^2 = 1.
Bad Circuit: \mathcal{S} = \{ \ket{+}, \ket{-} \}, \bra{+}Z\ket{+} = 0, \delta(H_0) = 0.



Proof of Lower bounds
Here, we dissect the proof of Theorem 1 (Proposition 3 in the text), which utilizes information-theoretic techniques to lower bound the hardness of the problem.
Proof Strategy: Le Cam’s Two-Point Method (Reduction to State Discrimination).






NoteDefinition



Hard-to-Distinguish Scenario The authors reduce the estimation problem to a discrimination problem. If we cannot distinguish between two specific states \rho_1 and \rho_2 using T samples, we certainly cannot estimate the expectation value accurately enough to tell them apart.

The maximally mixed state \rho_1 = \frac{\mathbb{I}}{2^n}.
A mixed state slightly biased by the Hamiltonian: \rho_x = \frac{\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon H_x}{2^n} where H_x is a version of H scaled by a small parameter a related to error \epsilon.

title: Magic based on Pauli spectrum
text:
Abstract
This paper defines a measure of magicness for pure states, introduces the Operator Magic (OSE) for an operation U, and highlights its properties:

It is subsystem additive, faithful, and invariant under Clifford operations.
It reflects the minimum number of T gates in circuit U and also constitutes a lower bound on the unitary stabilizer nullity of U.
It analytically calculates how the OSE of a local operator evolves over time under the XXZ Hamiltonian.
It analytically computes the OSE for Haar random unitaries.

title: Magic based on Pauli spectrum
text:
SRE and OSE
Since \sum_{P}\text{tr}^2(O P) = 2^n\text{tr}(O^2), then p_{\psi}(P) = [2^n\text{tr}(O^2)]^{-1} \text{tr}^2(O P) is a probability distribution.
Specifically,

For a pure state \psi, the function p_{\psi}(x) = \frac{1}{2^n} \text{tr}^2(\psi P_x) is a probability distribution, and stabilizer states uniformly support on |S| = 2^n stabilizers S.
For an operator O with \mathrm{tr}(OO^\dagger) = d, the function p_{O}(x) = \frac{1}{4^n} \text{tr}^2(O P_x) is a probability distribution, and Pauli operators are distributed over only one element.

Thus, the collision probability of this distribution clearly describes the stabilizer properties of pure states. We can also compute higher-order collisions to obtain Rényi-k stabilizer entropy.






NoteDefinition: Stabilizer Renyi Entropy



The k-stabilizer-Rényi Entropy for a pure state \psi is defined as: \begin{align*}
\mathrm{SRE}_k(\psi) &= \frac{1}{1 - k} \left[\ln \left(\sum_x p_{\psi}^k(x)\right) - \ln \left(\frac{1}{2^{kn}} \cdot 2^n\right)\right]= \frac{1}{1 - k} \mathrm{tr}(O^{\otimes k} T^{A}_{(12)(34)} \otimes T^{\bar{A}}_{(14)(23)})
\end{align*} For an operator O, the linearized entanglement is given by: 
E_{\mathrm{lin}}(O) = \mathrm{tr}(O^{\otimes 4} \cdot T^{A}_{(12)(34)} \otimes T^{\bar{A}}_{(14)(23)})



We compute the above average for TE-matching operators, considering O under Clifford operations. For simplicity, we consider O = \ket{0}\!\bra{0}^{\otimes r} \otimes Z^{n - r}. Using the result of the Clifford 4-fold average, we calculate: 
\mathrm{tr}[O^{\otimes 4} \Lambda^{\pm} T_{\pi}] = \pm d^{-2} \sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} \mathrm{tr}[(O \cdot P)^{\otimes 4} T_{\pi}] + \delta_{\pm,-} \mathrm{tr}(O^{\otimes 4} T_{\pi})
 It is worth noting the computation of \sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} (O \cdot P)^{\otimes 4} using symplectic notation for Pauli operators: 
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} \left[(\ket{0}\!\bra{0}^{\otimes s} \otimes Z^{n - s}) \cdot \sigma_{\mathbf r} \right]^{\otimes 4} &= \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}}\delta_{\mathbf{r}^{(s)}_x , \mathbf{0}^{(s)}} \left[\ket{0}\!\bra{0}^{\otimes s} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}^{(n-s)} + \mathbf{0}^{(n-s)}\mathbf{1}^{(n-s)}}\right]^{\otimes 4}\\
&=2^{s}\delta_{\mathbf{r}^{(s)}_x , \mathbf{0}^{(s)}}\sum_{\mathbf{r}^{(n-s)} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n-2s}} \left[\ket{0}\!\bra{0}^{\otimes s} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}^{(n-s)} + \mathbf{0}^{(n-s)}\mathbf{1}^{(n-s)}}\right]^{\otimes 4}
\end{aligned}

Dividing the permutation group S_4 into two categories, one containing only even cycles: [22] or [4], which totals to C_{4}^2/2 + 2C_3^2 = 9. The other category contains odd cycles: [1111],[211],[31], totaling 1 + C_4^2 + 2\times C_4^3 = 15.
