text: Abstract: Is there an advantage to using Clifford formalism in a vectorized space compared to using it directly?

title: Operator Stabilizer Formalism
text:
OSF and Its Advantages
We know that Clifford C performs a swap between Pauli operators P \to CPC^\dagger. Consider the Choi state of a Pauli operator |P\rangle\!\rangle \in \mathcal{H} \otimes \mathcal{H}^*, which undergoes a transformation under the action of C \otimes C^{*}: 
|P\rangle\!\rangle \to |Q\rangle\!\rangle = C \otimes C^{*}|P\rangle\!\rangle
 If we can map the Choi state of a Pauli operator |P\rangle\!\rangle through a unitary transformation U \in \mathcal{H} \otimes \mathcal{H}^* to the computational basis one-to-one, then all Clifford operations’ transformations U C \otimes C^* U^\dagger become coherence non-increasing gates. We find that such a transformation U exists:
\begin{align*}
    &\{I/\sqrt{2},Z/\sqrt{2},X/\sqrt{2},Y/\sqrt{2}\} \\
    &\xrightarrow{\mathcal{V}}\{\frac{\ket{00}_{ab}+\ket{11}_{ab}}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{\ket{00}_{ab}-\ket{11}_{ab}}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{\ket{01}_{ab}+\ket{10}_{ab}}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{-i\ket{01}_{ab}+i\ket{10}_{ab}}{\sqrt{2}}\}\\
    &\xrightarrow{U = CS_{ba}^\dagger H_bCNOT_{ba}}\{\ket{0}_a\ket{0}_b, \ket{0}_a\ket{1}_b, \ket{1}_a\ket{0}_b,\ket{1}_a\ket{1}_b\},\\
    &\xrightarrow{\mathcal{V}^{-1}}\{\ket{0}\!\bra{0}, \ket{0}\!\bra{1}, \ket{1}\!\bra{0},\ket{1}\!\bra{1}\}.
\end{align*}
Here, each single-qubit Pauli operator becomes a two-qubit system with qubits a,b, and \{I,X,Y,Z\} correspond to \ket{\mathbf{P}} \in \{\ket{00},\ket{10},\ket{01},\ket{11}\} respectively. This mapping precisely associates a,b with the number of X and Z operators. Under this substitution, it can be shown that common Clifford gates transform as follows:
\begin{align*}
    CNOT_{12}(\cdot)CNOT_{12} &\to \textbf{CNOT}_{a_1a_2} \textbf{CNOT}_{b_2b_1}(\cdot), \\
    S^\dagger(\cdot)S &\to \mathbf{CZ}_{ab}\mathbf{CNOT}_{ab}(\cdot),\\
    H(\cdot)H &\to \mathbf{CZ}_{ab}\textbf{SWAP}_{ab}(\cdot),\\
    T^\dagger(\cdot)T &\to \textbf{Z}_b\textbf{CH}_{ab}(\cdot),
\end{align*}
Thus, the problem of computing \mathrm{tr}(P C\ket{0}\!\bra{0}^{\otimes n}C^\dagger) is now transformed into calculating 2^{n/2} \bra{0+}^{\otimes n } \mathbf{C} \ket{\mathbf{P}}.
Note that the Original Physical Circuit has input on the left and output on the right. Its input is in the computational basis (representing the initial state), and its output is a Pauli operator (indicating which Pauli operator’s expectation value we care about). The Dual Circuit has input on the right and output on the left, both derived from the Original Physical Circuit. Each dual circuit input’s computational basis corresponds to the original physical circuit’s Pauli outputs according to the rules above, and each dual circuit’s final state (leftmost) is converted from the original physical circuit’s computational basis inputs, for example |0\rangle \to \frac{\mathbb{I} + Z}{2} \to \sqrt{2^{-1}}(\ket{00} + \ket{01}) = \ket{0}\ket{+}.
To this end, we can write a Python script to visualize the transformation of these circuits. Using this code, I demonstrated three types of circuits that are difficult to handle with ordinary Stabilizer Formalism but are simple within the OSF framework.


Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, QuantumRegister, ClassicalRegister
from qiskit.circuit import Qubit, Clbit

class DualCircuitConverter:
    def __init__(self, original_circuit: QuantumCircuit, 
                 input_state: str = None, 
                 output_pauli: str = None):
        """
        Initialize the converter.
        
        Args:
            original_circuit: Input physical circuit
            input_state: (Optional) Initial state of the original circuit, e.g., "00".
            output_pauli: (Optional) Output Pauli operator of the original circuit, e.g., "ZZ".
        """
        self.orig_qc = original_circuit
        self.n_qubits = original_circuit.num_qubits
        
        self.input_state_str = input_state
        self.output_pauli_str = output_pauli
        
        self.q_map = {q: i for i, q in enumerate(original_circuit.qubits)}
        
        self.dual_qc = None
        self._build_dual_circuit()

    def _build_dual_circuit(self):
        """
        Core translation logic: Build dual circuit according to Symplectic Mapping.
        Contains: Dual Input (Source) -> Reversed Unitaries -> Dual Output (Sink)
        """
        reg_a = QuantumRegister(self.n_qubits, 'a')
        reg_b = QuantumRegister(self.n_qubits, 'b')
        
        registers = [reg_a, reg_b]
        if self.input_state_str:
            creg = ClassicalRegister(2 * self.n_qubits, 'meas')
            registers.append(creg)
        
        self.dual_qc = QuantumCircuit(*registers)
        
        # ==========================================
        # 1. Set Dual Input (corresponds to Original Output Pauli)
        # ==========================================
        if self.output_pauli_str:
            if len(self.output_pauli_str) != self.n_qubits:
                raise ValueError("Output Pauli string length must match num_qubits.")
                
            for i, p_char in enumerate(self.output_pauli_str):
                p_char = p_char.upper()
                if p_char == 'Z':
                    self.dual_qc.x(reg_b[i])
                elif p_char == 'X':
                    self.dual_qc.x(reg_a[i])
                elif p_char == 'Y':
                    self.dual_qc.x(reg_a[i])
                    self.dual_qc.x(reg_b[i])
            
            self.dual_qc.barrier(label='Dual Input')

        # ==========================================
        # 2. Traverse and build Unitary in reverse
        # ==========================================
        for instruction in reversed(self.orig_qc.data):
            op_name = instruction.operation.name
            qubits = instruction.qubits
            
            indices = [self.q_map[q] for q in qubits]
            
            if op_name == 'h':
                idx = indices[0]
                self.dual_qc.swap(reg_a[idx], reg_b[idx])
                self.dual_qc.cz(reg_a[idx], reg_b[idx])
                
            elif op_name == 's':
                idx = indices[0]
                self.dual_qc.cx(reg_a[idx], reg_b[idx])
                self.dual_qc.cz(reg_a[idx], reg_b[idx])
                
            elif op_name == 't':
                idx = indices[0]
                self.dual_qc.ch(reg_a[idx], reg_b[idx]) 
                self.dual_qc.z(reg_b[idx])
                
            elif op_name == 'cx':
                c_idx, t_idx = indices[0], indices[1]
                self.dual_qc.cx(reg_a[c_idx], reg_a[t_idx])
                self.dual_qc.cx(reg_b[t_idx], reg_b[c_idx])
                
            elif op_name == 'barrier':
                mapped_qubits = []
                for idx in indices:
                    mapped_qubits.append(reg_a[idx])
                    mapped_qubits.append(reg_b[idx])
                self.dual_qc.barrier(*mapped_qubits)

        # ==========================================
        # 3. Set Dual Output (corresponds to Original Input State)
        # ==========================================
        if self.input_state_str:
            self.dual_qc.barrier(label='Dual Output')
            if len(self.input_state_str) != self.n_qubits:
                raise ValueError("Input state string length must match num_qubits.")

            for i, s_char in enumerate(self.input_state_str):
                if s_char == '0':
                    self.dual_qc.h(reg_b[i])
                elif s_char == '1':
                    self.dual_qc.h(reg_b[i]) 
            
            self.dual_qc.measure(reg_a, creg[:self.n_qubits])
            self.dual_qc.measure(reg_b, creg[self.n_qubits:])

    def draw_comparison(self, scale=1.0):
        """
        Draw side-by-side comparison. Title updates automatically if boundary conditions are defined.
        """
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12 * scale, 10 * scale))
        
        self.orig_qc.draw('mpl', ax=axes[0], style='iqp')
        
        in_txt = f"|{self.input_state_str}>" if self.input_state_str else "State"
        out_txt = f"<{self.output_pauli_str}>" if self.output_pauli_str else "Pauli"
        axes[0].set_title(f"Original Circuit: Input {in_txt} $\\rightarrow$ Measure {out_txt}", fontsize=13)
        axes[0].set_ylabel("Time $\\rightarrow$")

        self.dual_qc.draw('mpl', ax=axes[1], style='iqp', fold=-1)
        
        dual_in_txt = f"State({self.output_pauli_str})" if self.output_pauli_str else "Input"
        dual_out_txt = f"Project({self.input_state_str})" if self.input_state_str else "Output"
        axes[1].set_title(f"Dual Circuit: Input {dual_in_txt} $\\rightarrow$ Measure {dual_out_txt}", fontsize=13)
        axes[1].set_ylabel("Time $\\leftarrow$ (Reversed)")
        
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

# ==========================================
# Test case: Complete transformation with input and output
# ==========================================
if __name__ == "__main__":
    qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
    
    # Bell State
    qc.h(0)
    qc.s(1)
    qc.cx(0, 1)
    qc.barrier()
    
    # Phase gates
    qc.t(0)
    qc.t(1)
    qc.barrier()
    
    # Interference
    qc.cx(1, 0)
    qc.h(1)

    # Scenario: Original input |00>, we want to measure the expectation value of operator YZ
    converter = DualCircuitConverter(qc, input_state="00", output_pauli="YZ")
    
    # Expected result:
    # - Dual left side (Input): Corresponds to YZ.
    #   q0(Y) -> a0=1, b0=1 (X on a, X on b)
    #   q1(Z) -> a1=0, b1=1 (X on b)
    # - Middle: Gate sequence reversed (S -> CX -> H)
    # - Dual right side (Output): Corresponds to 00.
    #   H gate will be present in the b register for projection measurement
    converter.draw_comparison()









The advantages above stem from a special construction, allowing us to notice that the \mathbf{CH} gates in OSF can be simplified into H gates. Thus, the entire circuit becomes a Clifford circuit. A reasonable question is: For general circuits, how do we identify unnecessary T-gates and eliminate them?

title: Operator Stabilizer Formalism
text:
Simulating Noisy Circuits
Consider whether the above setup can be used for noisy circuits. This type of noise has been studied extensively, including:

Pauli-path simulation truncation
Random percolation based on graph states

Consider the simplest form of Pauli noise, \Lambda(\rho) = \sum_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_{2}^{2n}} 2^{-n}\lambda_{\mathbf{r}} \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \mathrm{tr}\left[\rho \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \right], which corresponds to a non-unitary matrix: \mathbf{\Lambda} := \sum_{P} 2^{-n}\lambda_{\mathbf{r}} \ket{\mathbf{r}} \!\bra{\mathbf{r}}. For local noise, it can even be written in the form \mathbf{\Lambda} = \bigotimes_{i=1}^n \Omega_i.
This matrix operation on quantum states is not a Clifford operation; forcing its use within the Clifford formalism would decompose it into an exponentially large sum of Cliffords, which introduces too much magic to the circuit and makes simulation exponentially hard.
If we adopt method 2 above, for the mean \langle P \rangle = \mathrm{tr}(\Lambda\circ\mathcal{U}_d \cdots \Lambda\circ\mathcal{U}_1[\rho] \cdot P):

First, convert it to an amplitude of a computational circuit using OSF: \langle P \rangle  =\bra{0+}^{\otimes n} 2^{n/2} \prod_{i=1}^d (\mathbf{\Lambda} \cdot \mathbf{U}_i)\ket{\mathbf{P}}
Then, move all the noise to act last: 
\langle P \rangle  = 2^{n/2}\bra{0+}^{\otimes n} \left(\prod_{i=1}^d \mathbf{\Lambda}_i \right) \cdot \left(\prod_{i=1}^d \mathbf{U}_i\right) \ket{\mathbf{P}}, \mathbf{\Lambda}_i := \left(\prod_{k = 1}^i \mathbf{U}_k \right)\mathbf{\Lambda} \left(\prod_{k = 1}^i \mathbf{U}_k \right)^\dagger


If the circuit \mathcal{U}_i does not contain a T gate, then it is manageable because each \mathbf{U}_i is an operation that does not generate superposition, and matrix \mathbf{\Lambda}_i will remain diagonal with each mapping \lambda^{(i)}_{\mathbf{r}}: \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}  \to \mathbb{R} being efficiently computable. This is entirely equivalent to tracking Pauli operators and updating the suppression of Pauli noise on these operators.
When a \mathbf{CH} gate exists in the circuit, it can be seen as splitting the computational basis \ket{P}. However, this is completely equivalent to method 1 above. Another approach is to examine updates: 
\mathbf{CH} \cdot \mathbf{\Lambda} \cdot \mathbf{CH}

However, note that this difficulty is purely classical. Consider introducing classical randomness into the OSF to accomplish this task.

title: Classical Shadows Based on Locally-Entangled Measurements
text: Citation: Matteo Ippoliti, “Classical shadows based on locally-entangled measurements”, Quantum 8, 1293 (2024)

title: Classical Shadows Based on Locally-Entangled Measurements
text:
Abstract and Overview
This paper introduces Bell shadows and related protocols that use locally-entangled measurements (rather than single-qubit measurements) for classical shadow tomography. The key innovation is using two-qubit Bell measurements, which achieves a quadratic improvement in sample complexity (from \sim 3^k to \sim 3^{k/2}) for compatible operators, at the cost of making some operators unlearnable. The paper shows how tuning the amount of entanglement creates a family of protocols interpolating between Pauli and Bell shadows.
Main contributions: 1. Bell shadows protocol using two-qubit entangled measurements 2. Characterization of compatible operators and their improved sample complexity 3. Extension to n-qubit GHZ measurements achieving \sim (3/2)^k scaling 4. Comparison with shallow shadows showing competitive performance

title: Classical Shadows Based on Locally-Entangled Measurements
text:
1.1 Rigorous Definitions & Intuitions






NoteDefinition 1: Shadow Channel



Given an ensemble of random unitaries \mathcal{U}, the shadow channel \mathcal{M} is the linear map relating the quantum state \rho to the expected snapshot: 
\mathbb{E}_{U \sim \mathcal{U}, b \sim U\rho U^\dagger}[\hat{\sigma}] = \mathcal{M}(\rho)
 where \hat{\sigma} = U^\dagger |b\rangle\langle b| U is a snapshot obtained by measuring U\rho U^\dagger in the computational basis with outcome b.
The inverted snapshot is defined as \hat{\rho} = \mathcal{M}^{-1}(\hat{\sigma}), which satisfies \mathbb{E}[\hat{\rho}] = \rho by construction.



Intuition & Example
Why this definition? The shadow channel \mathcal{M} captures how the measurement protocol “depolarizes” the quantum state. By inverting this channel, we can construct unbiased estimators for state properties.
Toy Example: For random Pauli measurements (measuring each qubit in X, Y, or Z basis randomly), the shadow channel factors as: 
\mathcal{M} = \mathcal{E}_1^{\otimes N}
 where each single-qubit channel \mathcal{E}_1 acts on Pauli matrices as: 
\mathcal{E}_1(\sigma^0) = \sigma^0, \quad \mathcal{E}_1(\sigma^\alpha) = \frac{1}{3}\sigma^\alpha \text{ for } \alpha \in \{x,y,z\}

This means the identity is preserved, but traceless Paulis are depolarized by a factor of 1/3 (because only 1 out of 3 random basis choices “hits” a given Pauli).
Physical interpretation: The shadow channel represents the information loss due to randomized measurements. The factor 1/3 arises because we randomly choose among 3 bases, and only the correct choice contributes useful information.







NoteDefinition 2: Shadow Norm



For a Pauli operator P in an N-qubit system with Pauli-invariant measurement ensemble, the shadow norm is: 
\|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2 = \frac{1}{2^N} \text{Tr}(P \mathcal{M}^{-1}(P))

This norm determines the sample complexity for learning \langle P \rangle to accuracy \epsilon: approximately \|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2/\epsilon^2 measurements are needed.




Intuition & Example
Why this definition? The shadow norm quantifies how “difficult” it is to learn an operator. The inverse channel \mathcal{M}^{-1} appears because we construct inverted snapshots, amplifying the depolarization effect.
Toy Example: For random Pauli measurements and a weight-k Pauli operator P: 
\|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2 = 3^k

This is because \mathcal{M}^{-1} inverts the depolarization: \mathcal{E}_1^{-1}(\sigma^\alpha) = 3\sigma^\alpha for \alpha \neq 0. Since P has k nontrivial Paulis, we get (1/3)^{-k} = 3^k.
Concrete calculation: For P = X_1 Z_2 (weight k=2): 
\mathcal{M}^{-1}(X_1 Z_2) = \mathcal{E}_1^{-1}(X_1) \otimes \mathcal{E}_1^{-1}(Z_2) = 3X_1 \otimes 3Z_2 = 9(X_1 Z_2)
 Thus \|X_1 Z_2\|_{\text{sh}}^2 = \frac{1}{4}\text{Tr}(X_1 Z_2 \cdot 9 X_1 Z_2) = \frac{9 \cdot 4}{4} = 9 = 3^2. ✓







NoteDefinition 3: Dimer Covering and Compatible Operators



A dimer covering is a partition of the N qubits into N/2 pairs (dimers).
A Pauli operator P is compatible with a dimer covering if its support intersects each dimer in either 0 or 2 sites. Otherwise, P is incompatible.




Intuition & Example
Why this definition? Bell measurements on a dimer can only measure operators that act nontrivially on both qubits or neither. Operators acting on only one qubit of a dimer cannot be learned.
Toy Example: Consider 4 qubits with dimer covering (1,2) and (3,4):
Compatible operators: - X_1 Z_2 (acts on both qubits of dimer 1, none of dimer 2) ✓ - X_1 Z_2 \otimes Y_3 Y_4 (acts on both qubits of both dimers) ✓ - I (acts on no qubits) ✓
Incompatible operators: - X_1 (acts on only one qubit of dimer 1) ✗ - X_1 Z_3 (acts on one qubit from each dimer) ✗
Geometric interpretation: On a 1D chain with nearest-neighbor dimers, compatible operators have “even support” - they touch each dimer an even number of times (0 or 2).







NoteDefinition 4: Bell Shadow Channel



For Bell measurements on dimers with local scrambling, the shadow channel factors as: 
\mathcal{M} = \mathcal{E}_2^{\otimes N/2}
 where each two-qubit channel \mathcal{E}_2 acts on a dimer as: 
\mathcal{E}_2(\sigma^\alpha \otimes \sigma^\beta) = \lambda_{\alpha\beta} \sigma^\alpha \otimes \sigma^\beta
 with eigenvalues: 
\lambda_{00} = 1, \quad \lambda_{0\bullet} = \lambda_{\bullet 0} = 0, \quad \lambda_{\bullet\bullet} = \frac{1}{3}
 where 0 denotes identity and \bullet denotes any traceless Pauli \{x,y,z\}.




Intuition & Example
Why these eigenvalues? - \lambda_{00} = 1: Identity is always preserved - \lambda_{0\bullet} = 0: Operators acting on only one qubit cannot be measured (incompatible!) - \lambda_{\bullet\bullet} = 1/3: For weight-2 operators, Bell measurements “hit” 3 out of 9 possibilities
Toy Example: For a dimer, there are 9 weight-2 Pauli operators: \{X,Y,Z\} \otimes \{X,Y,Z\}. A Bell measurement outcome (e.g., |XX\rangle = +1, |YZ\rangle = -1) tells us about 3 operators: - XX = +1 (measured directly) - YZ = -1 (measured directly) - ZY = XX \cdot YZ = -1 (inferred)
So we learn 3 out of 9 operators, giving probability 1/3 per dimer.
Verification: For P = X_1 X_2 on a single dimer: 
\mathcal{E}_2(X_1 X_2) = \lambda_{\bullet\bullet} X_1 X_2 = \frac{1}{3} X_1 X_2
 Thus \mathcal{E}_2^{-1}(X_1 X_2) = 3 X_1 X_2, giving \|X_1 X_2\|_{\text{sh}}^2 = 3 = 3^{2/2}. ✓

title: Classical Shadows Based on Locally-Entangled Measurements
text:
1.2 Main Theorems & Key Insights






ImportantTheorem 1: Bell Shadow Sample Complexity



For a weight-k Pauli operator P that is compatible with the dimer covering, the Bell shadow norm is: 
\|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2 = 3^{k/2}

This represents a quadratic improvement over random Pauli measurements (3^k).
For incompatible operators, \|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2 = \infty (not learnable).



Intuition of Validity
Why quadratic improvement? The key insight is that Bell measurements provide information about pairs of qubits simultaneously.
For a weight-k operator compatible with the dimer covering: - It acts nontrivially on k/2 dimers (since it touches each dimer on 0 or 2 sites) - Each dimer contributes a factor of 3 to the shadow norm (from \lambda_{\bullet\bullet}^{-1} = 3) - Total: (3)^{k/2} = 3^{k/2}
Comparison with Pauli shadows: - Pauli: Each of k qubits contributes factor 3 → 3^k - Bell: Each of k/2 dimers contributes factor 3 → 3^{k/2}
Why incompatible operators fail? If P acts on only one qubit of a dimer, that dimer contributes \lambda_{0\bullet}^{-1} = 1/0 = \infty.
Verification with toy example: For P = X_1 Z_2 \otimes Y_3 Y_4 (weight k=4, compatible with dimers (1,2) and (3,4)): 
\|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2 = \lambda_{\bullet\bullet}^{-1} \cdot \lambda_{\bullet\bullet}^{-1} = 3 \cdot 3 = 9 = 3^{4/2}

This means we need \sim 9/\epsilon^2 measurements instead of \sim 81/\epsilon^2 for Pauli shadows - a 9× improvement!







ImportantTheorem 2: Fraction of Learnable Operators



The fraction of Pauli operators that are compatible with a dimer covering is: 
\frac{10^{N/2}}{4^N} \approx 0.79^N

This fraction decreases exponentially with system size.




Intuition of Validity
Why this fraction? For each dimer, we can place: - \sigma^0 \otimes \sigma^0 (1 option) - identity on both - \sigma^\alpha \otimes \sigma^\beta with \alpha, \beta \in \{x,y,z\} (9 options) - nontrivial on both
Total: 1 + 9 = 10 compatible options per dimer.
Since there are N/2 dimers and each can independently have 10 options: 
\text{Compatible operators} = 10^{N/2}

Total Pauli operators: 4^N (each qubit can have \{I, X, Y, Z\}).
Fraction: 10^{N/2}/4^N = (10/16)^{N/2} = (5/8)^{N/2} \approx 0.79^N.
Trade-off interpretation: Bell shadows sacrifice exponentially many operators to achieve quadratic speedup on the remaining ones. This is worthwhile when the operators of interest are geometrically local and compatible with a natural dimer covering.







ImportantTheorem 3: GHZ Shadow Scaling



For n-qubit GHZ measurements (measuring n qubits in the GHZ basis), compatible weight-k operators achieve: 
\|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2 = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^k

This is the best possible scaling, but applies to an increasingly restricted set of operators as n grows.




Intuition of Validity
Why (3/2)^k? GHZ measurements on n qubits can measure 2^{n-1} out of 3^n weight-n operators (the stabilizer group of GHZ states has size 2^n, but we exclude the identity).
For large n, the ratio approaches: 
\frac{2^{n-1}}{3^n} \approx \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^n

For a weight-k operator touching k/n groups of n qubits: 
\|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2 \approx \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^k

Comparison: - Pauli shadows: 3^k - Bell shadows (n=2): 3^{k/2} = (\sqrt{3})^k \approx 1.73^k - GHZ shadows (large n): (3/2)^k = 1.5^k
Trade-off: As n increases, the scaling improves but the fraction of learnable operators decreases even faster: \sim (2/3)^{nN/n} = (2/3)^N for n-qubit groups.

title: Classical Shadows Based on Locally-Entangled Measurements
section: 2.1 Derivation of Bell Shadow Channel Eigenvalues
text:
2.1 Derivation of Bell Shadow Channel Eigenvalues






NoteDetailed Derivation (Click to expand)





We derive the eigenvalues \lambda_{\alpha\beta} of the Bell shadow channel \mathcal{E}_2.
Step 1: Express the channel
The channel acts on a dimer as: 
\mathcal{E}_2(\rho) = \sum_\alpha \int \text{d}u\, \text{d}v\, \langle\Phi^\alpha| u\otimes v \rho (u \otimes v)^\dagger |\Phi^\alpha\rangle \times (u \otimes v)^\dagger |\Phi^\alpha\rangle\langle\Phi^\alpha| u\otimes v

where \text{d}u, \text{d}v are Haar measures over U(2) (using 2-design property of Clifford gates), and |\Phi^\alpha\rangle are the four Bell states.
Step 2: Diagonality in Pauli basis
Due to local scrambling with random Clifford gates, the channel is diagonal in the Pauli basis: 
\mathcal{E}_2(\sigma^\alpha \otimes \sigma^\beta) = \lambda_{\alpha\beta} \sigma^\alpha \otimes \sigma^\beta

Step 3: Compute eigenvalues
The eigenvalue is: 
\lambda_{\alpha\beta} = \frac{1}{4} \text{Tr}[\sigma^\alpha \otimes \sigma^\beta \mathcal{E}_2(\sigma^\alpha\otimes \sigma^\beta)]

Substituting the channel expression and using \langle\Phi^0| B\otimes C|\Phi^0\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\text{Tr}(BC^T): 
\lambda_{\alpha\beta} = \frac{1}{4} \int\text{d}u\, \text{d}v\, [\text{Tr}(u\sigma^\alpha u^\dagger v \sigma^\beta v^\dagger)]^2

Key observation: The integrand depends only on u^\dagger v, so one rotation is redundant. We can integrate over u^\dagger v alone.
Step 4: Evaluate specific cases
Case 1: \alpha = \beta = 0 (both identity) 
\lambda_{00} = \frac{1}{4} \int\text{d}u\, [\text{Tr}(u u^\dagger)]^2 = \frac{1}{4} \cdot 4 = 1

Case 2: \alpha = 0, \beta \neq 0 (one identity, one traceless) 
\lambda_{0\bullet} = \frac{1}{4} \int\text{d}u\, [\text{Tr}(u \sigma^\beta u^\dagger)]^2

Since \sigma^\beta is traceless and u is Haar-random, \text{Tr}(u \sigma^\beta u^\dagger) = \text{Tr}(\sigma^\beta) = 0. Thus \lambda_{0\bullet} = 0.
Case 3: \alpha, \beta \neq 0 (both traceless)
Using the 2-design property, for traceless Paulis: 
\int\text{d}u\, (u\sigma^\alpha u^\dagger)_{ij} (u\sigma^\beta u^\dagger)_{kl} = \frac{1}{3}\delta_{\alpha\beta}(\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl} - \frac{1}{2}\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl})

After calculation: 
\lambda_{\bullet\bullet} = \frac{1}{3}

This completes the derivation of Eq. (1) in the paper.

title: Classical Shadows Based on Locally-Entangled Measurements
section: 2.2 Sample Complexity Analysis for Specific Operators
text:
2.2 Sample Complexity Analysis for Specific Operators






NoteApplication to 1D Pauli Strings (Click to expand)





Setup: Consider a 1D chain with N qubits. We want to learn Pauli string operators of the form P = \bigotimes_{i=1}^k \sigma^{\alpha_i}_{x_i} where x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_k are the support sites.
Dimer covering strategy: Use two dimer coverings: 1. Even covering: Dimers (1,2), (3,4), (5,6), \ldots 2. Odd covering: Dimers (2,3), (4,5), (6,7), \ldots
Key observation: Any Pauli string of even length k is compatible with at least one of these two coverings.
Proof: - If k is even and the string starts on an odd site, it’s compatible with the even covering - If k is even and the string starts on an even site, it’s compatible with the odd covering
Sample complexity: For even-length strings, we achieve: 
\|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2 = 3^{k/2}

Comparison with Pauli shadows: - Pauli: 3^k measurements - Bell (2 coverings): 2 \times 3^{k/2} measurements (factor 2 for two coverings)
Speedup: For k=10: Pauli needs \sim 59,000 measurements, Bell needs \sim 2 \times 243 = 486 measurements - a 120× improvement!
Limitation: Odd-length strings are incompatible with both coverings and cannot be learned.

title: Classical Shadows Based on Locally-Entangled Measurements
text:
2.3 Comparison with Shallow Shadows






NotePerformance Comparison (Click to expand)





Shallow shadows use variable-depth random circuits to interpolate between Pauli and Clifford measurements. For contiguous Pauli strings in 1D, they achieve: 
\|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2 \sim k \cdot 2^k
 when tuned to optimal depth \sim k.
Bell shadows achieve: 
\|P\|_{\text{sh}}^2 = 3^{k/2}

Comparison: - For k=4: Shallow \sim 64, Bell = 9 → Bell wins - For k=8: Shallow \sim 2048, Bell = 81 → Bell wins - For k=12: Shallow \sim 49152, Bell = 729 → Bell wins
Key advantage of Bell shadows: 1. Simpler protocol: Only requires two-qubit gates, no variable depth 2. Lower hardware requirements: Constant-depth circuit 3. Better scaling: 3^{k/2} vs k \cdot 2^k for many operators
Trade-off: Bell shadows only work for compatible operators (even-length strings with appropriate dimer covering), while shallow shadows work for all operators but with worse scaling.

title: Classical Shadows Based on Locally-Entangled Measurements
text:
Key Takeaways

Bell shadows achieve quadratic improvement in sample complexity (3^k \to 3^{k/2}) for compatible operators by using two-qubit entangled measurements.
The price is selectivity: Only \sim 0.79^N of all Pauli operators are learnable, but these include many physically-relevant operators (local strings, plaquettes, etc.).
The improvement comes from measuring pairs: Bell measurements provide information about 3 out of 9 weight-2 operators per dimer, vs 1 out of 3 per qubit for Pauli measurements.
Scaling can be further improved to (3/2)^k using n-qubit GHZ measurements, at the cost of even more restricted operator sets.
Practical advantage: Bell shadows can outperform shallow shadows for many physically-relevant tasks while requiring simpler hardware (constant-depth circuits with only two-qubit gates).
Design principle: Tuning the amount of entanglement in measurement bases creates a family of protocols with different trade-offs between sample complexity and operator coverage.

Abstract and My Thoughts
A family of Hamiltonians \{H(x): x \in [-1,1]^m\} is defined, where the parameter x can vary continuously over real numbers within a region where the gap of H remains constant. The ground state of H(x) is denoted by \rho(x). The author proves the following two conclusions:

If one can prepare quantum states \{\{\rho(x), x\}| x \in \mathcal{S}\} and then train a neural network using its classical shadow, it is possible to use a neural network in the Lazy zone to learn the behavior of any few-body operator’s ground state mean values at any x \in \mathcal{S}. This operation is also mentioned in the paper  [1].
If one attempts to use a classical algorithm \mathcal{A} to learn the behavior of single-operator means on the ground states of arbitrary two-dimensional H(x), it is NP-hard.

Interesting details/techniques worth learning are:

How to rigorously prove that learning a smooth function with a neural network is feasible?
What if this task is extended to quantum states using classical shadows and then transformed into some linear/nonlinear functions of the quantum state?
Is it really, on average, difficult to compute single-operator means on the ground states of smoothly gapped Hamiltonians? How does the paper prove this?

title: The Weingarten calculus
text:
由于任意算符的 k-fold Haar 随机是 k 点 SWAP 算符的线性组合，它可以分解在基底 \{\mathbb{P}^{d}_{\pi}\}_{\pi \in S_k} 上。然而，这不是一组正交归一基，因此分解系数涉及基于系数 \mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d}\cdot A) 的更复杂的计算。






注记引理 (Weingarten calculus)



对于 U \in U(d) 和 X \in (\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes t} \times (\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes t}，以下恒等式成立： 
\Phi_t(X) := \int_{\text{Haar}} U^{\otimes t} X U^{\dagger \otimes t} \, dU =\sum_{\tau,\sigma \in S_t} \text{tr}(X\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau}) \mathrm{Wg}(\tau\sigma^{-1} , d) \mathbb{P}^d_\sigma,
 其中系数 \mathrm{Wg}(\tau \sigma^{-1}, d) 由以下关系确定： 
\sum_{\tau\in S_t} \mathrm{Wg}(\tau \sigma^{-1}, d) \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} \mathbb{P}^{d}_{\rho})= \delta_{\sigma,\rho}.









注记Proof (点击展开)





根据定义，\Phi_t(X) 是 U^{\otimes t} X (U^\dagger)^{\otimes t} 在酉群上的 Haar 平均。 通过变量代换 U \to VU，可以证明对于所有 V \in U(d)，我们要有 V^{\otimes t} \Phi_t(X) (V^\dagger)^{\otimes t} = \Phi_t(X)。
根据 Schur-Weyl 对偶性 (Schur-Weyl duality)，任何与所有 V^{\otimes t} 对易的算符必须位于置换算符 \mathbb{P}^d_\rho (\rho \in S_t) 张成的空间中。 因此，我们可以写作 \Phi_t(X) = \sum_{\rho \in S_t} c_\rho \, \mathbb{P}^d_\rho。 在两边从右侧乘以 \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_\tau 并取迹，得到 \text{RHS} = \sum_{\rho \in S_t} c_\rho \, \text{Tr}( \mathbb{P}^d_\rho \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau})。
现在计算 LHS： 
\begin{aligned}
\text{LHS} = \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} \Phi_t(X))
&= \text{Tr} \left( \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} \int_{\text{Haar}} U^{\otimes t} X (U^\dagger)^{\otimes t} \, dU \right) = \int_{\text{Haar}} \text{Tr} \left( \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} U^{\otimes t} X (U^\dagger)^{\otimes t} \right) dU \\
&= \int_{\text{Haar}} \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^d_{\tau} X) \, dU = \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} X),
\end{aligned}
 这是因为迹在酉共轭和 Haar 测度积分下是不变的。因此，我们得到线性方程 \sum_{\rho \in S_t} c_\rho \, \text{Tr}( \mathbb{P}^d_\rho \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau})= \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} X)。 将每边乘以 \mathrm{Wg}(\sigma^{-1} \tau, d) 并对 \tau \in S_t 求和，得到： 
\sum_{\rho \in S_t} c_\rho \sum_{\tau\in S_t}  \mathrm{Wg}(\sigma^{-1} \tau, d)\text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} \mathbb{P}^d_\rho ) =  \sum_{\tau\in S_t}\mathrm{Wg}(\sigma^{-1} \tau, d)\text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} X) = \sum_{\rho \in S_t} c_\rho \delta_{\sigma,\rho} = c_{\sigma}.
 这里我们利用了以下事实：G_{\rho \tau}(d) \mathrm{Wg}_{\tau ,\sigma}(d) := \text{Tr}( \mathbb{P}^d_\rho \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau}) \mathrm{Wg}(\tau\sigma^{-1}, d) = \delta_{\rho,\sigma}。

title: The Weingarten calculus
text:
由于任意算符的 k-fold Haar 随机是 k 点 SWAP 算符的线性组合，它可以分解在基底 \{\mathbb{P}^{d}_{\pi}\}_{\pi \in S_k} 上。然而，这不是一组正交归一基，因此分解系数涉及基于系数 \mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{d}\cdot A) 的更复杂的计算。






注记引理 (Weingarten calculus)



对于 U \in U(d) 和 X \in (\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes t} \times (\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes t}，以下恒等式成立： 
\Phi_t(X) := \int_{\text{Haar}} U^{\otimes t} X U^{\dagger \otimes t} \, dU =\sum_{\tau,\sigma \in S_t} \text{tr}(X\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau}) \mathrm{Wg}(\tau\sigma^{-1} , d) \mathbb{P}^d_\sigma,
 其中系数 \mathrm{Wg}(\tau \sigma^{-1}, d) 由以下关系确定： 
\sum_{\tau\in S_t} \mathrm{Wg}(\tau \sigma^{-1}, d) \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} \mathbb{P}^{d}_{\rho})= \delta_{\sigma,\rho}.









注记Proof (点击展开)





根据定义，\Phi_t(X) 是 U^{\otimes t} X (U^\dagger)^{\otimes t} 在酉群上的 Haar 平均。 通过变量代换 U \to VU，可以证明对于所有 V \in U(d)，我们要有 V^{\otimes t} \Phi_t(X) (V^\dagger)^{\otimes t} = \Phi_t(X)。
根据 Schur-Weyl 对偶性 (Schur-Weyl duality)，任何与所有 V^{\otimes t} 对易的算符必须位于置换算符 \mathbb{P}^d_\rho (\rho \in S_t) 张成的空间中。 因此，我们可以写作 \Phi_t(X) = \sum_{\rho \in S_t} c_\rho \, \mathbb{P}^d_\rho。 在两边从右侧乘以 \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_\tau 并取迹，得到 \text{RHS} = \sum_{\rho \in S_t} c_\rho \, \text{Tr}( \mathbb{P}^d_\rho \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau})。
现在计算 LHS： 
\begin{aligned}
\text{LHS} = \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} \Phi_t(X))
&= \text{Tr} \left( \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} \int_{\text{Haar}} U^{\otimes t} X (U^\dagger)^{\otimes t} \, dU \right) = \int_{\text{Haar}} \text{Tr} \left( \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} U^{\otimes t} X (U^\dagger)^{\otimes t} \right) dU \\
&= \int_{\text{Haar}} \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^d_{\tau} X) \, dU = \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} X),
\end{aligned}
 这是因为迹在酉共轭和 Haar 测度积分下是不变的。因此，我们得到线性方程 \sum_{\rho \in S_t} c_\rho \, \text{Tr}( \mathbb{P}^d_\rho \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau})= \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} X)。 将每边乘以 \mathrm{Wg}(\sigma^{-1} \tau, d) 并对 \tau \in S_t 求和，得到： 
\sum_{\rho \in S_t} c_\rho \sum_{\tau\in S_t}  \mathrm{Wg}(\sigma^{-1} \tau, d)\text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} \mathbb{P}^d_\rho ) =  \sum_{\tau\in S_t}\mathrm{Wg}(\sigma^{-1} \tau, d)\text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau} X) = \sum_{\rho \in S_t} c_\rho \delta_{\sigma,\rho} = c_{\sigma}.
 这里我们利用了以下事实：G_{\rho \tau}(d) \mathrm{Wg}_{\tau ,\sigma}(d) := \text{Tr}( \mathbb{P}^d_\rho \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\tau}) \mathrm{Wg}(\tau\sigma^{-1}, d) = \delta_{\rho,\sigma}。

title: The Weingarten calculus
text:
2 Weingarten 系数的性质
现在我们展示 Weingarten 系数 \mathrm{Wg}(\pi\tau^{-1}, d):= \mathrm{Wg}_{\pi,\tau}(d) 的一些关键性质。通过定义矩阵 G_{\tau,\sigma} := \mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d}_{\tau}\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\sigma}) = d^{c(\tau \sigma^{-1})}，我们得出结论：如果 n!\times n! 矩阵 G 是可逆的，那么 \mathrm{Wg} 构成了 G 的逆。
然而，根据下文的 Lemma ，例如在 k>d 的情况下（比如 k=2 的单量子比特态上的 3-fold Haar 随机酉变换），G 是不可逆的。






注记引理 (G 的可逆条件)



Gram 矩阵 G_{\tau,\sigma}:= \text{tr}(\mathbb{P}^d_{\tau\sigma^{-1}})=d^{c(\tau \sigma^{-1})} 可逆当且仅当 t \leq d。这里 c(\tau \sigma^{-1}) 计数 \tau\cdot \sigma^{-1} 中的循环数。


在这种情况下，线性方程 \sum_{\pi \in S_t} G_{\pi,\rho} \, c_\pi = \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\rho} X) 的解不唯一。 此时，我们将 \mathrm{Wg}_{\rho,\sigma}(d) 定义为 G_{\pi,\rho} 的伪逆 (pseudo-inverse)，它仍然满足 \sum_{\rho} G_{\pi,\rho}\mathrm{Wg}_{\rho\sigma}(d) = \delta_{\pi,\sigma}。这表明它给出了 c_{\sigma} =\sum_{\rho} \mathrm{Wg}_{\rho\sigma}(d) \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\rho} X) 的其中一个解，但不是唯一的解。
接下来我们给出 \mathrm{Wg}_{\sigma,\pi} 的解析形式。






注记引理 (Weingarten 系数解析式)



给定 \pi,\sigma \in S_t，Weingarten 系数具有如下表达式： 
\mathrm{Wg}(\sigma\pi^{-1},d):= \frac{1}{(t!)^2}\sum_{\substack{\lambda \vdash t, \ell_m(\lambda)\leq d}}\frac{\chi^{\lambda}(1)^2\chi^\lambda(\sigma\pi^{-1})}{\text{dim}_U(\lambda)}









注记Proof (点击展开)





为了简便，我们将 \text{dim}_{S_t}(\lambda) 记为 \text{dim}\lambda，并使用 \text{dim}_{d}(\lambda):= \text{dim}_{S_t}(\lambda)\cdot \text{dim}_{U}(\lambda) 来表示嵌入在 \pi \to \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^d 表示中的 \lambda 型不可约表示 (irreps) 的维数。 根据定义，\mathrm{Wg}_{\sigma,\pi}(d) 是对称矩阵 G_{\tau,\sigma} =\text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^d_{\tau} \mathbb{P}^{d,\dagger}_{\sigma})=d^{c(\tau \sigma^{-1})} 的右伪逆。
考虑由 S_t 元素张成的线性空间，元素形式为 v = \sum_{\pi \in S_t} v_{\pi} \pi。元素 A_G = \sum_{\pi \in S_t} d^{c(\pi)} \pi 在这些向量上诱导了一个线性变换，其矩阵表示为 (A_G)_{\tau,\sigma}= d^{c(\tau \sigma^{-1})}，因为： 
A_G \cdot v = \sum_{\sigma \in S_t} v_{\sigma} A_G \cdot \sigma = \sum_{\sigma \in S_t} v_{\sigma}\sum_{\pi \in S_t} d^{c(\pi)} \pi \cdot \sigma = \sum_{\sigma \in S_t} v_{\sigma}\sum_{\tau \in S_t} d^{c(\tau \sigma^{-1})} \tau = \sum_{\tau \in S_t}\left(\sum_{\sigma}(A_G)_{\tau,\sigma}v_\sigma\right) \tau.
 因此，首先找到 A_G 的群逆（记为 A_{G^{-1}}）就足够了，然后在同一基底上表示它，给出 A_{G^{-1}} = \sum_{\pi\in S_t}f(\pi)\cdot\pi，其矩阵表示为 (A_{G^{-1}})_{\tau,\sigma}= f(\tau\sigma^{-1})。 结合定义可得结果： 
A_G A_{G^{-1}} = e \Rightarrow \sum_{\pi,\sigma}d^{c(\pi)}f(\sigma)\pi \sigma = e \Rightarrow \sum_{\sigma} f(\sigma) d^{c(r\sigma^{-1})} = \sum_{\sigma} f(\sigma) G_{r, \sigma}= \sum_{\sigma}  G_{r,\sigma} f(\sigma)=  \delta_{e,r}
 这意味着 f(\sigma) = \mathrm{Wg}_{\sigma,e}(d) 且 \mathrm{Wg}(\sigma \pi^{-1},d) = f(\sigma \pi^{-1})。
注意到 g A_G g^{-1} = A_G，因为 \pi 的循环结构在群共轭下是不变的，我们得出结论 [A_G,g] = 0,\forall g \in S_t。根据 Schur 引理 (Schur’s Lemma)，A_G 的所有不可约表示 \forall \lambda \vdash t 必须正比于单位元。即： 
\hat{A}_G(\lambda) = \sum_{\pi \in S_t}d^{c(\pi)} \hat{R}_{\lambda}(\pi) =  \eta_{\lambda} \cdot \mathbb{I}_{\text{dim}(\lambda)} \Rightarrow \eta_{\lambda} = \sum_{\pi \in S_t} d^{c(\pi)} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi)/\text{dim} \lambda.
 基于 Lemma (注：此处引用了原文中未列出的引理)，我们得出结论 \text{tr}(P_{\lambda}) = \left({\text{dim} \lambda}/{t!}\right) \sum_{\pi \in S_t} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) d^{c(\pi)} = \text{dim}_d \lambda。这给出了恒等式 \eta_{\lambda} = t!\cdot {\text{dim}_d \lambda}/{(\text{dim}\lambda)^2} = t!\cdot {\text{dim}_U \lambda}/{\text{dim}\lambda}。
注意到 \text{dim}_U \lambda= \prod_{(i,j) \in \lambda}(d+j-i)/h(i,j)，根据 Lemma (注：原文未列出)。如果杨表 (Young-tableaus) \lambda 的最长行满足 \ell_m(\lambda)>d，则该值为零。 这展示了 \hat{A}_{G} 的不可逆性质，因此 A_G 亦然。我们可以通过设定若 \eta_{\lambda} =0 则 \eta_{\lambda}^{-1} = 0 来找到右伪逆 \hat A_{G^{-1}}。 这确定了 A_{G^{-1}} 的所有不可约表示为： 
\hat{A}_{G^{-1}}(\lambda)= \begin{cases}\left[(\text{dim}\lambda)/\left(t!\cdot \text{dim}_U \lambda\right)\right]\cdot \mathbb{I}_{\text{dim}(\lambda)} &\text{if~}\ell_m(\lambda)\leq d\\ 0&\text{if~}\ell_m(\lambda)>d\end{cases}
 知道了 A_{G^{-1}} 的所有不可约表示，根据 Lemma (注：原文未列出) 即可确定系数： 
\begin{aligned}
    f(\pi) &= \frac{1}{t!} \sum_{\lambda \vdash t} \text{dim}(\lambda) \text{tr}\left( \hat{A}_{G^{-1}}(\lambda) \hat R_\lambda(\pi) \right) = \frac{1}{t!} \sum_{\substack{\lambda \vdash t, \ell_m(\lambda)\leq d}} \text{dim}(\lambda) \text{tr}\left( \frac{\text{dim}(\lambda)}{t! \cdot \text{dim}_U(\lambda)}  \hat{R}_\lambda(\pi) \right) \\
    & = \frac{1}{(t!)^2} \sum_{\substack{\lambda \vdash t, \ell_m(\lambda)\leq d}}  \frac{(\text{dim}(\lambda))^2 \chi^\lambda(\pi)}{\text{dim}_U(\lambda)}.
\end{aligned}





2.1 例子 (Examples)
在 t = 2, d\geq 2 的情况下，我们得到两种类型的置换 e, (12)，其中 \text{dim}_U([1^2]) ={d(d-1)}/{2}, \text{dim}_U([2]) = {d(d+1)}/{2} 且 \text{dim}([1^2]) = 1 =\text{dim}([2])。基于 S_2 的特征标表，我们列出 Weingarten 系数如下：

\mathrm{Wg}(e, d) &= \frac{1}{(2!)^2} \left[ \frac{(\chi_{[2]}(e))^2 \chi_{[2]}(e)}{\text{dim}_U([2])} + \frac{(\chi_{[1,1]}(e))^2 \chi_{[1,1]}(e)}{\text{dim}_U([1,1])} \right] \\

\mathrm{Wg}((12), d) &= \frac{1}{(2!)^2} \left[ \frac{(\chi_{[2]}(e))^2 \chi_{[2]}((12))}{\text{dim}_U([2])} + \frac{(\chi_{[1,1]}(e))^2 \chi_{[1,1]}((12))}{\text{dim}_U([1,1])} \right] \\

\begin{aligned}
    \dim_U([3]) &= \frac{d(d-1)(d-2)}{6}, \dim_S([3]) = 1 \\
    \dim_U([2,1]) &= \frac{d(d^2-1)}{3},  \dim_S([2,1]) = 2 \\

基于 S_3 的特征标表，我们列出 Weingarten 系数如下：

&= \frac{d^2-2}{d(d^2-1)(d^2-4)}, \\[1em]
\mathrm{Wg}((12), d) &= \frac{1}{(3!)^2} \left[ \frac{1^2 \cdot (-1)}{\dim_U([3])} + \frac{2^2 \cdot 0}{\dim_U([2,1])} + \frac{1^2 \cdot 1}{\dim_U([1^3])} \right] \\
&= \frac{-1}{(d^2-1)(d^2-4)}, \\[1em]
\mathrm{Wg}((123), d) &= \frac{1}{(3!)^2} \left[ \frac{1^2 \cdot 1}{\dim_U([3])} + \frac{2^2 \cdot (-1)}{\dim_U([2,1])} + \frac{1^2 \cdot 1}{\dim_U([1^3])} \right] \\
&= \frac{2}{d(d^2-1)(d^2-4)}.
\end{aligned}



在 t = 3, d=2 的情况下，由于 \dim_U([3])=0，我们要找伪逆。这消除了杨表 \lambda = [3] 并导致以下结果： 
\mathrm{Wg}(e, d) = \frac{17}{144},\quad \mathrm{Wg}((12), d) =\frac{1}{144},\quad \mathrm{Wg}((123), d)=-\frac{7}{144}

在 X = \ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}^{\otimes t} 的情况下，我们选择能够统一 k>d 和 k<d 两种情况的结果。






注记引理 (态 \ket{\psi} 的酉轨道)




\mathbb{E}_{\psi \sim \mathrm{Haar}(d)} \ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}^{\otimes t} =  \frac{\sum_{\pi \in S_t} S_t(d)}{(t+d-1)(t+d-2)\cdots(d-1) d},
 其中 S_t(d) = \sum_{\pi \in S_t} \mathbb{P}^d_\pi。如果 t \leq d，则此分解是唯一的。








注记Proof (点击展开)





根据 Lemma ，我们得出结论 \forall \rho \in S_t： 
\sum_{\pi \in S_t}\text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}_{\rho^{-1}}^d \mathbb{P}_\pi^d) \, c_\pi = \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}^d_{\rho^{-1}} X) =1
 我们首先假设算符 c_{\pi} 不依赖于 \pi，这给出了 c_\pi 的解如下： 
\text{Tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_t} \mathbb{P}^d_{\rho^{-1}\pi} \right)c =  \text{Tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_t} \mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \right)c=1.
 解 c_\pi = c 是线性方程的解之一。 为了证明此解是唯一的，我们利用事实：G_{\pi, \sigma} := \text{Tr}(\mathbb{P}_{\pi^{-1}}^d \mathbb{P}_\sigma^d) 是一个可逆矩阵。 注意到 (t!)^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_t} \mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} 是到 t-fold 对称空间的投影算符，其维数为 C_{t+d-1}^t（即，将 t 个物体放入 d 个篮子的方法的数量）。这给出了结果： 
\text{Tr}\left(\sum_{\pi \in S_t} \mathbb{P}^d_{\pi} \right) = (t!)C_{t+d-1}^t = (t+d-1)(t+d-2)\cdots(d-1) d.










注记引理 (n-fold Weingarten 演算)



取独立同分布 (i.i.d.) V_i \sim \text{Haar}(d), i = 1,\cdots,n，X \in \text{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{kn}))，并定义 B_{\mathbf{v}}:= \bigotimes_{i =1}^{n} \left(\mathbb{P}_{v_i}^{d}\right) 其中 \mathbf{v} = (v_1,\cdots,v_n) \in S_k^n，则以下恒等式成立： 
\Phi_k^{\otimes n}(X):= \mathbb{E}_{V_i \sim \text{Haar}(d)} \left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^n V_i^{\otimes k}\right) X \left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^n V_i^{\dagger\,\otimes k}\right) = \sum_{\mathbf u, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{F}_2^n} \text{Wg}^{n}(\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}^{-1}, d)  \text{tr}\left( B_{\mathbf{u}} X\right)\cdot  B_{\mathbf{v}},
 其中积 Weingarten 系数由 \sum_{\mathbf{v}} \text{Wg}^{n}(\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}^{-1}, d) \text{tr}\left(B_{\mathbf{u}}B_{\mathbf{r}}^\dagger\right) = \delta_{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{r}} 确定，其解析表达式为 \mathrm{Wg}^{n}(\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}^{-1}, d) = \prod_{i=1}^n\mathrm{Wg}({v}_i{u}_i^{-1}, d)。具体来说：
对于所有 \mathbf u,\mathbf v \in S_2^n： 
\mathrm{Wg}^{n}(\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}^{-1}, d) = \left(\frac{1}{d^2 -1}\right)^n \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{d}\right)^{|\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}^{-1}|},\text{~其中~}|\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}^{-1}| = \#\{i|v_i \neq u_i\}

对于所有 \mathbf u,\mathbf v \in S_3^n： 
\mathrm{Wg}^{n}(\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}^{-1}, d) = \left(\frac{d^2-2}{d(d^2 -1)(d^2-4)}\right)^n \cdot \left(\frac{-d}{d^2-2}\right)^{\#\{i|v_i u_i^{-1} \in [21]\}}\left( \frac{2}{d^2-2}\right)^{\#\{i|v_i u_i^{-1} \in [3]\}}

3 应用

令U_{AB}和U_{BC}是两个支持在不同系统上的酉算符，考察unitary ensemble \{V_{ABC}= U_{AB}U_{BC}\}_{U \sim \mathrm{Haar}}。 有： 
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_{\mathcal{E}^*}(X) &= \mathbb{E}_{U_{AB}} \left[ U_{AB}^{\otimes k} \left( \mathbb{E}_{U_{BC}} \left[ U_{BC}^{\otimes k} X U_{BC}^{\dagger \otimes k} \right] \right) U_{AB}^{\dagger \otimes k} \right]\\

&= \sum_{\sigma, \tau} \text{Wg}_{BC}(\sigma\tau^{-1}) \cdot \mathbb{E}_{U_{AB}} \left[ U_{AB}^{\otimes k} \left(\text{Tr}_{BC}\left( X (I_A \otimes \sigma_{BC}^{-1}) \right) \otimes \tau_{B} \right) U_{AB}^{\dagger \otimes k} \right]\otimes \tau_{C}\\

title: Decoding in classical space
text:
A classical error correction code is a mapping from a shorter string \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{F}_2^k to a longer string \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{F}_2^n, where n > k. This information, with added length redundancy, can suppress errors in the following ways:

Valid strings must satisfy \mathbf{H} \cdot \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}.
A string where an error \mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{F}_2^n has occurred must satisfy \mathbf{H} \cdot (\mathbf{c} + \mathbf{e}) = \mathbf{H} \cdot  \mathbf{e} := \mathbf{s}, where \mathbf{s} is the observed syndrome.
It guarantees that for all errors with |\mathbf{e}| < d, \mathbf{H} \cdot \mathbf{e} \neq \mathbf{0}. In other words, the linear system \mathbf{H} \cdot \mathbf{e} = \mathbf{s} has a unique solution under the constraint |\mathbf{e}| < d.
Decoding refers to finding the string \mathbf{c} such that \mathbf{H} \cdot \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{s} given the syndrome \mathbf{s}. This has a unique solution assuming the error weight does not exceed d, meaning exact decoding is possible from an information-theoretic perspective.
However, in reality, the error weight may exceed d, and solving this system of equations for an arbitrary error correction code is NP-complete. Therefore, approximate decoding algorithms are considered.

The figure below shows a classical error correction code and its Tanner graph representation: 
For the classical decoding problem:

H[j,i]: Does the i-th error trigger the j-th syndrome?
p[i]: The probability of the i-th error occurring.

In error correction, there is an additional element: L[j,i]: Does the i-th error flip the j-th logical operator? If it does not flip it, it is not considered an error regardless of its length.
There are two types of decoding algorithms:

MLD
BP




For cases where |\mathbf{e}_i| > 2, MLD can be reduced to hypergraph-MWPM, but determining the existence of a hypergraph matching is NP-hard.
Considering approximate algorithms for hypergraph-MWPM, there are the following inapproximability theorems:

Unless P=NP, there is no \Omega(r(G)/\ln(r(G))) approximation algorithm, where r(G) is the maximum size of hyperedges in hypergraph G ([Hazan et al., 2006]).
Unless P=NP, there is no \mathcal{O}(|V(G)|^{1/2−\varepsilon}) approximation algorithm.

Examining the difficulty of the \text{MLD} problem itself:

MLD is NP-complete.
Even when restricted to Reed-Solomon Codes, MLD is NP-hard.


For hypergraphs with special structures, many related algorithms have been designed recently, for example:
http://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13587 http://arxiv.org/abs/2312.08813

title: Toolbox for proving lower bounds
text:
The lower bound does not rely on a specific strategy. But it tells us why we cannot do better. This impossibility always stems from the fact that the lack of information.
In this chapter, we first discuss the necessary information to distinguish between two distributions. Many algorithms for complex problems have been proved to violate this lower bound, thus proving a no-go theorem for reaching the lower bound.


We first upper bound the ability to distinguish two classical distributions p and q, as shown in Lemma [lemma:TV_bound] below.






重要Lemma



 If two distributions p,q on set S = \{1,\cdots,n\} has total variance distance (TVD) \|p - q\|_{\mathrm {TV}}:=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i = 1}^n|p(i) - q(i)| \leq \varepsilon, then there is no single sample algorithm \mathcal{A}: S \to \{p,q\} that \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing, in other words, satisfied \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq 1/2 + \varepsilon/2 and \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq 1/2 + \varepsilon/2.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. It is sufficient to show that for an arbitrary algorithm \mathcal{A}, either \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq (1-\varepsilon)/2 or \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq  (1-\varepsilon)/2. Notice that \begin{align}
        \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] + \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] & = 1 - \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] +\text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p]\\
        &\geq 1 - \sup_{U \subseteq S} \left |\text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[U] -\text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[U]\right |\\
        &= 1 - \|p - q\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \geq 1 - \varepsilon.

Given an implementable POVM set \mathcal{M} = \{\{F_s\}|\{F_s\} \text{~satisfied the restriction.}\}, we can implement those POVMs multiple times, carefully design their order, and even implement them adaptively. Any description of such an adaptive learning protocol are called a \mathcal{M}-restrained adaptive strategy. It has the Tree representation  [1]. Roughly speaking, the adaptive structure will first induce a decision tree \mathcal{T}. Each branching edges in \mathcal{T}, which we denoted as \{(u,v_1),\cdots,(u,v_{s_u})\}, was labeled by one of the restrained POVMs \{F^{u}_{v_{i}}\}_{i = 1}^{s_u} \in \mathcal{M}. Then any c-copies of state \rho \in \mathcal{H}(d^c) will induce a probability distribution p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(v) on each vertex v of the decision graph \mathcal{T}.






注记Definition



Consider an adaptive learning strategy with T-rounds of c-replica POVMs restrained on \mathcal{M}. The tree representation of it is

A T-level decision tree \mathcal{T} with root node r.
Edges between node u and its child nodes s_1,\cdots,s_{N_u} represents a POVM \{F^{u}_s\}_{s =1}^{N_u} \in \mathcal{M} with the measurement outcomes \{1,\cdots,N_u\}.
Each node u is assigned a probability p_{\mathcal{T},\rho}(u) based on the updating rule p_{\rho}(u) = p_{\rho}(u|s)p_{\rho}(s), where p_{\rho}(s|u) = \text{tr}(F^u_{s} \rho) and p_{\rho}(r) = 1.

To prove that any \mathcal{M}-restrained adaptive strategy \mathcal{T} cannot distinguish the states \rho from a set of state \mathcal{S} with 1/2 + \varepsilon successful rate, it is sufficient to show that \forall \mathcal{T}, the distribution p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l) and the distribution ensemble \{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(l)\}_{\sigma \in \mathcal{E}} cannot be distinguished \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing. This recasts the problem in a form that is solvable by applying Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound]. Thus, the distinguishability between \rho and \mathcal{S} is tightly lower-bounded by TVD as \begin{align}
\label{eq:tvd}
    \delta_{\mathrm{tvd}} :=\max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\|p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}-\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim\mathcal{E}} p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\end{align} where \mathcal{E} is an arbitrary distribution on the set \mathcal{S}. The analysis of \delta_{\mathrm{tvd}} requires brute-force calculation of leaves distribution p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l),\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim\mathcal{E}} p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(l) on a deep decision tree. We can eschew this by constructing upper-bounds for TVD using the Leaves Likelihood L(l) and the Edges Likelihood L(u,s) of the decision tree. \begin{align}
    L_{\sigma}(l) := \frac{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(l)}{p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l)} ,\quad L_{\sigma}(u,s):= \frac{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)}{p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)}.
\end{align}






重要Lemma



 Given distribution p^{(0)}(l) and distribution ensemble p^{(a)}(l),a \sim \mathcal{E} with L_a(l):=p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l), then for any \beta \in (0,1), the TVD satisfied \begin{align}
    \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 1 - \min_{l}\mathbb{E}_a L_a(l), \quad
    \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \text{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E},l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) \leq \beta] + (1 - \beta)
\end{align}








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. By definition, we have \begin{align}
        \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} &:= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} |p^{(0)}(l) - \mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}(l)| = \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max\{0, 1 -\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l)\}\\
        &\leq \mathbb{E}_a \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max\{0, 1 -p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l)\}\\
        &=\left[\sum_{\substack{a,l \in \text{leaf}\\\text{~s.t.~}L_a(l)\leq \beta}}p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max \{0,1 - L_a(l)\}+\sum_{\substack{a,l \in \text{leaf}\\\text{~s.t.~}L_a(l)>\beta}}p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max \{0,1 - L_a(l)\}\right].
\end{align} Here in the first line, we directly get the first inequality because \begin{align}
        \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max\{0, 1 -\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l)\} \leq \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \left( 1 - \min_{l}\mathbb{E}_a L_a(l) \right) = 1 - \min_{l}\mathbb{E}_a L_a(l).
\end{align} In the second line, we use the fact that \max \{0, 1- x\} is a convex function, thus f(\mathbb{E}_a x_a) \leq \mathbb{E}_a f(x_a). Because for any \beta \in (0,1), we have \begin{cases}

\end{align} ◻

重要Theorem

\end{align} Sometimes we use a loosing lower bound T > c \cdot \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S} \sim \mathcal{E}}^{-1} where \begin{align}

重要Lemma



 Given two state ensemble \mathcal{E}_1,\mathcal{E}_2. If 
\|\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_1}[\rho^{\otimes k}] - \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_2}[\rho^{\otimes k}]\|_1 \\
:= \|\mu^{(k)}_1 - \mu^{(k)}_2\|_{1}\geq \varepsilon,

Proof. Define function f(A):=\|A\|_1. Since f(A) is a closed and convex function, we conclude that f(A) = \max_{O}\left[\mathrm{tr}(O\cdot A) - f^*(O)\right]. The conjugate function writes: f^{*}(A) = \begin{cases}0 &\text{if~}\|A\|_{\infty}<1\\ +\infty &\text{if else}. \end{cases}, thus we have \|A\|_{1} = \max_{\|O\|_{\infty}<1}\mathrm{tr}(O\cdot A). Thus, the condition \|\mu^{(k)}_1 - \mu^{(k)}_2\|_{1}\geq \varepsilon is equivalent to the existence of O, \|O\|_{\infty}<1 such that \mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}_1) - \mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}_2) \geq \varepsilon. This means that we can measure operator O on k-replica state \rho^{\otimes k} and construct a direct estimator \hat{o} for \mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}). If the estimator \hat{o} has \leq \varepsilon/2 additive error, then it solves the discrimination problem. The condition O, \|O\|_{\infty}<1 means that -1<\mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}) < 1. We then can use Hoeffding inequality in Theorem [theo:Hoeff_inq] to bound the sampling complexity N < 2\varepsilon^{-2} \ln(2 \delta^{-1}) to constructing \hat{o} with \leq \varepsilon/2 additive error. ◻

To do this, to first defined an \eta-covering set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} on the n-qubit pure states, as illustrated in Lemma [lemma:covering_on_nqubit].






重要Lemma



  An \eta-covering set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} on the n-qubit pure states is a finite set of n-qubit pure states such that 
\forall \ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}_n, \exists \ket{\psi} \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta}, \\
\text{s.t.~} \|\ket{\phi} - \ket{\psi}\|_2 \leq \eta.
 The cardinality of \mathcal{N}_{\eta} is upper bounded by |\mathcal{N}_{\eta}| \leq (1 + 2/\eta)^{2^{n+1}}.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. The set of n-qubit pure states corresponds to the unit sphere in the Hilbert space \mathcal{H}(n) \cong \mathbb{C}^{2^n}. This complex space of dimension 2^n is equivalent to a real space of dimension D = 2 \cdot 2^n = 2^{n+1}. The states are thus points on the unit sphere S^{D-1} in \mathbb{R}^D. Let \mathcal{N}_{\eta} = \{\ket{\psi_1}, \ket{\psi_2}, \dots, \ket{\psi_M}\} be a maximal set of n-qubit pure states such that the Euclidean distance between any two distinct states in the set is greater than \eta. This is known as an \eta-packing. We first argue that this set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} is also an \eta-covering net. If it were not, then \exists \ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}_n such that \forall \ket{\psi_i} \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta} ,\|\ket{\phi} - \ket{\psi_i}\|_2 > \eta, which contradicts the assumption that \mathcal{N}_{\eta} is a maximal set. Therefore, any maximal \eta-packing is an \eta-covering net. The problem is now reduced to finding an upper bound on the size M = |\mathcal{N}_{\eta}| of such a packing. Consider a set of open balls \{B(\ket{\psi_i}, \eta/2)\}_{i=1}^M of radius \eta/2 centered at each point of our set \mathcal{N}_{\eta}. Since for any i \neq j, we have \|\ket{\psi_i} - \ket{\psi_j}\|_2 > \eta, the triangle inequality implies that these balls are disjoint. All these disjoint balls are contained within a larger ball of radius 1 + \eta/2 centered at the origin. This is because each \ket{\psi_i} is on the unit sphere (norm 1), and any point in the ball B(\ket{\psi_i}, \eta/2) has a norm of at most \|\ket{\psi_i}\|_2 + \eta/2 = 1 + \eta/2. The total volume of these M disjoint balls cannot exceed the volume of the larger containing ball. Let V_D(r) be the volume of a D-dimensional ball of radius r. We have \sum_{i=1}^M V_D(\eta/2) \le V_D(1 + \eta/2). Since all the small balls have the same volume, this simplifies to M \cdot V_D(\eta/2) \le V_D(1 + \eta/2). The volume of a D-dimensional ball of radius r is given by C_D r^D for some constant C_D that depends only on the dimension D. Thus, we can write M \cdot C_D (\eta/2)^D \le C_D (1 + \eta/2)^D. Canceling the constant C_D and substituting back the dimension D = 2^{n+1}, we get the upper bound on M \begin{align}

重要Lemma



 Defined \text{dim}(\lambda) as the number of standard Young tableaus of shape \lambda \vdash k and alphabet [k]. Then \text{SW}_{\rho}^k(\lambda)= \text{dim}(\lambda) \cdot s_\lambda (\eta_1,\cdots,\eta_d) with \eta the spectrum of \rho. Specifically, we have \text{SW}_{d^{-1}\mathbb{I}}^k(\lambda) = {(\text{dim} (\lambda))^2}{(k!)^{-1}} {d^{\uparrow \lambda}}({d^k})^{-1}, where denots d^{\uparrow \lambda}: = \prod_{(i,j) \in [\lambda]} (d + j - i) with i,j labeling the position of all the lattices in Young tableaus of shape \lambda \vdash n,








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. \begin{align}
\label{eq:Schur_prob}
        \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) = (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \text{tr}( \text{SWAP}_\pi \rho^{\otimes k}).
\end{align} If \pi has l cycles with cycle length \kappa_1\cdots\kappa_l and \rho has eigenvalues \eta_1,\cdots,\eta_{d}, we noted that \begin{align}
        \text{tr}( \text{SWAP}_\pi \rho^{\otimes k}) = \text{tr}(\rho^{\kappa_1})\times \cdots\times\text{tr}(\rho^{\kappa_l}) = M_{\kappa}(\eta).
\end{align} Plug into Eq. [eq:Schur_prob] gives \begin{align}
        \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) &= (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) M_{\kappa}(\eta)\\
        &=(\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \sum_{\omega \vdash k}\chi_{\omega}(\pi)s_{\omega}(\eta)\\
        &=(\text{dim}\lambda) \cdot s_{\lambda}(\eta).
\end{align} Here in the second equality, we use Lemma [lemma:sym_poly_decomp]. In the third equality, we use the orthorgonal equation of group characters |G|^{-1} \sum_{g \in G} \chi_{p}^*(g)\chi_{q}(g) = \delta_{pq}. ◻

title: Toolbox for proving lower bounds
text:
We first upper bound the ability to distinguish two classical distributions p and q, as shown in Lemma [lemma:TV_bound] below.






重要Lemma



 If two distributions p,q on set S = \{1,\cdots,n\} has total variance distance (TVD) \|p - q\|_{\mathrm {TV}}:=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i = 1}^n|p(i) - q(i)| \leq \varepsilon, then there is no single sample algorithm \mathcal{A}: S \to \{p,q\} that \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing, in other words, satisfied \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq 1/2 + \varepsilon/2 and \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq 1/2 + \varepsilon/2.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. It is sufficient to show that for an arbitrary algorithm \mathcal{A}, either \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq (1-\varepsilon)/2 or \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq  (1-\varepsilon)/2. Notice that \begin{align}
        \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] + \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] & = 1 - \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] +\text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p]\\
        &\geq 1 - \sup_{U \subseteq S} \left |\text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[U] -\text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[U]\right |\\
        &= 1 - \|p - q\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \geq 1 - \varepsilon.
\end{align} Then either \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = q] \geq   (1-\varepsilon)/2 or \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \geq  (1-\varepsilon)/2, which means that either \text{Pr}_{x \sim p}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \leq   (1+\varepsilon)/2 or \text{Pr}_{x \sim q}[\mathcal{A}(x) = p] \leq  (1+\varepsilon)/2. ◻



A slight generalization of Lemma [lemma:TV_bound] is to distinguish a unique distribution p_0 and multiple distributions p_1,\cdots,p_l for L =\{1,\cdots,l\}, where p_i are all distributions over set S=\{1,\cdots,n\}. We prove a generalized no-go theorem below:






重要Lemma



 If there exists a distribution \mathcal{D} over L such that \delta_{\mathcal{D}}:=\|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} \leq \varepsilon, then there is no single-sampling algorithm that distinguishes p_0 between p_1,\cdots,p_l such that it is \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. We first directly prove this result using lemma [lemma:TV_bound]. If it exists, we can use it as an algorithm that distinguishes the distribution q(i):=\mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}(i)] with p_0(i) and it is \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing. This contradicts the fact that \|p_0 - q\|_{\mathrm {TV}} =\|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}}  \leq \varepsilon according to Lemma [lemma:TV_bound]. ◻



In Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound], we can try all kinds of distribution \mathcal{D} over L and choose the hardest one \delta_{\mathrm{w}} = \min_{\mathcal{D}}\delta_{\mathcal{D}}. This reflects the worst case information complexity of this discrimination problem.


In general, this problem is much harder than two-point discrimination, as we are designing a unified algorithm that dealt with multiple two-point discrimination (p_0,p_1),\cdots,(p_0,p_L) at the same time. One can relax this problem by ensuring that the distribution p_i only appears following a fixed distribution \mathcal{D}. This reduces the problem to a two-point discrimination (p_0,\mathbb{E}_{r \sim \mathcal{D}}p_r). Then the value \delta_{\mathcal{D}} in Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound] is tight. We call it the average case information complexity under problem ensemble \mathcal{D}. Similarly, we can define multiple-to-multiple tasks that discriminate a set of distribution \mathcal{A} from the other set of distribution \mathcal{B}, whose average case hardness is defined by \|\mathbb{E}_{r \sim \mathcal{D}(A)}p_{r} -\mathbb{E}_{r \sim \mathcal{D}(B)} q_{s}\|_{\mathrm{TVD}} for problem ensemble \mathcal{D}(\mathcal A) and \mathcal{D}(\mathcal B).



One confusing point is the discrimination of the distribution p_0 = \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}] and a set of distribution \{p_{r}\} with problem ensemble {r \sim \mathcal{D}}. By Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound], we cannot distinguish them with probability greater than 1/2 given one-sample. However, under k-samples, this is equivalent to the discrimination of p_0(t_1)\cdots p_0(t_k) and a set of distribution \{p_{r}(t_1)\cdots p_{r}(t_k)\} with problem ensemble {r \sim \mathcal{D}}. We can check that 
\mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}} \left[p_{r}(t_1)\cdots p_{r}(t_k)\right] \neq p_0(t_1)\cdots p_0(t_k) \\
=  \left[\mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}p_{r}(t_1)\right]\cdots \left[\mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}p_{r}(t_k)\right],
 thus can be estimated with probability greater than 1/2.



Intuitively, distinguishing two fine-grained distributions is never more difficult than distinguishing their coarse-grained versions. With TVD, we quantify this intuition as Lemma [lemma:TVD_corse].






重要Lemma



 Given two distribution \mathbf{p}:=\{p_1,\cdots,p_M\},\mathbf{q}:=\{q_1,\cdots,q_M\} and their coarse graining \mathbf{P}:=\bigcup_{s}\{p_{1,s},\cdots,p_{M,s}\},\mathbf{Q}:=\bigcup_{s}\{q_{1,s},\cdots,q_{M,s}\} such that \sum_{s} p_{k,s} = p_k,\sum_{s} q_{k,s} = q_k, \forall k \in \{1,\cdots,M\}. Then \|\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Q}\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \geq \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. Since \|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} = 2^{-1}\|\cdot\|_{1}, we conclude that \|\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{Q}\|_{1} = \sum_{k,s}\|p_{k,s} - q_{k,s}\|_{1} \geq  \sum_{k}\|\sum_{s}p_{k,s} - \sum_{s}q_{k,s}\|_{1} = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\|_{1} ◻



The most general form of the lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound] is Le Cam’s bound. We prove this theorem and show that lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound] is a special case of the Le-Cam theorem [theo:Le_Cam] for completeness.






重要Theorem



 Given a measurable space x \in \mathcal{X} and a family of measures P \in \mathcal{P}, P: 2^\mathcal{X} \to [0,1]. Let \hat \theta:\mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^p be an arbitrary estimator of the parameters of this family of distributions \theta: \mathcal{P} \to \mathbb{R}^p. Let D[\cdot,\cdot]:\mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} be a pseudo-metric of the parameter space that is symmetric and satisfies the triangular inequality D(x,y)+D(y,z) \geq D(x,z). Take two arbitrary subsets \mathcal{P}_1, \mathcal{P}_2 \subset \mathcal{P} that satisfied \inf_{\substack{P_1 \in \mathcal{P}_1,P_2 \in  \mathcal{P_2}} } D\left[\theta(P_1), \theta(P_2)\right] \geq 2\delta, then the inequality is true: \begin{align}
        \sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP(x)\cdot D\left[\hat \theta(x),\theta(P)\right]\right] \\
        &\geq \delta\cdot \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \left[1 - \frac{1}{2}\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} [dP_1(x) - dP_2(x)]\right].
\end{align}








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. We first noted that \begin{align}
          2\sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P)\right]\right] \\
          &\geq  \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP_1(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_1)\right] \\
          &\quad + \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP_2(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_2)\right].
\end{align} Based on the triangular inequality, we have D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_1)\right]  + D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P_2)\right] \geq D\left[\theta(P_1),\theta(P_2)\right]\geq 2\delta. Thus, for a fixed point x, the tuple (f_1/2\delta,f_2/2\delta), \text{where }\begin{cases}f_1(x) =D[ \hat \theta(x),\theta(P_1)], \\f_2(x) =D[ \hat \theta(x),\theta(P_2)],\end{cases} is in the convex set \mathcal{S} =\{(r_1,r_2)\in \mathbb{R}^2| r_1,r_2\geq 0,r_1+r_2 \geq  1\}. Then \forall P_1 \in \mathcal{P}_1,\forall P_2 \in \mathcal{P}_2, we write the inequality \begin{align}
          2\sup_{P \in \mathcal{P}} \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} dP(x)\cdot D\left[\hat\theta(x),\theta(P)\right]\right] \\
          &\geq 2\delta\cdot \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{[r_1(x),r_2(x)] \in \mathcal{S}} \left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) +  dP_2(x)\cdot r_2(x)\right]\right]\\
          &\geq   \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } 2\delta\cdot \\
          &\quad \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{[r_1(x),r_2(x)] \in \mathcal{S}} \left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) +  dP_2(x)\cdot r_2(x)\right]\right].
\end{align} The RHS satisfied the identity \begin{align}
         \text{RHS} &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\
         &\quad \left[\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{ \substack{r_1(x),r_2(x)\geq 0,\\r_1(x)+r_2(x) =  1}} \left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) +dP_2(x)\cdot r_2(x)\right]\right]\\
          &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\
          &\quad \left[1 +\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \inf_{ r_1(x)\in [0, 1]}\left[dP_1(x)\cdot r_1(x) -  dP_2(x)\cdot  r_1(x)\right]\right]\\
         &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\
         &\quad \left[1- \int_{\substack{x \in \mathcal{X}\\P_2(x) \geq P_1(x)}} dP_2(x) -  dP_1(x) \right]\\
         &=2\delta \sup_{\substack{P_1 \in \text{cov~}\mathcal{P}_1\\P_2 \in \text{cov~} \mathcal{P_2}} } \\
         &\quad \left[1- \frac{1}{2} \int_{\substack{x \in \mathcal{X}}} |dP_2(x) -  dP_1(x)| \right].
\end{align} This completes the proof. ◻









重要Lemma



The lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound] is a special case of the Le-Cam theorem [theo:Le_Cam].








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. Take the special case that \mathcal{X} = \{1,\cdots,n\}, \mathcal{P}_0 =\{p_0(x)\}, \mathcal{P}_1 =\{p_1(x),\cdots,p_l(x)\} and \theta(p_i) :=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }i =0,\\1&\text{else}.\end{cases} The estimator and metric are taken as \hat \theta(\cdot): \mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\} and \begin{align}
    D(\cdot,\cdot): \{0,1\}^{2} \to \{0,1\}, \\
    (\theta_1,\theta_2) &\hookrightarrow \begin{cases}1&\text{if }(\theta_1,\theta_2)=(1,0),(0,1),\\ 0 &\text{else}.\end{cases}
\end{align} It is easy to see that D(\cdot,\cdot) is indeed symmetric and satisfies the triangular inequality. This strategy distinguished the \mathcal{P}_0 and \mathcal{P}_1 with success probability \begin{align}
    p_{\text{succ}}  &=\min_{i=1,\cdots,l}\left\{ \text{Pr}_{x \sim p_0}[\hat \theta(x) =0 ],\text{Pr}_{x \sim p_i}[\hat \theta(x) =1 ]\right\} \\
    &= 1 - \max_{i = 1,\cdots,l}\left\{ \text{Pr}_{x \sim p_0}[\hat \theta(x) =1 ],\text{Pr}_{x \sim p_i}[\hat \theta(x) =0 ]\right\}\\
    &=1 - \max_{p \in \mathcal{P}} E_{x \sim p} D[\hat \theta(x),\theta(p)].
\end{align} Based on Lemma [theo:Le_Cam], we conclude the inequality \begin{align}
    \max_{p \in \mathcal{P}} E_{x \sim p} D[\hat \theta(x),\theta(p)] \geq \delta\cdot [1 - \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} ].
\end{align} Notice that \inf_{\substack{P_1 \in \mathcal{P}_1,P_2 \in  \mathcal{P_2}} } D\left[\theta(P_1), \theta(P_2)\right] \geq 1, we take \delta = 1/2, which combine to the final result \begin{align}
    p_{\text{succ}} \leq 1 -\frac{1 - \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} }{2} = \frac{1 + \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} }{2} .
\end{align} Then if \|p_0 - \mathbb{E}_{r\sim \mathcal{D}}[p_{r}]\|_{\mathrm {TV}} \leq \varepsilon, we conclude that p_{\text{succ}}\leq (1+\varepsilon)/2 and cannot \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing. ◻

title: Toolbox for proving lower bounds
text:
Now we specify different POVM restrain \mathcal{M} = \{\{F_s\}|\{F_s\} \text{~satisfied the restriction.}\}. In general, we can keep c copies of identical state \rho^{\otimes c}, and implement a c-replica measurement. Such a strategy are specified by as set of POVM operators \{F_s \in \mathrm{Herm}(d^c)\}_{s \in \mathcal{S}}, with s \in \mathcal{S} specified the measurement results and \forall s \in \mathcal{S}, F_s \geq 0, \sum_s {F_s} = \mathbb{I}(d)^{\otimes c}. We first show that we can always restrain the form of \{F_{s}\}_{s} on rank-1 operator set \{w_{s}\ket{\psi_{s}}\!\bra{\psi_{s}}\}_{s} without loss of generality. This is because arbitrary POVMs can be simulated by rank-1 POVMs through grouping the results.






重要Lemma



 Any POVM \{F_s\}_s can be simulated through rank-1 POVM \{w_{sp}\cdot\ket{\psi_{sp}}\!\bra{\psi_{sp}}\}_{sp} by classical post-grouping \ket{\psi_{sp}}\!\bra{\psi_{sp}} \to F_s.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. Do Cholesky decomposition. Trivial. ◻



This equivalence means that given an arbitrary state \rho, the classical distribution generated by \{w_{sp}\cdot\ket{\psi_{sp}}\!\bra{\psi_{sp}}\}_{sp} is a coarse graining of that of \{F_s\}_s. Using Lemma [lemma:TVD_corse], we conclude that it is sufficient to consider rank-1 POVMs only.
Based on different experiment restriction, F_s might only supports on a subset of space \mathrm{Herm}(d^c). Here below we characterized some typical restriction.


We first focus on the k-memory c-replica strategies. It is a c-replica measurement but with finite quantum-storage, as formally defined below.






注记Definition



 A (c,k) adaptive strategy repeats T rounds of sampling. Within each round, as shown in the process diagram [eq:procc_diag], it repeatedly adds new copies of n-qubits \rho to the k-qubits memory \sigma^{(i)} and adaptively implements n+k \to k qubits POVMs \{M_s^{u}\}. \begin{align}
\label{eq:procc_diag}
        \left[\rho \xrightarrow{\{M_{s_1}\}} \sigma^{(1)} \xrightarrow{\text{Add } \rho}  \rho \otimes \sigma^{(1)}\xrightarrow{\{M_{s_1,s_2}\}} \sigma^{(2)} \xrightarrow{\text{Add } \rho} \cdots  \rho \otimes \sigma^{(c)}\xrightarrow{\{M_{s_1,\cdots,s_c}\}} R_r \right]_{\times T}
\end{align}


At the end of each round in a (c,k)-adaptive strategy, we get the result s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_c, corresponding to the POVM branch 
\begin{aligned}
&\{M_{s_1}:\mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{n}),\mathcal{H}(d^{k_1})), \\
&\quad M_{s_1,s_2}:\mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{n + k_1}),\mathcal{H}(d^{k_2})), \cdots, \\
&\quad M_{s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_c}:\mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{n + k_{c-1}}), \mathbb{C})\}.
\end{aligned}
 Here the parameter satisifed k_1 = \min\{n,k\}, k_2 = \min\{n+k_1,k\},\cdots,k_{c-1} = \min\{n+k_{c-2},k\}. The POVM operator \{F_{\mathbf{s}}\} belongs to the linear space \mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{cn})). When k = (c-1)\cdot n, we have k_1 = n,k_2 = 2n,\cdots,k_{c-1} = (c-1)n. This means that the last POVM operator supports on the whole linear space M_{s_1,s_2,\cdots,s_c}:\mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{cn}), \mathbb{C}). Thus, the round-POVM operators \{F_s\} cover the whole space \mathrm{Lin}(\mathcal{H}(d^{cn})) and are equivalent to first storing c-copies of n-qudit states followed by c-copies collective measurements. If k < (c-1)n, \{F_s\} is restricted which we denoted as the set \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k}. We show that every element of \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k} can be realized by rank-1 POVMs within \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k} and post coarse-graining of the measurement results. Thus, it is sufficient to lower bounding all the rank-1 \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k} POVMs \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^k = \{F_{j}:= 2^{cn}w_j|L_j\rangle\!\langle L_j|\}_{j}, with \sum_{j}F_j = \mathbb{I}(d^{cn}).






重要Lemma



 \{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k} has decomposition \{F_s:= d^{nc}\sum_{a_c}w_{s,a_c}|L_{s,a_c}\rangle\!\langle L_{s,a_c}|\}_s, where \ket{L_{s,a_c}} is a normalized MPS vector on c \cdot n qudits with at most d^{k_j} bond dimension.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. The operator F_s can be constructed from those M_s operators through the identity: \begin{align}
    \mathrm{tr}(\rho^{\otimes c} F_s) = \sum_{a_c \in [d^{n+k}]}\begin{quantikz}[row sep=0.1cm, column sep=0.1cm]
        \setwiretype{n}&&&\gate[2]{M_{s_1, s_2}}&\gate[1]{M_{s_1}\vphantom{M_{s_1}^\dagger}}\setwiretype{c}&\gate[1]{\rho}\setwiretype{q}&\gate[1]{M_{s_1}^\dagger}\gategroup[4,steps=6,style={dashed,rounded corners,inner sep=-1pt},label style={label position=below, yshift=0.65cm, xshift=-0.7cm}]{$\ket{L_{s,a_c}}$}&\gate[2]{M_{s_1, s_2}^\dagger}\setwiretype{c}\\
        \setwiretype{n}&&\gate[2]{\cdots}\setwiretype{n}&\setwiretype{c}&\setwiretype{q}&\gate[1]{\rho}&&&\gate[2]{\cdots}\setwiretype{c}\\
        \setwiretype{n}&\gate[2]{M_{s_1,\cdots,s_c}}&\setwiretype{c}&\setwiretype{q}&&\gate[1]{\cdot\!\!\cdot\!\!\cdot}&&&&\gate[2]{M_{s_1,\cdots,s_c}^\dagger}\setwiretype{c}\\
        \lstick{$a_c$|\!|\!\!\!}\setwiretype{c}&&\setwiretype{q}&&&\gate[1]{\rho}&&&&&\setwiretype{c}&\rstick{\!\!\!|\!|$a_c$}
    \end{quantikz} \label{eq:tensor_network_MPS}
\end{align} Here we use single line to indicate the d-dimensional bond and double line to indicate the k_j-dimensional bond. The restriction of such (c,k)-POVM operators, which we denoted as the set \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^{k}, is equivalent to state that \{F_s:= d^{nc}\sum_{a_c}w_{s,a_c}|L_{s,a_c}\rangle\!\langle L_{s,a_c}|\}_s with \ket{L_{s,a_c}} a normalized MPS vector on c \cdot n qudits with d^{k_j} bond dimension: \begin{align}
    &\ket{L_{s,a_c}} =\sum_{a_j\in [d^{k_j}]} \ket{L_{s,a_1}}\ket{L_{s,a_1,a_2}}\cdots \ket{L_{s,a_{c-2},a_{c-1}}}\ket{L_{s,a_{c-1},a_c}}, \text{~where~} \forall \ket{e} \in \mathcal{H}(d^n),\\
    &\langle e|{L_{s,a_1}}\rangle := \langle e|M_{s_1}^{\dagger}|a_1\rangle,\quad \langle e|{L_{s,a_{j-1},a_{j}}}\rangle := \langle e,a_{j-1}|M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}^{\dagger}|a_{j}\rangle,\forall j>1.
\end{align} The trace-preserving condition \sum_{s_j} M^{\dagger}_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j} = \mathbb{I}(d^n) now transformed into \begin{align}
    \sum_{a_j,s_j} \langle e|{L_{s,a_{j-1},a_{j}}}\rangle \langle {L_{s,a_{j-1},a_{j}}}|f\rangle  &=  \sum_{a_j}\langle e,a_{j-1}|M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}^{\dagger}|a_{j}\rangle\langle a_{j}|M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}|f,a_{j-1}\rangle\\
    &=\sum_{s_j}\langle e,a_{j-1}|M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}^{\dagger}M_{s_1,\cdots,s_j}|f,a_{j-1}\rangle = \delta_{e,f} \\
    &\hspace{-5em}\Rightarrow \forall j = 1,\cdots,c,\quad \sum_{a_j,s_j} |{L_{s,a_{j-1},a_{j}}}\rangle \langle {L_{s,a_{j-1},a_{j}}}|= \mathbb{I}(d^n).
\end{align} Thus, \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^k can be implemented through rank-1 MPS-POVMs \mathcal{M}_{c,n}^k = \{F_{j}:= 2^{cn}w_j|L_j\rangle\!\langle L_j|\}_{j=(s,a_c)}, with \sum_{j}F_j = \mathbb{I}(d^{cn}), followed by classical post-processing rule j=(s,a_c) \to s. ◻



Given a pure quantum state \ket{L} that supports on c identical quantum systems with subsystem S \subset \{1,\cdots,c\}. Define P^S as the tensor product of Pauli operator P on the subsystem s if s \in S otherwise identity. We say the Pauli operator P are \varepsilon-correlated on the subsystem if and only if |\bra{L} P^{S} \ket{L}|^2 \geq \varepsilon. For a 2^k-bonded MPS states \ket{L}, we show that the \varepsilon-correlated Pauli is only taking no more than \varepsilon^{-1}2^{-n + k} proportion within all possible Pauli operators, as rigorously stated in Lemma [lemma:MPS_Paulicorrelation].






重要Lemma



 Define the average Pauli correlation on subsystem S \subset \{1,\cdots,c\} as \mathcal{P}(S):= 4^{-n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} |\bra{L} P^{\otimes S} \ket{L}|^2. Then if \ket{L} is an MPS state with no more than 2^k bond dimension, we have \mathcal{P}(S) \leq 2^{-n + k}. In the special case |S| = 1, \mathcal{P}(S) \leq 2^{-n}.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. In the simplest case c = 2,d= 2, a MPS state with \leq 2^k bond dimension always has Schmidt decomposition \ket{L} = \sum_{a = 1}^{2^k} \sqrt{\lambda_a} \ket{\phi_a} \otimes \ket{\psi_a} with \sum_a \lambda_a = 1. Take P^{\{1,2\}} = P \otimes P,P^{\{1\}} = P \otimes \mathbb{I}_n, then \begin{align}
    \mathcal{P}(\{1,2\}) &=  2^{-2n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n}  \left|\sum_{a,a'}\sqrt{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a}P\ket{\phi_{a'}}\bra{\psi_a}P \ket{\psi_{a'}}\right|^2\notag\\
    &\leq 2^{-2n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} \left( \sum_{a,a'}\left|\sqrt{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a}P\ket{\phi_{a'}}\right|^2\right)\cdot \left(\sum_{a,a'}\left|\bra{\psi_a}P \ket{\psi_{a'}}\right|^2\right) \notag\\
    &\leq 2^{-2n + k}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n}  \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}\left|\bra{\phi_a}P\ket{\phi_{a'}}\right|^2 = 2^{-n + k} \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}\bra{\phi_a\phi_{a'}}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} 2^{-n}P \otimes P\ket{\phi_{a'}\phi_a}\notag\\
    &=2^{-n + k} \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}\bra{\phi_a\phi_{a'}}\ket{\phi_{a}\phi_{a'}} =2^{-n + k},\\
    \mathcal{P}(\{1\}) &= 2^{-2n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n}  \left|\sum_{a,a'}\sqrt{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a}P\ket{\phi_{a'}}\bra{\psi_a}\ket{\psi_{a'}}\right|^2 = 2^{-2n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n}  \left|\sum_{a}{\lambda_a}\bra{\phi_a}P\ket{\phi_{a}}\right|^2 \notag\\
    &=2^{-n}  \sum_{a}{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a\phi_{a'}}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} 2^{-n}P \otimes P\ket{\phi_{a}\phi_{a'}}= 2^{-n}  \sum_{a}{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a\phi_{a'}}\ket{\phi_{a'}\phi_{a}}\leq 2^{-n}.
\end{align} This generalized to c>2 case by noticing that \ket{L} = \sum_{a = 1}^{2^k} \sqrt{\lambda_a} \ket{\phi_a} \otimes \ket{\psi_a} is satisfied for bipartition \{1,\cdots,l\} \cup \{l+1,c\}. Take l being the least on in set S. For special case |S| = 1, it is trivially the same as c = 2 case. For |S| \geq 2, the same procedure followed: \begin{align}
    \mathcal{P}(S) &=  2^{-2n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n}  \left|\sum_{a,a'}\sqrt{\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}}\bra{\phi_a}P^{\{l\}}\ket{\phi_{a'}}\bra{\psi_a}P^{S - \{l\}} \ket{\psi_{a'}}\right|^2\leq 2^{-2n + k}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n}  \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}\left|\bra{\phi_a}P^{\{l\}}\ket{\phi_{a'}}\right|^2 \notag \\
