    &= 2^{-n + k} \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}\bra{\phi_a\phi_{a'}}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} 2^{-n}P^{\{l\}} \otimes P^{\{l\}}\ket{\phi_{a'}\phi_a}\leq 2^{-n + k} \sum_{a,a'}\lambda_a\lambda_{a'}=2^{-n + k}.
\end{align} ◻



In the case of c =2, we also have the inequality below:






重要Lemma



 \begin{align}
    \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}^{k}_{2,n}} \sum_{s} \frac{\left[\mathrm{tr}(F_s \mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n})\right]^2}{\mathrm{tr}(F_s)} \leq 2^{k+n}
\end{align}








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. ◻

title: Toolbox for proving lower bounds
text:
Given an implementable POVM set \mathcal{M} = \{\{F_s\}|\{F_s\} \text{~satisfied the restriction.}\}, we can implement those POVMs multiple times, carefully design their order, and even implement them adaptively. Any description of such an adaptive learning protocol are called a \mathcal{M}-restrained adaptive strategy. It has the Tree representation  [1]. Roughly speaking, the adaptive structure will first induce a decision tree \mathcal{T}. Each branching edges in \mathcal{T}, which we denoted as \{(u,v_1),\cdots,(u,v_{s_u})\}, was labeled by one of the restrained POVMs \{F^{u}_{v_{i}}\}_{i = 1}^{s_u} \in \mathcal{M}. Then any c-copies of state \rho \in \mathcal{H}(d^c) will induce a probability distribution p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(v) on each vertex v of the decision graph \mathcal{T}.






注记Definition



Consider an adaptive learning strategy with T-rounds of c-replica POVMs restrained on \mathcal{M}. The tree representation of it is

A T-level decision tree \mathcal{T} with root node r.
Edges between node u and its child nodes s_1,\cdots,s_{N_u} represents a POVM \{F^{u}_s\}_{s =1}^{N_u} \in \mathcal{M} with the measurement outcomes \{1,\cdots,N_u\}.
Each node u is assigned a probability p_{\mathcal{T},\rho}(u) based on the updating rule p_{\rho}(u) = p_{\rho}(u|s)p_{\rho}(s), where p_{\rho}(s|u) = \text{tr}(F^u_{s} \rho) and p_{\rho}(r) = 1.






Illustrations of a (c = 3, k < n) adaptive learning strategy and its tree representation 𝒯. Refer to .


To prove that any \mathcal{M}-restrained adaptive strategy \mathcal{T} cannot distinguish the states \rho from a set of state \mathcal{S} with 1/2 + \varepsilon successful rate, it is sufficient to show that \forall \mathcal{T}, the distribution p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l) and the distribution ensemble \{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(l)\}_{\sigma \in \mathcal{E}} cannot be distinguished \varepsilon/2 better than random guessing. This recasts the problem in a form that is solvable by applying Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound]. Thus, the distinguishability between \rho and \mathcal{S} is tightly lower-bounded by TVD as \begin{align}
\label{eq:tvd}
    \delta_{\mathrm{tvd}} :=\max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\|p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}-\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim\mathcal{E}} p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
\end{align} where \mathcal{E} is an arbitrary distribution on the set \mathcal{S}. The analysis of \delta_{\mathrm{tvd}} requires brute-force calculation of leaves distribution p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l),\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim\mathcal{E}} p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(l) on a deep decision tree. We can eschew this by constructing upper-bounds for TVD using the Leaves Likelihood L(l) and the Edges Likelihood L(u,s) of the decision tree. \begin{align}
    L_{\sigma}(l) := \frac{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(l)}{p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l)} ,\quad L_{\sigma}(u,s):= \frac{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)}{p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)}.
\end{align}






重要Lemma



 Given distribution p^{(0)}(l) and distribution ensemble p^{(a)}(l),a \sim \mathcal{E} with L_a(l):=p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l), then for any \beta \in (0,1), the TVD satisfied \begin{align}
    \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 1 - \min_{l}\mathbb{E}_a L_a(l), \quad
    \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \text{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E},l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) \leq \beta] + (1 - \beta)
\end{align}








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. By definition, we have \begin{align}
        \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} &:= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} |p^{(0)}(l) - \mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}(l)| = \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max\{0, 1 -\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l)\}\\
        &\leq \mathbb{E}_a \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max\{0, 1 -p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l)\}\\
        &=\left[\sum_{\substack{a,l \in \text{leaf}\\\text{~s.t.~}L_a(l)\leq \beta}}p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max \{0,1 - L_a(l)\}+\sum_{\substack{a,l \in \text{leaf}\\\text{~s.t.~}L_a(l)>\beta}}p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max \{0,1 - L_a(l)\}\right].
\end{align} Here in the first line, we directly get the first inequality because \begin{align}
        \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \max\{0, 1 -\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}(l)/p^{(0)}(l)\} \leq \sum_{l \in \text{leaf}} p^{(0)}(l)\cdot \left( 1 - \min_{l}\mathbb{E}_a L_a(l) \right) = 1 - \min_{l}\mathbb{E}_a L_a(l).
\end{align} In the second line, we use the fact that \max \{0, 1- x\} is a convex function, thus f(\mathbb{E}_a x_a) \leq \mathbb{E}_a f(x_a). Because for any \beta \in (0,1), we have \begin{cases}
        \max\{0, 1 - L_a(l)\} \leq 1 - \beta, &\text{for } l \text{ s.t. } L_a(l) > \beta,\\
        \max\{0, 1 - L_a(l)\} \leq 1, &\text{for } l \text{ s.t. } L_a(l) \leq \beta,
    \end{cases}, we obtain \begin{align}
        \|p^{(0)}-\mathbb{E}_a p^{(a)}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}  &\leq \sum_{\substack{a,l \in \text{leaf}\\L_a(l)\leq \beta}} p^{(0)}(l) +  (1 - \beta) \sum_{\substack{a,l \in \text{leaf}\\L_a(l)> \beta}} p^{(0)}(l)\\
        &=  \text{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E},l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) \leq \beta] +(1 - \beta)\cdot \text{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E},l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) > \beta]\\
        &\leq \text{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E},l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) \leq \beta] + (1 - \beta).
\end{align} ◻



Then we can simply prove that \forall l, \mathbb{E}_{\sigma\sim \mathcal{E}} L_{\sigma}(l) \geq 1 - \delta. Then use the first inequality in Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD], we have \|p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}-\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim\mathcal{E}} p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq \delta. Or we can prove a fine-tuned upper bound for the probability \text{Pr}_{\sigma\sim \mathcal{E}, l \sim p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(l)}[L_{\sigma}(l) \leq \beta]. This is found by the proportion of Edges Likelihood L_{\sigma}(u,s), as illustrated by the inequality in the Lemma [lemma:UB_Ltail].






重要Lemma



 If \forall u satisfied \mathbb{E}_{a\sim \mathcal{E}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim p^{(0)}(s|u)}[(L_{a}(u,s) - 1)^2] \leq \delta, then for every constant c_1 \in (0,1/3), c_2 >0, there exists a constant c_3>0 such that \begin{align}
       \mathrm{Pr}_{a\sim \mathcal{E}, l \sim p^{(0)}}[L_a(l) \leq 1 - c_1] \leq c_2+ c_3\delta T.
\end{align}








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. ◻



Now we are set to give a lower bound on Eq.[eq:tvd], which immediately lower bounding the measurement times T of the adaptive strategy \mathcal{T}, as shown in Theorem [theo:mart_distinguish_lb] blow:






重要Theorem



 To distinguish \rho and a set of state \mathcal{S} for a constant success rate 1/2 + \varepsilon, with restrained POVMs \mathcal{M} and classical adaptive strategy, the adaptive measurement rounds T must be lower bounded by chi-squared divergence T > c \cdot \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S}}^{-1}, where \begin{align}
        \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S}} = \min_{\mathcal{E} \text{~on~} \mathcal{S}} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2.
\end{align} Sometimes we use a loosing lower bound T > c \cdot \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S} \sim \mathcal{E}}^{-1} where \begin{align}
     \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S} \sim \mathcal{E}} := \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2.
\end{align}








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. We first defined the likelihood function below: \begin{align}
\label{eq:likelihood_func}
  \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho) := \max_{u}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \mathbb{E}_{s \sim p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)} \left[\frac{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)}{p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}}(s|u)} - 1\right]^2 = \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \max_{u}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s}^{u})} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s}^{u})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s}^{u})} - 1\right]^2
\end{align} Combining Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD] and Lemma [lemma:UB_Ltail], this function upper-bounds the TVD through inequality \begin{align}
    \forall \mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},c_1 \in (0,1/3),c_2>0,&~\|p_{\rho,\mathcal{T}} - \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq c_2 + c_3 \cdot \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho) \cdot T + c_1,\\
    \Rightarrow \forall c_1 \in (0,1/3),c_2>0,&~\delta_{\mathrm{tvd}} \leq c_2 + c_3 \cdot \max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho) \cdot T + c_1.
\end{align} Using Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound], the correct probability 1/2 + \varepsilon to distinguish p_{\rho, \mathcal{T}} from \{p_{\sigma,\mathcal{T}}\}_{\sigma \in \mathcal{E}} must satisfy \begin{align}
    &1/2 + \varepsilon < 1/2 + \delta_{\mathrm{tvd}}/2 \leq 1/2+{(c_1+c_2)}/{2} + (1/2)c_3\cdot\max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho)T\\
    & \Rightarrow T > \frac{2 \varepsilon - c_1 -c_2}{c_3}\left[\max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho)\right]^{-1} \geq c \cdot \left[\min_{\mathcal{E}}\max_{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E},\rho)\right]^{-1}.
\end{align} Here in the last inequality we use the max-min inequality \max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{F} \leq \min_{\mathcal{E}}\max_{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{F}. As long as \varepsilon is a constant, we can always tune the value of c_1 \in (0,1/3),c_2>0 such that the lower bound T > c\cdot \max_{\mathcal{T}}\min_{\mathcal{E}}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E}, \rho) is meaningful (i.e., c>0). Plug in the definition of \mathcal{F}, we get the equation T \geq c \cdot \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S}}^{-1}, where \begin{align}
    \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S}} = \min_{\mathcal{E}}\max_{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{E}, \rho)
    &=\min_{\mathcal{E}} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \max_{\mathcal{T}}\max_{u}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s}^{u})} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s}^{u})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s}^{u})} - 1\right]^2 \\
    &=\min_{\mathcal{E}} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2.
\end{align} Here in the last line, we consider all possible adaptive strategy with POVM restriction \{F_s^{u}\} \in \mathcal{M}, \forall u, thus the maximum can be unioned. Sometimes we ignore the minimization over all possible ensemble \mathcal{E} over the state set \mathcal{S} and give a loose lower bound for the measurement times. We denoted this as: \begin{align}
    \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S}} \leq \delta_{\mathcal{M},\rho,\mathcal{S} \sim \mathcal{E}} := \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \mathbb{E}_{\sigma \sim \mathcal{E}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2.
\end{align} ◻



Before dived into complex prove of distinguishability lower bound, it is necessary to build an intuition about which ensemble is hard to distinguished.






重要Lemma



 Given two state ensemble \mathcal{E}_1,\mathcal{E}_2. If 
\|\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_1}[\rho^{\otimes k}] - \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_2}[\rho^{\otimes k}]\|_1 \\
:= \|\mu^{(k)}_1 - \mu^{(k)}_2\|_{1}\geq \varepsilon,
 then there exists strategy that distinguishes \mathcal{E}_1 and \mathcal{E}_2 using k-replica measurement for O(1/\varepsilon^2) times.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. Define function f(A):=\|A\|_1. Since f(A) is a closed and convex function, we conclude that f(A) = \max_{O}\left[\mathrm{tr}(O\cdot A) - f^*(O)\right]. The conjugate function writes: f^{*}(A) = \begin{cases}0 &\text{if~}\|A\|_{\infty}<1\\ +\infty &\text{if else}. \end{cases}, thus we have \|A\|_{1} = \max_{\|O\|_{\infty}<1}\mathrm{tr}(O\cdot A). Thus, the condition \|\mu^{(k)}_1 - \mu^{(k)}_2\|_{1}\geq \varepsilon is equivalent to the existence of O, \|O\|_{\infty}<1 such that \mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}_1) - \mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}_2) \geq \varepsilon. This means that we can measure operator O on k-replica state \rho^{\otimes k} and construct a direct estimator \hat{o} for \mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}). If the estimator \hat{o} has \leq \varepsilon/2 additive error, then it solves the discrimination problem. The condition O, \|O\|_{\infty}<1 means that -1<\mathrm{tr}(O \mu^{(k)}) < 1. We then can use Hoeffding inequality in Theorem [theo:Hoeff_inq] to bound the sampling complexity N < 2\varepsilon^{-2} \ln(2 \delta^{-1}) to constructing \hat{o} with \leq \varepsilon/2 additive error. ◻



For more general task to distinguish set S_1 form S_2, it is equivalent to build all possible distribution on S_1,S_2 and check the hardness of these constructed ensemble on S_1 and S_2. However, Lemma [lemma:hard_necess1] is only a necessary condition. Even if two ensembles have similar rank-k property, their might still exist efficient k-replica measurement strategy. An example is \mathbb{I}/d and \{\ket{\mathbf{s}}\!\bra{\mathbf{s}}\}_{\mathbf{s}} with \mathbf{s} uniformly distributed on \mathbb{F}_2^{n}. This is because although \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_1}[\rho^{\otimes k}] = \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_2}[\rho^{\otimes k}], we still have 
\mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_1}[\prod_{i = 1}^{T}\mathrm{tr}(O_i\rho^{\otimes k})] \\
\neq \mathbb{E}_{\rho \sim \mathcal{E}_2}[\prod_{i = 1}^{T}\mathrm{tr}(O_i\rho^{\otimes k})].

With this intuition in mind, now we reviewed the information lower bound to distinguish Haar random state ensembles. Perhaps the most simple one are the maximum mixed state \mathbb{I}(d)/d with operator mixed ensemble.

title: Toolbox for proving lower bounds
text:
Given access to either (i). A set of state {S}_{\mathcal{O}}:=\{(\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon O_x)/d\}_{x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}} or (ii) \rho = \mathbb{I}/2^n, try to distinguish between these two cases with an error of at most 1/2-\varepsilon.

This problem determines the lower bound of classical shadow of \{O_x\}_{x \in \{1,\cdots,M\}} and has a special case for discrimination of \mathbb{I}/d and Pauli mixed state \rho = (\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon P)/2^n with P \in \mathcal{P}_n.
We first get intuition of this task based on Lemma [lemma:hard_necess1]. If we choose distribution on \mathcal{O} supports on Z_1 operators only, we conclude that the value \|\mu_1^{(1)} - \mu_2^{(1)}\|_1 are separately \|3\varepsilon Z_1/2^n\|_1 = \mathrm{tr}\left({3\varepsilon \mathbb{I}/2^n}\right) = 3\varepsilon and 
\|4^{-n}\sum_{P \in \mathcal{P}}3\varepsilon P/2^n\|_1 \\
= 3\varepsilon \left[\mathrm{tr}\left(\sqrt{AA^\dagger}\right) \right]^{n} \\
= 3\varepsilon(\sqrt{3}/2)^n \sim \mathcal{O}(2^{-n}).
 Here we use \mathrm{tr}\left(\sqrt{AA^\dagger}\right) = \sum_{\lambda(A)}|\lambda(A)| and \begin{align}
A = \frac{I+X+Y+Z}{4} =4^{-1} \begin{pmatrix}2&1- i\\1+i&0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \lambda(A) = {\frac{1 - \sqrt{3}}{4},\frac{1 + \sqrt{3}}{4}}.
\end{align} This means that even though there exists easy distribution \mathrm{Pr}(P)=\delta(P - Z_1) on Pauli operators that can be distinguished with \mathbb{I}/d with single replica strategy, there also has distribution \mathrm{Pr}(P) = 4^{-n} that might be hard. Based on this intuition, we set up hard distributions as uniform distribution on signed operators \{+1,-1\}\times \mathcal{O}. This ensures its average is exactly \mathbb{I}/d, thus being hard for 1-replica strategy.





For shadow tomography of general operator set \{O_1,\cdots,O_M\} where O_j is an arbitrary n-qubits operator, we build hard distribution by rotating Pauli Z operators with independent Haar random unitary: \begin{align}
    O_{1},\cdots,O_{M/2} &= U_1Z_1U_1^{\dagger}, \cdots, U_{M/2}Z_{M/2}U_{M/2}^{\dagger},\\
    O_{M/2+1},\cdots,O_{M} &= -U_1Z_1U_1^{\dagger}, \cdots, -U_{M/2}Z_{M/2}U_{M/2}^{\dagger},
\end{align} where U_1,\cdots,U_{M/2} are independent Haar random unitaries. The signature is to ensure its average is \mathbb{I}/d such that Lemma [lemma:hard_necess1] cannot give effective single copy strategy. According to Lemma [lemma:mult_TV_bound], to distinguish (i) and (ii) with 2/3 correction rate, which is \delta= 1/6 better that 1/2, we must have 1/3=2\delta \leq \|\mathbb{E}_{x} p_{\rho_x} - p_{2^{-n}\mathbb I}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}, where x is an arbitrary distribution on 1,\cdots,M. It is sufficient to take the uniform distribution of x. Based on Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD], 1/3\leq \|\mathbb{E}_{x} p_{\rho_x} - p_{2^{-n}\mathbb I}\|_{\mathrm{TV}} \leq 1 - \min_{l} \mathbb{E}_{x} L_{x}(l). According to the rank-1 reduction in Lemma [lemma:POVM_r1_reduction], we calculate the leaves’ likelihood \forall l as \begin{align}
\mathbb{E}_{x} L_{x}(l) &= \frac{\mathbb{E}_{x} p_{\rho_x}(l)}{p_{2^{-n}\mathbb I}(l)} = \mathbb{E}_{x} \prod_{t = 1}^T \frac{w_{s_t}^{u_t}\bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\rho_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}}{2^{-n}w_{s_t}^{u_t}}=\mathbb{E}_{x} \prod_{t = 1}^T \left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\notag\\
&=\mathbb{E}_{x} \text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T \ln\left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\right]\geq \text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T \mathbb{E}_{x} \ln\left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\right]\notag\\
&=\text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T M^{-1} \ln \left(\prod_{x = 1}^{M/2}\left(1+ 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\left(1- 3\varepsilon\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}\right)\right)\right]\notag\\
&=\text{exp}\left[\sum_{t = 1}^T M^{-1} \sum_{x = 1}^{M/2}\ln \left(1- 9\varepsilon^2\cdot \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}^2\right)\right] \notag\\
&\geq \text{exp}\left[-9\varepsilon^2\sum_{t = 1}^T \frac{2}{M}\sum_{x = 1}^{M/2} \bra{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}} O_x \ket{\psi_{s_t}^{u_t}}^2\right] \geq \text{exp}\left[-9\varepsilon^2 T \sup_{\ket{\phi}}\frac{2}{M}\sum_{x = 1}^{M/2} \bra{\phi} O_x \ket{\phi}^2\right] \label{eq:sig_canc_TVlb}
\end{align} Here we use \ln(1 - x)\geq -2x, \forall x \in [0,0.796]. This condition is satisfied if and only if 9\varepsilon^2<0.796, \varepsilon <0.29. Thus for \beta =\text{exp}\left[-9\varepsilon^2 T \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M)\right], we have \text{Pr}_{l \sim p^{(0)}}[L(l) \leq \beta] = 0, which gives the inequality use the fact that 1 - x \leq e^{-x},\forall x \in \mathbb{R}. \begin{align}
&1/3\leq 0 +(1 - \beta) = 1 - e^{-9\varepsilon^2 T \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M)}  \leq 9\varepsilon^2 T \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M) \notag\\
&\Rightarrow T \geq \Omega(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^2 \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M)}), \text{~where~} \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M):= \sup_{\ket{\phi}} \frac{2}{M}\sum_{i =1}^{M/2}\bra{\phi} O_i \ket{\phi}^2. \label{eq:LB_shadow_eq}
\end{align} Now we calculate the value \delta(O_1,\cdots,O_M). Noted that the random variable \bra{\phi} O_i \ket{\phi},\{O_i\}_i \sim \mathcal{O} and \bra{\psi_i} Z_n \ket{\psi_i}, \ket{\psi_i} \sim \text{Haar} has the same distribution. Thus, it is sufficient to discuss the property of function f(\ket{\psi}):= \bra{\psi} Z_n \ket{\psi} with Haar random inputs.






重要Lemma



  Given function f(\ket{\psi}):= \bra{\psi} Z_n \ket{\psi} with independent Haar random inputs, we conclude that \begin{align}
        &\text{Pr}\left[\left|\frac{1}{R}\sum_{i =1}^{R} f(\ket{\psi_i})^2 - \mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi} \sim \text{Haar}}\left[ f(\ket{\psi})^2\right]\right| \geq t\right] \leq 2 e^{-R \min(t^2/\lambda^2, t/\lambda)},\\
        & \text{where~} \lambda = 288\pi^3/2^n,\quad \mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi} \sim \text{Haar}} [f(\ket{\psi_i})^2] = \frac{1}{2^n + 1}
\end{align}








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. ◻



Now given one state \ket{\phi}, we proved that with high probability \sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2 will not deviate from its expectation too much, according to the Lemma [lemma:expon_cent_ineq]. Nevertheless, we hope to prove this property for all states \phi, that is, to bound the deviation of \sup_{\ket{\phi}}\sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2. To do this, to first defined an \eta-covering set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} on the n-qubit pure states, as illustrated in Lemma [lemma:covering_on_nqubit].






重要Lemma



  An \eta-covering set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} on the n-qubit pure states is a finite set of n-qubit pure states such that 
\forall \ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}_n, \exists \ket{\psi} \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta}, \\
\text{s.t.~} \|\ket{\phi} - \ket{\psi}\|_2 \leq \eta.
 The cardinality of \mathcal{N}_{\eta} is upper bounded by |\mathcal{N}_{\eta}| \leq (1 + 2/\eta)^{2^{n+1}}.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. The set of n-qubit pure states corresponds to the unit sphere in the Hilbert space \mathcal{H}(n) \cong \mathbb{C}^{2^n}. This complex space of dimension 2^n is equivalent to a real space of dimension D = 2 \cdot 2^n = 2^{n+1}. The states are thus points on the unit sphere S^{D-1} in \mathbb{R}^D. Let \mathcal{N}_{\eta} = \{\ket{\psi_1}, \ket{\psi_2}, \dots, \ket{\psi_M}\} be a maximal set of n-qubit pure states such that the Euclidean distance between any two distinct states in the set is greater than \eta. This is known as an \eta-packing. We first argue that this set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} is also an \eta-covering net. If it were not, then \exists \ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}_n such that \forall \ket{\psi_i} \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta} ,\|\ket{\phi} - \ket{\psi_i}\|_2 > \eta, which contradicts the assumption that \mathcal{N}_{\eta} is a maximal set. Therefore, any maximal \eta-packing is an \eta-covering net. The problem is now reduced to finding an upper bound on the size M = |\mathcal{N}_{\eta}| of such a packing. Consider a set of open balls \{B(\ket{\psi_i}, \eta/2)\}_{i=1}^M of radius \eta/2 centered at each point of our set \mathcal{N}_{\eta}. Since for any i \neq j, we have \|\ket{\psi_i} - \ket{\psi_j}\|_2 > \eta, the triangle inequality implies that these balls are disjoint. All these disjoint balls are contained within a larger ball of radius 1 + \eta/2 centered at the origin. This is because each \ket{\psi_i} is on the unit sphere (norm 1), and any point in the ball B(\ket{\psi_i}, \eta/2) has a norm of at most \|\ket{\psi_i}\|_2 + \eta/2 = 1 + \eta/2. The total volume of these M disjoint balls cannot exceed the volume of the larger containing ball. Let V_D(r) be the volume of a D-dimensional ball of radius r. We have \sum_{i=1}^M V_D(\eta/2) \le V_D(1 + \eta/2). Since all the small balls have the same volume, this simplifies to M \cdot V_D(\eta/2) \le V_D(1 + \eta/2). The volume of a D-dimensional ball of radius r is given by C_D r^D for some constant C_D that depends only on the dimension D. Thus, we can write M \cdot C_D (\eta/2)^D \le C_D (1 + \eta/2)^D. Canceling the constant C_D and substituting back the dimension D = 2^{n+1}, we get the upper bound on M \begin{align}
    |\mathcal{N}_{\eta}| = M \le \frac{(1 + \eta/2)^D}{(\eta/2)^D} = \left(\frac{1 + \eta/2}{\eta/2}\right)^D = \left(1 + \frac{2}{\eta}\right)^D.
\end{align} ◻



Then the low-deviation condition that satisfied for arbitrary \ket{\phi} \in \mathcal{H}(n) also satisfied on set \mathcal{N}_{\eta}, only with a |\mathcal{N}_\eta| larger error probability. After this, we show that the function g(\ket{\phi}):=\sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2 is Lipschitz continuous, which means that the difference of function value is upper bounded by the variables difference. Combining the Lipschitz continuity and the property of the \eta-covering, we show upper bounds for the value \sup_{\ket{\phi}}\sum_{O \in \mathcal{O}} |\mathcal{O}|^{-1}\bra{\phi} O \ket{\phi}^2, as rigrously illustrated in Lemma [lemma:point_to_uniform].






重要Lemma



  Given an L-Lipschitz continuous function f:V \to \mathbb{R} on metric space V and an \eta-covering set \mathcal{N}_{\eta} of V, if \forall x \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta}, |f(x) - c| < t, then \forall x \in V, |f(x) - c| < t + L \eta.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. By definition, we know that \forall x \in V, \exists r_x \in \mathcal{N}_{\eta} \text{~s.t.~} |r_x - x| \leq \eta. Then we conclude \begin{align}
        \forall x \in V, |f(x) - c| &\leq |f(x) - f(r_x)| + |f(r_x) - c|\leq L\|x - r_x\| + t \leq L\eta + t.
\end{align} ◻



If we further






重要Theorem



Given a uniform distribution on M Pauli observables \mathcal{A}:=\{P_1,\cdots,P_M\}, any single-copy learning algorithm that predict \{\text{tr}(\rho P)\}_{P \sim \mathcal{A}} with \varepsilon-additive error and 2/3 success probability must use T \geq \Omega \left(\varepsilon^{-2} \min\{M/\log M, 2^n\}\right) samples.






 Given a subset \mathcal{O} \subset \mathcal{P}(n), try to discriminate (i). A set of state {S}_{\mathcal{O}}:=\{\sigma_{P}:=(\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon P)/d\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}} and (ii) \rho = \mathbb{I}/2^n with confidence 1 - \delta.




Similarly, we set up hard distributions as uniform distribution on signed Pauli operators \{+1,-1\}\times \mathcal{O}, where \mathcal{O} \subset \{\mathbb{I},X,Y,Z\}. Follow the same procedure of Eq.[eq:sig_canc_TVlb], we then calculate its rank-1 POVM leaves likelihood as: \begin{align}
    \mathbb{E}_{s,P} L_{s,P}(l)  \geq \exp\left[-18\varepsilon^2T \sup_{\ket{\phi}} \mathbb{E}_{P\in \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{O})} \bra{\phi} P \ket{\phi}^2\right].
\end{align} In the case of \mathcal{O} = \mathcal{P}_n, we use the identity 
\mathbb{E}_{P\in \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{P}_n)} \bra{\phi} P \ket{\phi}^2 \\
=\bra{\phi}\bra{\phi} 4^{-n}\sum_{P\in \mathcal{P}_n}P \otimes P\ket{\phi}\ket{\phi}
 and \sum_{P\in \mathcal{P}_n}P \otimes P = 2^{n}\mathrm{SWAP}^{\otimes n}. We conclude that \mathbb{E}_{s,P} L_{s,P}(l) \geq e^{-18\varepsilon^2 T 2^{-n}},\forall l. Use Lemma [lemma:UB_TVD], we conclude that for all choice of single-copy POVM, \|p_{\mathbb{I}/d} - \mathbb{E}_{s,P}p_{\rho_{s,P}}\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \leq 1 - e^{-18\varepsilon^2 T 2^{-n}}. This means that to reach confidence 1/2 + \delta/2, we have to set 1 - e^{-18\varepsilon^2 T 2^{-n}} \geq \delta \Rightarrow T \geq 18^{-1}\times 2^n \varepsilon^{-2}\ln(1 - \delta).
According to Theorem [theo:mart_distinguish_lb], we can also calculate its \chi-squared divergence given ensemble \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O} on the subset of Pauli operators \mathcal{O}: \begin{align}
    \delta_{\mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} &:= \max_{\{F_s\}_s \in \mathcal{M}}\mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} \mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\sigma_P F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\rho F_{s})} - 1\right]^2= \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s}  \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{d}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\frac{\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon P}{d}F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})/d} - 1\right]^2 \notag\\
    &= 9\varepsilon^2 \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s}  \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{d}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}({P}F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}\right]^2 = {9\varepsilon^2} \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \sum_{s} \frac{\left[\mathrm{tr}({P}F_{s})\right]^2}{{d}\cdot \mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}.
\end{align} Since F_s includes all the rank-1 POVMs and each POVMs with rank greater than 1 can be equivalently realized using rank-1 POVMs with undecreasing discrimination efficiency, as shown in Lemma [lemma:POVM_r1_reduction]. We can plug in F_s = 2^{n}w_s \ket{\psi_s}\!\bra{\psi_s} with \{w_s\} a valid distribution and conclude the same result: \begin{align}
    \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \sum_{s} \frac{\left[\mathrm{tr}({P}F_{s})\right]^2}{{d}\cdot \mathrm{tr}(F_{s})} &= \max_{\ket{\psi_s}}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} \sum_{s}w_s{\left[\bra{\psi_s}{P}\ket{\psi_s}\right]^2} = \max_{\ket{\phi}}\mathbb{E}_{P \sim \mathcal{D}_\mathcal{O}} {\bra{\phi}{P}\ket{\phi}^2}
    \\
    &\sim \Omega(2^{-n}) \text{~if~} \mathcal{O} = \mathcal{P}_n, \mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{O}} = \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{O}).
\end{align} Then based on Lemma [theo:mart_distinguish_lb], T\geq 2^n. Note that such a martingale analysis do not directly applied to purity-identity test, which has a constant \chi-squared divergence, as calculated below: \begin{align}
    \delta_{\mathrm{Haar}} &= \max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s}  \frac{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})}{d}\mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi}\sim \mathrm{Haar}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})/d} - 1\right]^2=\max_{F_s \succ 0 }\sum_{s}  \mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi}} \left[\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}^{\otimes 2}F_{s}\otimes F_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(F_{s})/d}\right]- 1\\
    &=\max_{\ket{\psi_s} }\sum_{s}   d^2w_s\mathbb{E}_{\ket{\psi}} \left[{\mathrm{tr}({\psi}^{\otimes 2} \psi_s^{\otimes 2})}\right]- 1 = \frac{2d^2}{d(d+1)} - 1 = \frac{d-1}{d+1} \sim \Omega(1).
\end{align} This great difference between ensemble supports on \{(\mathbb{I}+ 3\varepsilon O)/2^n\}_{O \in \mathcal{O}} and Haar random state supports on \{\psi\} is because the probability of the latter one is more concentrated. \begin{align*}
    p_{\mathrm{Haar}}(\psi_s) =\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\ket{\psi}\!\bra{\psi}\psi_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{I}/d\cdot \psi_{s})}= d |\langle {\psi}|{\psi_s}\rangle|^2 \in[0,d], \, p_{\mathcal{P}}(\psi_s) =\frac{\mathrm{tr}(\frac{\mathbb{I} + 3\varepsilon P}{d}\psi_{s})}{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbb{I}/d\psi_{s})}=1 + 3\varepsilon\langle{\psi_s}|P|{\psi_s}\rangle \in [1- 3\varepsilon, 1+ 3\varepsilon].
\end{align*}

title: Toolbox for proving lower bounds
Toolbox for proving lower bounds
text:
If there is no restriction on the memory-number and the replica number, we can lower-bound the strategy through the symmetric of the property. We first define general testing strategy rigorously.






注记Definition



A property \mathcal{P} \subset \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}) is a set of quantum states. A two-outcome POVM \{E,\mathbb{I} - E\} on k-copies of n-qubit states tests the property \mathcal{P} iff for certain 1>\varepsilon_B \geq \varepsilon_A >0 and \delta = \Theta(1), \begin{align}
         d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P})  \leq \varepsilon_A \Rightarrow \text{tr}(E \rho^{\otimes k}) \geq 1/2 +\delta,\\
       d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P})  \geq \varepsilon_B \Rightarrow \text{tr}(E \rho^{\otimes k}) \leq 1/2 - \delta.
\end{align}


Now suppose the testing property \mathcal{P}, which is a set of state within n-qubit space, is invariant under unitary operation U(G) , which is a subgroup of U(2)^{\otimes n}. Namely, \begin{align}
    \forall \sigma \in \mathcal{P},\forall V \in U(G), V\sigma V^\dagger \in \mathcal{P}.
\end{align} Then we are prepared to show that it is enough to consider the symmetric version of the strategy rather than an arbitrary POVM within n-qubit space, as stated by Lemma [lemma:symmtric_M] below






重要Lemma



 Given a k-replica strategy \{E, \mathbb{I } - E\} for the U(G)-symmetric property \mathcal{P} on n-qubits, the symmetric strategy \{\Phi(E), \mathbb{I } - \Phi(E)\} with \Phi(E) := |U(G)|^{-1}\sum_{V \in U(G)} V^{\dagger,\otimes k}EV^{\otimes k} and \Phi_k(E) := |S_k|^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_k} \text{SWAP}_\pi E\cdot\text{SWAP}_\pi has non-decreasing efficiency.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. Because the unitary invariant property of \mathcal{P} and the non-decreasing property of trace distance under unitary transformation d_{\text{tr}}(\cdot,\cdot) = d_{\text{tr}}(U\cdot U^\dagger,U\cdot U^\dagger), we conclude that \begin{align}
       d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P})  \leq  \varepsilon_A &\Rightarrow \forall U \in U(G),  d_{\text{tr}}(U\rho U^\dagger, \mathcal{P}) \leq  \varepsilon_A \\
       &\Rightarrow  \forall U \in U(G),\text{tr}( EU^{\otimes k}\rho^{\otimes k} U^{\dagger,\otimes k}) \geq 1/2 + \Theta(1),\\
       &\Leftrightarrow  \forall U \in U(G),|U(G)|^{-1}\sum_{V \in U(G)}\text{tr}(U^{\dagger,\otimes k} EU^{\otimes k}\rho^{\otimes k} ) \geq 1/2 + \Theta(1),\\
       &\Leftrightarrow  \forall U \in U(G),\text{tr}(\bar E\rho^{\otimes k} ) \geq 1/2 + \Theta(1)
\end{align} Similarly, we can prove that d_{\text{tr}}(\rho, \mathcal{P})  \geq \varepsilon_B \Rightarrow \text{tr}(\bar E \rho^{\otimes k}) \leq 1/2 - \Theta(1). The same procedure is applied for \bar{E} := |S_k|^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_k} \text{SWAP}_\pi E\cdot\text{SWAP}_\pi. Thus, we prove that the symmetric strategy \{\bar{E}, \mathbb{I } - \bar{E}\} will have at least the same testing efficiency. ◻



Then we discuss the symmetry for the estimation problem.






注记Definition



A quantitative property of states is a map f: \rho \to \mathbb{R} with \rho \in \mathcal{S}(\mathcal{H}) . Given a POVM \{M_m\}_{m \in R} on k-replica space, an k-replica estimator of f is an observable O \in \text{End}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}) such that \text{tr}(O \rho^{\otimes k}) = f(\rho). An estimator O is efficient k-replica strategy iff \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O)\leq \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O') for all O \in \text{End}(\mathcal{H}^{\otimes k}).


We say a quantitative property f is invariant under unitary operation U(G) iff f(U\cdot U^\dagger) = f(\cdot), \forall U \in U(G). The we gives the symmetric strategy for estimate problem.






重要Lemma



 If O is a k-replica estimator for property f. Then the symmetrized estimators \begin{align}
        \Phi(O):=  |U(G)|^{-1}\sum_{V \in U(G)} V^{\dagger,\otimes k}OV^{\otimes k},\Phi_{k}(O):= |S_k|^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_k} \mathbb{P}_\pi^{d,\dagger} \cdot O\cdot \mathbb{P}_\pi^{d},
\end{align} always satisfied \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(\Phi(O))\leq \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O),\text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(\Phi_k(O))\leq \text{Var}_{\rho^{\otimes k}}(O).








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. We will show a more general statement for arbitrary channel that is unital (\Phi(\mathbb{I}) = \mathbb{I}), positive (\forall \rho \succeq 0, \Phi(\rho) \succeq 0), and satisfied \forall O \in \text{Herm}(\mathcal{H}), \text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)) = \text{tr}(\rho O). By definition, \text{Var}_{\rho}(\Phi(O)) = \text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)^2) - \text{tr}^2(\rho \Phi(O))  = [\text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)^2) - \text{tr}(\rho O^2)]+ \text{Var}_{\rho}(O). According to Theorem [theo:KS_ineq], \Phi(O^2)-\Phi(O)^2\succeq 0, which shows that \text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O)^2)<\text{tr}(\rho \Phi(O^2)) = \text{tr}(\rho O^2). This directly gives the result \text{Var}_{\rho}(\Phi(O)) \leq \text{Var}_{\rho}(O). ◻



Thanks to the Lemma [lemma:symmtric_M] and Lemma [lemma:symmetric_O] , if we find the lower bound of the sample complexity of all the symmetric POVM and operators, any strategy’s sample complexity is lower bounded by this value.


The simplest case are properties that is invariant under a unitary transformation. The lemma [lemma:symmtric_M] is useful because any spectrum testing strategy \{M,\mathbb{I} - M\} now can be restated as weak Schur sampling followed by classical post-processing  [2], as stated by the theorem below.






重要Lemma



 Given a testing strategy \{M, \mathbb{I } - M\} for unitary invariant property \mathcal{P} such that: \begin{align}
        \tr(M \rho^{\otimes k}) &\geq 1 - \delta,\forall \rho \in \mathcal{P};\\
         \tr(M \rho^{\otimes k}) &\leq 1 - f(\varepsilon),\forall \rho ~\varepsilon \text{-far from~} \mathcal{P}.
\end{align} Another strategy \bar{M} such that [\bar M,U^{\otimes k}] =0 and [\bar M,\text{SWAP}_\pi]=0 can be constructed with non-decreasing efficiency.








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. M_s =|S_k|^{-1} \sum_{\pi \in S^k}\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n}\cdot  M \cdot\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n} have unchanged efficiency because \mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n}\cdot  \rho^{\otimes k} \cdot\mathbb{P}_{\pi}^{2^n} = \rho^{\otimes k}. Combined with lemma [lemma:symmtric_M] proves the result. ◻



This construction simplified the analysis because we can reduce arbitrary strategy to a canonical one-weak Shur sampling. To see this, we first cite the lemma in  [3], according to the famous Schur-Weyl duality.






重要Lemma



 Given the symmetry group S_k , use \kappa \vdash k labels the conjugate classes K(\kappa) and \lambda \vdash k label the irreducible representation with the character function \chi_{\lambda}(\cdot) and dimension \text{dim}~\lambda. Define the projective measurements P_\lambda and the conjugate-class observables O_{\kappa} as \begin{align}
         P_{\lambda} := (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1} \sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \mathbb{P}_\pi^d,\quad O_{\kappa} := |K(\kappa)|^{-1} \sum_{\pi \in K(\kappa)}  \mathbb{P}_\pi^d.
\end{align} If \forall U \in \mathbb{C}^{k} and \forall \pi \in S_k, the operator M on the space (\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes k} satisfies [M,U^{\otimes k}] =0 and [M,\mathbb{P}_\pi^d]=0, then M can be decomposed as \begin{align}
         M &= \sum_{\lambda \vdash k} \alpha_{\lambda} P_\lambda,\quad M = \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} O_\kappa, \label{eq:M_decomp} \\
&\text{where~}O_{\kappa} = \sum_{\lambda}{(\text{dim}\lambda)^{-1}}\chi_{\lambda}(\kappa) P_{\lambda}. \label{eq:relation_PM}
\end{align}








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. The proof of this theorem is separated into three steps. First, by Schur-Weyl duality, we know that [M,U^{\otimes k}]=0 iff M is a linear superposition of SWAP gates: \begin{align}
\label{eq:M_decomp_mid}
        M &= \sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) \cdot \text{SWAP}_g.
\end{align}
Then we show that linear combination of SWAP gates commute with all the SWAP gates iff the superposition coefficient is a class function. According to Eq. [eq:M_decomp_mid], M is the image of group algebra m = \sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) g under representation \rho(g) = \text{SWAP}_g. Then m must commute with arbitray element in S_k. \forall~ h \in S_k, notice that: \begin{align}
        hmh^{-1} &= \sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) \cdot{hgh^{-1}} =\sum_{t \in S_k} f(h^{-1} t h) \cdot{t} =\sum_{g \in S_k} f(g) \cdot g = m
\end{align} This then imply f(g) = f(h^{-1} t h) for all h \in S_k and f is a class function. Last, given that character functions forms a orthonormal basis for class function, we obtain f(g) = \sum_{\lambda}c_{\lambda} \chi_{\lambda}(g). Plug into Eq. [eq:M_decomp_mid] gives: \begin{align}
             M &=  \sum_{\lambda}c_{\lambda}  \sum_{g \in S_k}\chi_{\lambda}(g)\cdot \text{SWAP}_g =\sum_{\lambda} \alpha_{\lambda} \frac{\text{dim}(V_\lambda)}{k!} \sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \text{SWAP}_\pi = \sum_{\lambda} \alpha_{\lambda} P_\lambda
\end{align} This is indeed a projector based on Lemma [lemma:projector_in_lambda] proved before. To prove the conclusion (ii), we first noted that \begin{align}
     \sum_{\lambda}\frac{1}{\text{dim~}\lambda}\chi_{\lambda}(\kappa) P_{\lambda} &=  \sum_{\pi \in S_k} ({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\lambda}\chi_{\lambda}(\kappa)  \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \mathbb{P}^d_\pi\\
     &=|K(\kappa)|^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in K(\kappa)}  \mathbb{P}^d_\pi = O_{\kappa}
\end{align} Here in the second line we use the second orthogonal identity |G|^{-1}\sum_{p}\chi_{p}(\kappa_j)\chi_{p}(\kappa_k) = |K(\kappa_k)|^{-1}\delta_{jk}. Then plug in Eq. [eq:M_decomp] we get \begin{align}
    \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} O_\kappa =\sum_{\lambda\vdash k}\frac{1}{\text{dim}~\lambda}\left[ \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} \chi_{\lambda}(\kappa)\right] P_{\lambda}= \sum_{\lambda \vdash k} \alpha_{\lambda} P_\lambda.
\end{align} This implys the transformation (\text{dim}\lambda)\cdot \alpha_{\lambda} =  \sum_{\kappa \vdash k} \beta_{\kappa} \chi_{\lambda}(\kappa). ◻






When k = 2, the group S_2 only has two conjugate class (2,0) and (1,1). The corresponding projectors are P_{(2,0)} = 2^{-1}{(\mathbb{I} + \text{SWAP}_{(1,2)})},P_{(1,1)} = 2^{-1}{(\mathbb{I} - \text{SWAP}_{(1,2)})}. This is just the SWAP test of two identical states, which is widely used for purity test. For larger t, the computation of those exact projector is proved to be #P-hard  [4]. Fortunately, the realization of projective measurement \{P_\lambda\} can be implemented in time \text{Poly}(k,\ln d) with generalized phase estimation circuit  [5], which is efficient for n-qubits property testing with d = 2^n. This is called the weak Schur sampling (WSS). Now we characterize the result of WSS by polynomials of density matrix’s spectrum.






注记Definition



 Let \mu,\lambda\vdash k be a partition of the replica number k. Let \mathcal{T} be the set of all semi-standard Young tableaus with shape \lambda and alphabet \{1,\cdots,d\}. Let \#(T,i) be the number of times that the character i occurs in the semi-standard Young tableau T. Two rank-k symmetric polynomials of d variables \mathbf{x}=(x_1,\cdots,x_d) can be defined below.

Schur polynomial (SP) is a rank-k symmetric polynomial that s_{\lambda}(\mathbf x):= \sum_{T}\prod_{i=1}^d x_i^{\#(T,i)}
Power sum polynomial (PSP) is a rank-k symmetric polynomial that M_{\mu}(\mathbf{x}):=\prod_{i=1}^{l(\mu)} \sum_{j=1}^d x_j^{\mu_i}






If we take \lambda = (k,0,\cdots), we get the \sum_{j = 1}^d x_j^k. SP and PSP can decompose each other, as shown in Lemma [lemma:sym_poly_decomp] below.






重要Lemma



 Any rank-k power sum polynomial can be decomposed with the rank-k symmetric Schur polynomial through M_{\mu}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{\lambda \vdash k}\chi_{\lambda}(\mu)s_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}).








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. ◻



Refer to  [6], the distribution of \text{tr}(P_{\lambda} \rho^{\otimes k}) only relates to the spectrum \eta of \rho, as proved in Lemma [lemma:WSS_res] below. Thus, we use \text{SW}_{\rho}^k(\lambda) to denote the weak Schur sampling probability \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) where \lambda is the eigenvalue of the density matrix \rho.






重要Lemma



 Defined \text{dim}(\lambda) as the number of standard Young tableaus of shape \lambda \vdash k and alphabet [k]. Then \text{SW}_{\rho}^k(\lambda)= \text{dim}(\lambda) \cdot s_\lambda (\eta_1,\cdots,\eta_d) with \eta the spectrum of \rho. Specifically, we have \text{SW}_{d^{-1}\mathbb{I}}^k(\lambda) = {(\text{dim} (\lambda))^2}{(k!)^{-1}} {d^{\uparrow \lambda}}({d^k})^{-1}, where denots d^{\uparrow \lambda}: = \prod_{(i,j) \in [\lambda]} (d + j - i) with i,j labeling the position of all the lattices in Young tableaus of shape \lambda \vdash n,








注记Proof (Click to expand)





Proof. \begin{align}
\label{eq:Schur_prob}
        \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) = (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \text{tr}( \text{SWAP}_\pi \rho^{\otimes k}).
\end{align} If \pi has l cycles with cycle length \kappa_1\cdots\kappa_l and \rho has eigenvalues \eta_1,\cdots,\eta_{d}, we noted that \begin{align}
        \text{tr}( \text{SWAP}_\pi \rho^{\otimes k}) = \text{tr}(\rho^{\kappa_1})\times \cdots\times\text{tr}(\rho^{\kappa_l}) = M_{\kappa}(\eta).
\end{align} Plug into Eq. [eq:Schur_prob] gives \begin{align}
        \text{tr}(P_\lambda \rho^{\otimes k}) &= (\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) M_{\kappa}(\eta)\\
        &=(\text{dim}\lambda)({k!})^{-1}\sum_{\pi \in S_k} \chi_{\lambda}(\pi) \sum_{\omega \vdash k}\chi_{\omega}(\pi)s_{\omega}(\eta)\\
        &=(\text{dim}\lambda) \cdot s_{\lambda}(\eta).
\end{align} Here in the second equality, we use Lemma [lemma:sym_poly_decomp]. In the third equality, we use the orthorgonal equation of group characters |G|^{-1} \sum_{g \in G} \chi_{p}^*(g)\chi_{q}(g) = \delta_{pq}. ◻

title: Multiple-copy Shadow tomography
text:
We have proved the inefficiency of single-copy strategy while an efficient two-copy Bell strategy exists. In analogy, we try to break the lower bound in the last section by extending the single-copy shadow tomography method into the multi-copy case.






ImportantTheorem(Non-local Pauli shadow tomography)



 Let \mathcal{P}_n be the n-qubit Pauli group. Let \mathbb{P}^{d}_{\pi} be the permutation operator on 2k replica of n-qubits (d = 2^n) and \pi =(\mathrm{odds})(\mathrm{even}) is 2-cycle permutation on odd labels (1,3,5,\cdots,2k-1) and even labels (2,4,\cdots,2k) respectively. For any P \in \mathcal{P}_n, define the operator: A_P =\mathrm{sym}_{\pi}\left[P^{\otimes 2} \otimes (I^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes (k-1)} \right] \cdot \mathbb{P}^{d}_{\pi}. The family of observables \mathcal{A} = \{A_P\}_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n} is a commuting family, i.e., [A_P, A_Q] = 0 for all P, Q \in \mathcal{P}_n. Furthermore, its expectation value on \rho^{\otimes 2k} is \mathrm{tr}(A_P \rho^{\otimes 2k}) = [\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^k)]^2. Therefore, a single projective measurement in the common eigenbasis of \mathcal{A} allows for the simultaneous estimation of |\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^k)| for all P \in \mathcal{P}_n.








NoteProof (Click to expand)





We first prove the commutativity of the family \mathcal{A}. Let S_P = \mathrm{sym}_{\pi}\left[P^{\otimes 2} \otimes (I^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes (k-1)} \right] and abbreviate \pi = \mathbb{P}^d_{\pi}. The operators are A_P = S_P \pi and A_Q = S_Q \pi. First, \pi commutes with S_P, \forall P \in \mathcal{P} since S_P is symmetrized under repeat operation of \pi. Now, the commutator [A_P, A_Q] became: \begin{align*}
        [A_P, A_Q] &= (S_P \pi) (S_Q \pi) - (S_Q \pi) (S_P \pi) \\
        &= S_P (S_Q \pi) \pi - S_Q (S_P \pi) \pi \quad \text{(since $\pi$ commutes with $S_P$ and $S_Q$)} \\
        &= [S_P, S_Q]\pi^2.
\end{align*} Finally, we show that [S_P, S_Q] = 0. This is because each term within S_P = \mathrm{sym}_{\pi}\left[P^{\otimes 2} \otimes (I^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes (k-1)} \right] and S_Q = \mathrm{sym}_{\pi}\left[Q^{\otimes 2} \otimes (I^{\otimes 2})^{\otimes (k-1)} \right] either have commutators of operators on disjoint subsystems or have two-replica terms with [P^{\otimes 2}, Q^{\otimes 2}] = [P \otimes P, Q \otimes Q] = 0. Thus we have [S_P, S_Q] = 0 for all Pauli operators P, Q . Thus, [S_P, S_Q] = \mathbf{0}, which implies [A_P, A_Q] = \mathbf{0}. We now calculate \begin{align*}
        \mathrm{tr}(A_P \rho^{\otimes 2k}) &= \mathrm{tr}[\mathrm{sym}_{\pi}(P^{\otimes 2} \otimes \mathbb{I}^{\otimes 2k-2}) \pi \rho^{\otimes 2k}] = \mathrm{tr}[(P^{\otimes 2} \otimes \mathbb{I}^{\otimes 2k-2}) \pi \rho^{\otimes 2k}]\\
        &=\mathrm{tr}[(P\rho \otimes \rho^{\otimes k-1}) \mathbb{P}^{d}_{(\mathrm{odds})} \otimes (P\rho \otimes \rho^{\otimes k-1}) \mathbb{P}^{d}_{(\mathrm{even})}]\\
        &=[\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^k)]^2
\end{align*} Thus, measuring the commuting family \{A_P\} simultaneously yields estimates for |\mathrm{tr}(P\rho^k)| for all P \in \mathcal{P}_n. ◻









ImportantLemma (Signal estimation)



 If we can estimate |\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)|, \forall P \in \mathcal{O} \subset \mathcal{P}_n within constant additive error \varepsilon, then using a \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}\log(|\mathcal{O}|)) times k-replica strategy with k \cdot n ancilla qubits, we can construct an estimator E_P such that |E_P - \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^{k})| \leq 3\varepsilon.








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Denoting f_P = |\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)|. We then construct the quantum state \sigma such that \left||\mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k)|- f_P\right| \leq \varepsilon. Such a state \sigma always exist and can be constructed if we knew an \varepsilon additive error estimator for \{f_P\}_{P \in \mathcal{O}}, but might cannot be found computationally efficient. Then we estimate \mathrm{tr}(\rho^k P)\cdot \mathrm{tr}(\sigma^k P) by measuring the commuting family \{A_P\}_{P\in \mathcal{O}} on state \rho^{\otimes k} \otimes \sigma^{\otimes k} for \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4}\log(|\mathcal{O}|)) times. This will give us an estimator g_P such that |g_P - \mathrm{tr}(\rho^k P)\cdot \mathrm{tr}(\sigma^k P)|\leq \varepsilon^2. Now we set E_P = 0 if f_P \leq \varepsilon and E_P = g_P/\mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k) if else. We thus noted that: \begin{align*}
        \text{If~} f_P < 2\varepsilon, \quad  |E_P - \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)| &= |\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)| \leq ||\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)| - f_P| + |f_P| \leq 3\varepsilon \\
        \text{If~} f_P \geq 2\varepsilon, \quad |E_P - \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)| &=   
            |g_P/\mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k) -\mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)| \\
            &= \frac{|g_P - \mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k) \cdot \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)|}{|\mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k)|}\\
            &\leq  \frac{|g_P - \mathrm{tr}(P \sigma^k) \cdot \mathrm{tr}(P \rho^k)|}{f_P - \varepsilon}  \leq \frac{\varepsilon^2}{2\varepsilon - \varepsilon} \leq 3\varepsilon.
\end{align*} 











ImportantLemma: 4-Copy Measurement Strategy for k=2



For the case k = 2, there exists a measurement protocol on 4 copies of the quantum state that can estimate the commutants A_{\mathbf{r}} through a shared eigenbasis measurement. The eigenbasis states \ket{\Psi^{s}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}} with eigenvalues \lambda_{(s,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})} :=s \cdot 2^{-1}[(-1)^{[\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{a}]} + (-1)^{[\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{b}]}] (where s = \pm 1) can be measured using a combination of local gates, computational basis measurements, and GHZ measurements.





A 4-copy strategy for non-linear shadow tomography








NoteConstruction and Proof (Click to expand)





Step 1: Define the commutants
For k = 2, the commutants we choose writes \{A_{\mathbf{r}} := {2}^{-1}{(\sigma_{\mathbf{r}}\sigma_{\mathbf{r}}\mathbb{I}_n\mathbb{I}_n + \mathbb{I}_n\mathbb{I}_n\sigma_{\mathbf{r}}\sigma_{\mathbf{r}})} \mathrm{S}_{13}\mathrm{S}_{24}\}_{\mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}}.
Step 2: Construct the eigenbasis
Since \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \otimes \sigma_{\mathbf{r}} \ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}}} = (-1)^{[\mathbf{r},\mathbf{a}]}\ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}}}, the shared eigenbasis of \mathcal{A} has the form: 
\begin{align*}
   \ket{\Psi^{s}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}}&=
   \begin{cases}
    {2^{-1/2}}\left[{\ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z}} \otimes \ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{b}_x\mathbf{b}_z} }+s \ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{b}_x \mathbf{b}_z}} \otimes \ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}_x\mathbf{a}_z}}}\right] & \text{if~} \mathbf{a} < \mathbf{b}, \\
    \ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z}}\ket{\Phi_{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z}}& \text{if~} \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b}.
\end{cases}
\end{align*}
 with eigenvalues \lambda_{(s,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})} :=s \cdot 2^{-1}[(-1)^{[\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{a}]} + (-1)^{[\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{b}]}] and s = \pm 1.
Step 3: Measurement protocol
After implementing the measurement \left\{\ket{\Psi^{s}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}} \bra{\Psi^{s}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}}\right\}_{s \in \{+,-\}, \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{2n}} for T times and recording the results \{(s_t,\mathbf{a}_t, \mathbf{b}_t)\}_{t = 1}^{T}, the average of A_{\mathbf{r}} = \sum \lambda_{(\pm,\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})} \ket{\Psi^{\pm}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}} \bra{\Psi^{\pm}_{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}} can then be estimated by calculating the estimator T^{-1}\sum_{t = 1}^{T} \lambda_{(s_t, \mathbf{a}_t,\mathbf{b}_t)}. To realize such a measurement, we refer to construction in  [liu2024auxiliary?] and noted that 
\begin{align*}
    \ket{\Psi^{s}_{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}}}&= \mathrm{CNOT}_{34}\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{H}_1 \cdot
\begin{cases}
    2^{-1/2} \left[{\ket{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z\mathbf{b}_x\mathbf{b}_z} +s \ket{\mathbf{b}_x \mathbf{b}_z\mathbf{a}_x\mathbf{a}_z}}\right] &\text{if~} \mathbf{a} < \mathbf{b}\\
    \ket{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z\mathbf{b}_x\mathbf{b}_z}&\text{if~} \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b}
\end{cases},\\
&= \mathrm{CNOT}_{34}\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{H}_1 \mathrm{CNOT}_{13}\mathrm{CNOT}_{24}\cdot
\begin{cases}
    2^{-1/2} \left[{\ket{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z} +s \ket{\mathbf{b}_x \mathbf{b}_z}} \right]\ket{\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}} &\text{if~} \mathbf{a} < \mathbf{b}\\
    \ket{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z} \ket{\mathbf{0} \mathbf{0}}&\text{if~} \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b}
\end{cases},\\
&= \mathrm{CNOT}_{34}\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{H}_1 \mathrm{CNOT}_{13}\mathrm{CNOT}_{24}\cdot
\begin{cases}
    2^{-1/2} \left[{\ket{\mathbf{a}^{I}} +s \ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{I}}}\right] \ket{\mathbf{a}^{E}}\ket{\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}} &\text{if~} \mathbf{a} < \mathbf{b}\\
    \ket{\mathbf{a}_x \mathbf{a}_z} \ket{\mathbf{0} \mathbf{0}}&\text{if~} \mathbf{a} = \mathbf{b}
\end{cases}.
\end{align*}

This disentangles the qubits on the third and fourth copies. Thus, we can locally implement the gate sequence \mathrm{CNOT}_{13}\mathrm{CNOT}_{24}\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{H}_1\mathrm{CNOT}_{12}\mathrm{CNOT}_{34} and then measure the 3rd and 4th copies in the computational basis \ket{\mathbf{s}_{3}\mathbf{s}_4}.
Step 5: Extract measurement outcomes
The computational basis measurement gives the difference of vectors \mathbf{a} and \mathbf{b} through: 
\mathbf{s}_{3} = \mathbf{a}_x + \mathbf{b}_x,\quad \mathbf{s}_{4} = \mathbf{a}_z + \mathbf{b}_z

This information indicates a partition of the 1st and 2nd copies of qubits \{1,\cdots,2n\} = E \cup I, where: - E := \{i \in [2n]| a_i = b_i\} (equal indices) - I:= \{i \in [2n]| \bar{a}_i = b_i\} := \{i_1<i_2<\cdots<i_{|I|}\} (inverted indices)
We then implement: 1. Computational basis measurement \ket{\mathbf{s}^{E}} on qubits in set E 2. GHZ state measurement s^{I} on qubits in set I, formalized by the circuit:

\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left[{\ket{\mathbf{a}^{I}} + s\ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{I}}} \right] &=
    \begin{cases}
        \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(\bigotimes_{i \in I} X_i + Z_{i_1}\right) \ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{I}}  &\text{if~} s = -1,\\
        \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \left(\bigotimes_{i \in I} X_i + Z_{i_1}\right) \ket{{\mathbf{a}}^{I}}  &\text{if~} s = +1,
    \end{cases}\\
    &=\left(\prod_{i = i_1}^{i_{|I|-1}}\mathrm{CNOT}_{i,i+1}\right)^{\dagger} H_{i_1} \left(\prod_{i = i_1}^{i_{|I|-1}}\mathrm{CNOT}_{i,i+1}\right) \begin{cases}\ket{\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{I}} &\text{if~}s = -1,\\\ket{{\mathbf{a}}^{I}} &\text{if~}s = 1.\end{cases}
\end{align*}
 Here we use the fact that since \mathbf{a}< \mathbf{b}, we have a_{i_1} = 0. This then gives the \mathbf{a} vector through \mathbf{a}^{E} = {\mathbf{s}^{E}} and s = +1, \mathbf{a}^{I} = {s}^{I} if a_{i_1} = 0, s = -1, \mathbf{a}^{I} = \bar{s}^{I} if a_{i_1} = 1.






The construction above is useful in generalization to general non-linear shadow  [liu2024auxiliary?]. To get a classical shadow of \hat{\rho^t}, analogically, we sample h(\mathbf b,V):=\mathcal{M}^{-1}(V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V) with pseudo-probability \text{Pr}(V)\cdot\text{Pr}(\mathbf b|V): = \text{Pr}(V)\cdot\bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b}. This gives the result \mathbb{E}_{V \sim \mathcal{U}}\sum_{\mathbf b}\mathcal{M}^{-1}(V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V) \bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} = \rho^{t}. But \text{Pr}(\mathbf b|V): = \bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} is not a valid probability distribution. Fortunately, it can be effectively realized based on the estimator of \bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} in Lemma [lemma:gen_swap_est]. Note that the computational projective operator \{\ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}\}_{\mathbf b \in \{0,1\}^{n}} is mutually commutant and the operator set \{Q_{\mathbf b}\}_{\mathbf b}, where Q_{\mathbf{b}}:=\text{sym}(\ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}) = t^{-1} \sum_{i =1}^{t} \ket{\mathbf{b}}\!\bra{\mathbf{b}}_i fully distinguished the spectrum of \text{SWAP}_t^{\otimes n}. We use the common eigenvectors \ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}} of the operator set \{\text{SWAP}_{t}^{\otimes n}\}\cup \{Q_{\mathbf b}\}_{\mathbf b \in \{0,1\}^n} and calculates 
\begin{align*}
\bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} =f(\mathbf{x})\text{Pr}(\mathbf b | \mathbf x)\text{Pr}(\mathbf x | \mathbf V) , \text{~where~}\left\{\begin{aligned} &f(\mathbf{x}):= \bra{\psi_{\mathbf x}}\text{SWAP}_{t}^{\otimes n}\ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}}, \\ &\text{Pr}(\mathbf b | \mathbf x):=\bra{\psi_{\mathbf x}}Q_{\mathbf b}\ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}},\\ &\text{Pr}(\mathbf x | \mathbf V):=\bra{\psi_{\mathbf x}}(V\rho V^\dagger)^{\otimes t}\ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}}.\end{aligned}\right.
\end{align*}
 Here \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n\cdot t} labeled different eigenvectors. Then sampling h(\mathbf b,V) with pseudo-probability \bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} then is equivalent to sample f(\mathbf{x})h(\mathbf b,V) with probability \text{Pr}(\mathbf b | \mathbf x)\text{Pr}(\mathbf x | \mathbf V)\text{Pr}(V). If we can build an efficient quantum circuit \mathcal{R}\ket{\mathbf x} = \ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}}, this sampling can be realized. Based on this, we first give the form of common eigenvectors \ket{\psi_{\mathbf x}} and then discuss the efficient implementation of \mathcal{R}. Because (\text{SWAP}_{t})^{t} = \mathbb{I}, \text{SWAP}_t must have eigenvalue e^{i2\pi/t}. This conclusion generalized to Lemma [lemma:eigvec_QSWAP] below.






ImportantLemma(Common eigenvectors of SWAP and QSWAP)



 Given \mathbf{z} = (\mathbf{z}_1,\cdots,\mathbf{z}_t) \in (\{0,1\}^{n})^t with set [\mathbf{z}]:= \{\mathbf z,\tau(\mathbf z),\cdots,\tau^{|[\mathbf z]|-1}(\mathbf z)\}, where the t-cyclic permutation \tau satisfied \tau\circ(\mathbf{z}_1,\cdots,\mathbf{z}_t) = (\mathbf{z}_{\tau(1)},\cdots,\mathbf{z}_{\tau(t)})=(\mathbf{z}_t,\mathbf{z}_1\cdots,\mathbf{z}_{t-1}), the operators \{\text{SWAP}_{t}^{\otimes n}\}\cup \{Q_{\mathbf b}\}_{\mathbf b \in \{0,1\}^n} have common eigenvectors labeled by [\mathbf{z}],k =0,\cdots, |[\mathbf{z}]|-1 as \ket{\Psi_{[\mathbf z]}^{k}} = \sqrt{|[\mathbf{z}]|^{-1}} \sum_{r = 0}^{|[\mathbf{z}]| - 1}e^{\frac{(2\pi i)rk}{|[\mathbf{z}]|}} \ket{\tau^{r}(\mathbf z)}, with eigenvalue \{e^{-2k\pi i/|[\mathbf{z}]|}\} \cup \{t^{-1}\cdot \# (\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{z}_i)\}.








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. This can be proved by direct calculation. \begin{align*}
        &\text{SWAP}_{t}^{\otimes n} \ket{\Psi_{[\mathbf z]}^{k}} = \sqrt{|[\mathbf{z}]|^{-1}} \sum_{r = 0}^{|[\mathbf{z}]| - 1}e^{\frac{(2\pi i)rk}{|[\mathbf{z}]|}} \ket{\tau^{r+1}(\mathbf z)} = e^{-2k\pi i/|[\mathbf{z}]|}\ket{\Psi_{[\mathbf z]}^{k}}.\\
        &Q_{\mathbf b}\ket{\Psi_{[\mathbf z]}^{k}} = \sqrt{|[\mathbf{z}]|^{-1}} \sum_{r = 0}^{|[\mathbf{z}]| - 1}e^{\frac{(2\pi i)rk}{|[\mathbf{z}]|}} Q_{\mathbf b}\ket{\tau^{r}(\mathbf z)} = t^{-1}\cdot \# (\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{z}_i) \ket{\Psi_{[\mathbf z]}^{k}}.
\end{align*} ◻



Take t = 2, the eigenvectors writes \{\ket{\mathbf{s}\mathbf{s}}\}_{\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{F}_2^{n}} \cup \{\sqrt{2^{-1}}(\ket{\mathbf{s}_1{\mathbf{s}_2}}+\ket{{\mathbf{s}_2}\mathbf{s}_1}), \sqrt{2^{-1}}(\ket{\mathbf{s}_1{\mathbf{s}_2}}-\ket{{\mathbf{s}_2}\mathbf{s}_1})\}_{\mathbf{s}_1\neq \mathbf{s}_2 \in \mathbb{F}_2^n}, which counts 2^n + 2^n(2^n - 1) numbers of linearly independent basis, thus being complete. This leads us to find circuit that transform the 2n-qubits computational basis into these bases. Specifically, \begin{align*}
    \mathcal{R} \ket{\mathbf{s}_1 \mathbf{s}_2} =
    \left\{
        \begin{aligned}
        &\ket{\mathbf{s}_1 \mathbf{s}_2} &&\text{~if~} \mathbf{s}_1 = \mathbf{s}_2 \\
        &\sqrt{2^{-1}}(\ket{\mathbf{s}_1{\mathbf{s}_2}}+\ket{{\mathbf{s}_2}\mathbf{s}_1}) &&\text{~if~} \mathbf{s}_1 < \mathbf{s}_2 \\
        &\sqrt{2^{-1}}(-\ket{\mathbf{s}_1{\mathbf{s}_2}}+\ket{{\mathbf{s}_2}\mathbf{s}_1}) &&\text{~if~} \mathbf{s}_1 > \mathbf{s}_2.  
        \end{aligned}
        \right.
\end{align*} This pinned down the measurement cirucit by two steps: (i).Check whether \mathbf{s}_1 = \mathbf{s}_2 by transversal CNOT gates, (ii).On the different parts, with length l < n and most significant position p_{m}, implements \bar{H}:= \sqrt{2^{-1}} (X^{\otimes l} +Z_{p_m}) on those qubits. The step(ii) involved non-local operation within one of the copies. This is why we named it non-local multi-copy (NLMC) shadow.


As summarized in Lemma [lemma:var_nonlocal_nonlinear_shadow], the variance of NLMC shadow to estimate \text{tr}(O \rho^t) with unitary sampled from V \sim \mathcal{E} is upper bounded by the variance of single-copy shadow to estimate \text{tr}(O \rho) with the same unitary ensemble V. This means that if O is (i).low weight Pauli operators or (ii)low rank operators, NLMC shadow will have \text{poly}(n) sample complexity by taking \mathcal{E} = \text{Cliff}_{n}, \text{Cliff}(2)^{\otimes n} separately, which is exponentially faster compared to single copy shadow tomography in Eq.[eq:singlecp_shadow_nonlinear].






ImportantLemma(Variance of non-local Pauli shadow)



 Given (\mathbf x, \mathbf b, V) sampled from distribution \text{Pr}(\mathbf b | \mathbf x)\text{Pr}(\mathbf x | V)\text{Pr}(V), the random variable \hat{o}_t(\mathbf x, \mathbf b, V) := \text{tr}\left(\mathcal{M}^{-1}(V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V) O\right)\cdot f(\mathbf x) is an unbiased estimator for \text{tr}(O\rho^t). The variance of this estimator satisfied \begin{align*}
     \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf x, \mathbf b, V} \hat{o}_t^2 \leq \mathbb{E}_{V \sim \text{Pr}(V)} \sum_{\mathbb{b}} \bra{\mathbf{b}}V\rho V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b} \text{tr}^2\left(O \mathcal{M}^{-1}\left(V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V\right)\right).
\end{align*} Here the RHS related to the variance to estimate \text{tr}(O \rho) with unitary ensemble V \sim \text{Pr}(V).








NoteProof (Click to expand)





Proof. To show the unbiasedness, according to Eq.[eq:tpower_shadow], we noted that \begin{align*}
        \mathbb{E}_{V \sim \mathcal{E}} \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{b}) \sim \text{Pr}(\mathbf{b}|\mathbf{x})\text{Pr}(\mathbf{x}|V)}f(\mathbf x) \cdot V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V = \mathbb{E}_{V \sim \mathcal{E}}\bra{\mathbf b} V \rho^t V^\dagger\ket{\mathbf b} \cdot V^\dagger \ket{\mathbf b}\!\bra{\mathbf b}V = \mathcal{M}(\rho^t).
\end{align*} ◻
